arXiv:2607.10102v2 [math.PR] 21 Sep 2026
Dynamical mean-field limit and replica-symmetric free energy for the orthogonally-invariant SK model
Zhou Fan
,
Theodor Misiakiewicz
,
Leda Wang
and
Garrett G. Wen
Address: Yale University, Department of Statistics and Data Science
Email address: zhou.fan@yale.edu
Email address: theodor.misiakiewicz@yale.edu
Email address: leda.wang@yale.edu
Email address: gang.wen@yale.edu
Abstract.
We study a class of diffusion processes on \mathbb{R}^{n} interacting through a
symmetric matrix \mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} . When eigenvectors of
\mathbf{X} are random and uniformly distributed on the orthogonal group, we derive a
dynamical mean-field limit for the empirical law of sample paths,
extending a classical characterization due to Sompolinsky and Zippelius for
\mathbf{X}\sim\operatorname{GOE} . This limit takes the form of a generalized Langevin equation
with correlated Gaussian noise and memory, whose correlation and response
kernels relate to those of the original diffusion process through a system of
convolution equations depending on \mathbf{X} via the free cumulants of its eigenvalue
distribution.
Specializing to the overdamped Langevin diffusion \{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0}
for a Gibbs measure
\mu(\boldsymbol{\theta})\propto\exp\Big(\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}\Big)\prod_{i=1}^{n}\nu(\mathrm{d}\theta_{i}),
we analyze this mean-field limit under an assumption that the dynamics are rapidly
mixing. In this regime, the correlation/response kernels admit
time-translation-invariant approximants which satisfy a
fluctuation-dissipation relation. The generalized Langevin equation admits a
Markovian approximation with coupling to an auxiliary multivariate OU-process,
and converges in time to a replica-symmetric prediction for the
empirical law of coordinates under \mu . The correlation structure of
the auxiliary process may be understood through the infinitesimal generator of a
Markov semigroup for the lifted process of path histories
\boldsymbol{\xi}^{t}=\{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}\}_{s:s\leq t} .
Consequently, we show that the free energy of the Gibbs measure
converges to a replica-symmetric limit under an explicit
high-temperature condition, which for an Ising model is
\|\mathbf{X}\|_{\mathrm{op}}<1/2.
By recent dynamical universality results, this implies that the same characterization of the free energy holds in fully deterministic models without random disorder, as long as
\mathbf{X} satisfies a set of deterministic delocalization conditions.

1. Introduction
Let \mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} be a (deterministic or random) symmetric matrix.
Consider a diffusion process or gradient flow in \mathbb{R}^{n} interacting through \mathbf{X} ,
(1.1)
\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}=[f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t})+\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}]\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{b}^{t}
where f is a scalar function applied coordinate-wise. Under suitable mean-field
assumptions for \mathbf{X} to be specified, the first goal of our work is to obtain
an asymptotic characterization of the empirical distribution of coordinates of
(1.1) in the limit n\to\infty . Applying this
characterization to study Langevin dynamics for the Gibbs measure
(1.2)
\mu(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta})=\frac{1}{\mathcal{Z}}\exp\Big(\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}\Big)\prod_{i=1}^{n}\nu(\mathrm{d}\theta_{i}),
the second goal of our work is to obtain an asymptotic characterization of the
free energy and replica overlaps of (1.2)
in a regime where these dynamics are rapidly mixing.
For models where \mathbf{X} has
independent Gaussian entries up to transposition symmetry, such
questions are richly studied in the physics and mathematics literatures on spin
glasses and disordered systems. A dynamical mean-field limit for a prototypical
example of (1.1) was first derived by Sompolinsky and
Zippelius in [64],
and is given by the law of a scalar generalized
Langevin equation
(1.3)
\mathrm{d}\theta^{t}=\left[f(\theta^{t})+\int_{0}^{t}R_{\theta}(t,s)\theta^{s}\mathrm{d}s+g^{t}\right]\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\mathrm{d}b^{t},\qquad\{g^{t}\}\sim\operatorname{GP}(0,C_{\theta}),
with correlated Gaussian noise \{g^{t}\} and self-consistently defined
correlation and response kernels (C_{\theta},R_{\theta}) .
Convergence in empirical law of the sample paths of (1.1) to
(1.3), and an associated annealed large deviations
principle, was first proved mathematically by Ben Arous and Guionnet
in [3, 40]. The Ising case of the Gibbs measure (1.2)
with \nu(\mathrm{d}\theta) supported on \{\pm 1\} corresponds to the classical
Sherrington-Kirkpatrick (S-K) model [63], for which the form of the asymptotic
free energy was famously conjectured by Parisi in [60]
and proved by
Guerra and Talagrand [39, 67]; we refer to
[68, 69, 58] for textbook treatments
of this model and its rich history. Universality over classes of random
matrices \mathbf{X} having independent non-Gaussian entries (up to symmetry)
has been shown for the free energy of the S-K model in [12] and for
dynamics similar to (1.1) in
[18, 20].
Arguably, this universality class of disorder matrices with independent entries remains quite limited, raising a question of whether analogous results hold under more general mean-field structure. In this work, we aim to extend some of these developments to a class of disorder
matrices \mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} that are orthogonally-invariant in law —
i.e. whose matrix of eigenvectors is uniformly distributed on the orthogonal
group — and to an associated universality class that encompasses examples of
deterministic matrices \mathbf{X} . Our contributions are threefold:
1.
For the dynamics (1.1) with
orthogonally-invariant \mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} having a compactly supported
asymptotic spectral law \Lambda , we develop an extension of the
mean-field limit (1.3).
This extension has the same structural form as (1.3),
(1.4)
\mathrm{d}\theta^{t}=\left[f(\theta^{t})+\int_{0}^{t}R_{g}(t,s)\theta^{s}\mathrm{d}s+g^{t}\right]\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\mathrm{d}b^{t},\qquad\{g^{t}\}\sim\operatorname{GP}(0,C_{g}),
with correlation and response kernels (C_{g},R_{g}) now defined from the kernels (C_{\theta},R_{\theta}) which characterize the correlation and response of \{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} via convolution equations and the free cumulants of
\Lambda (cf. Definition 2.3). We establish almost-sure
convergence of the empirical law of sample paths of (1.1) to this limit, when f has bounded derivatives up to 3^{\text{rd}} order.
2.
We carry out an analysis of this mean-field limit (1.4)
for the overdamped Langevin dynamics of the Gibbs measure
(1.2) when \nu(\mathrm{d}\theta)=e^{-U(\theta)}\mathrm{d}\theta
has a smooth potential,
under an assumption that these dynamics converge at an
exponential dimension-free rate from both an equilibrium and an independent
random initialization (cf. Assumption 2.5).
In this dynamical regime, we prove that the preceding kernels (C_{g},R_{g}) have
time-translation-invariant limits (c_{g},r_{g}) as t\to\infty ,
which satisfy a fluctuation-dissipation relation
(1.5)
r_{g}(t)={-}c_{g}^{\prime}(t).
In contrast to the mean-field limit of Sompolinsky-Zippelius in
(1.3), the correlation kernel c_{g}(\cdot) may not have a
mixture-of-exponentials form. We instead establish a sequence of approximations
c_{g}(t)\approx u_{m}^{\top}e^{-tA_{m}}u_{m} with non-diagonal, asymmetric matrices
A_{m}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m} , leading to a sequence of Markovian
approximations of (1.4),
(1.6)
\displaystyle\mathrm{d}\theta^{t}
\displaystyle=[f(\theta^{t})+u_{m}^{\top}x^{t}+z]\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{d}b^{t}
\displaystyle\mathrm{d}x^{t}
\displaystyle={-}A_{m}[x^{t}-u_{m}\theta^{t}]\mathrm{d}t+\Sigma_{m}\,\mathrm{d}b_{x}^{t}.
Via these approximations, we show that
\{\theta^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} in (1.4) converges to an equilibrium
law that coincides with a replica-symmetric prediction for the empirical distribution of coordinates under the Gibbs measure
(1.2).
3.
A sufficient condition ensuring Assumption 2.5
is a log-Sobolev inequality for the Gibbs measure, which
may be verified under an explicit high-temperature condition
[6]. From this, we prove replica-symmetric
limits for the overlaps and free energy of (1.2).
Concretely, for the Ising model with \nu(\mathrm{d}\theta)\propto e^{h}\delta_{\theta=1}+e^{-h}\delta_{\theta=-1} where h\in\mathbb{R} is an external field,
we establish this result under the high-temperature assumption
(1.7)
\|\mathbf{X}\|_{\mathrm{op}}<1/2.
(In the setting of the classical S-K model where \mathbf{X}=\beta\mathbf{J} and \mathbf{J}\sim\operatorname{GOE}(n) , this corresponds to the assumption \beta<1/4 , which is a subset of the full replica-symmetric regime [49].)
Leveraging the dynamical universality results of
[26, 71], we deduce
that the same conclusion holds when h=0 for a general class of
purely deterministic matrices \mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} satisfying delocalization
conditions (cf. Assumption 2.9), and for arbitrary h\in\mathbb{R} when \mathbf{X} is a “semi-random” matrix conjugated by a diagonal matrix of
random \{\pm 1\} signs.
These results are presented in Section 2.
1.1. Existing literature
Dynamics.
The form of the mean-field limit (1.4) for the
diffusion equation (1.1) with orthogonally-invariant \mathbf{X}
may be anticipated from the analysis of Opper,
Çakmak, and Winther [55], who computed the dynamical mean-field
equations for an analogous class of discrete-time dynamics.
The mean-field limit (1.4) and convolutional structure of its
correlation and response kernels may be understood as a passage of this
result to continuous time.
A particular class of discrete-time dynamics — analogous
to Approximate Message Passing (AMP) algorithms [43, 24] and TAP iterations
[9] in models with Gaussian disorder \mathbf{X} — was highlighted in
[55] as having purely Gaussian limiting dynamics. For this AMP class,
convergence to the mean-field limit was proved mathematically in
[35],
extending an approach of iterative conditioning of Haar-orthogonal matrices
previously developed in [50, 66, 61] to analyze a simpler family of divergence-free
“vector-AMP” algorithms. Alternative proofs and extensions of
the result of [35] have since been obtained in [48, 38], and universality
over semi-random and deterministic disorder matrices \mathbf{X} has been shown
in increasingly general contexts in
[26, 71, 38].
It was shown by Celentano, Cheng, and Montanari [13], in an analogous
statistical model with i.i.d. Gaussian disorder, that the
mean-field limit of general discrete-time iterative algorithms may be
deduced from that of AMP, and also that the mean-field limit of
continuous-time gradient flow dynamics may be proved using an approach different
from [3, 40]. This approach relies on a reduction to AMP dynamics via
time-discretization, and a passage to the continuous-time limit through
verifying contractivity of the dynamical
fixed-point equations in a suitably defined Banach metric.
The approach has been extended to derive mean-field limits for
broad families of discrete-time iterative algorithms in
[37, 41, 14, 16]
and for continuous-time Langevin diffusions and stochastic gradient dynamics
in [30, 33, 54]. We apply a similar proof strategy in our work, to pass the
characterization of AMP in [35] to continuous time.
Mathematical analysis of aging in the dynamical mean-field limit of a
spherical 2-spin model was carried out in [2],
of convergence in time of the Cugliandolo-Kurchan/Crisanti-Horner-Sommers
equations of the spherical p-spin model to an FDT equilibrium in [19],
and of convergence in time of these equations under disorder-dependent initial
conditions in [21, 22]. For non-spherical models, aging dynamics and their connection to the static replica-symmetry-breaking structure of the Gibbs mesaures was analyzed using (non-rigorous) statistical physics techniques in [1]. A mathematical analysis for a non-spherical model with Gaussian disorder
was carried out in [31]
in a dynamical rapid-mixing regime similar to our work; we build upon several ideas
of [31], discussed in Section 1.2.
Free energy. The Ising case of the model (1.2)
was introduced by Marinari, Parisi, and Ritort [52] as a model which may
exhibit similar mean-field phenomena as models with deterministic disorder.
Replica-symmetric and 1-RSB predictions for the asymptotic
free energy of this model were computed in
[52, 15].
TAP equations for the magnetization were derived in [59] using a
high-temperature expansion and in [56] using an alternative
cavity method. [51] extended the former analysis to a broad class of
statistical models with orthogonally-invariant random disorder, and discussed its
connection to dynamical algorithms.
Mathematical proofs of such predictions remain scarce in the
literature, even in high temperature. For a
high-temperature regime of the Ising model without external field, where
quenched and annealed free energies coincide, a replica-symmetric limit for the free
energy was proved in [8] using the second-moment method. This was extended to an Ising
model with external field h\in\mathbb{R} in [34] via a conditional
second-moment method analogous to that of [10] for the S-K model and
[23] for the Ising perceptron, conditioning on the filtration of a
TAP iteration for computing the magnetization. This result of
[34]
showed, for \mathbf{X}=\beta\mathbf{J} where the asymptotic spectral law of \mathbf{J} converges to
\bar{\Lambda} , that the free energy converges to its replica-symmetric prediction
under a high-temperature condition of the form
\beta\in(0,\beta_{0}) for some
\beta_{0}\equiv\beta_{0}(\operatorname{Law}(\bar{\Lambda})).
As the analysis of the second-moment variational problem in [34] was
perturbative around \beta=0 , it is difficult to glean a more explicit bound for
\beta_{0} , and we believe that this bound would be substantially smaller than
our explicit guarantee in (1.7). In a related statistical generalized linear model with orthogonally-invariant design, replica-symmetric predictions for the free energy were derived in [44, 65]. This was proved mathematically for a linear model with design factorizable through Gaussian randomness in [5], via a Gaussian interpolation approach.
The replica-symmetric ground state energy for convex potentials was also proved in
[36]
via analysis of a vector AMP algorithm for convex optimization.
One perspective on the challenge of using a dynamical approach to prove
properties of the Gibbs measure is in certifying the optimality of the dynamics.
For example, in the
context of (1.2) and related statistical models,
AMP algorithms/TAP iterations that conjecturally converge to the magnetization
are known [55, 61, 11], but this convergence has thus far only been
certified in high-temperature regimes analogous to that of
[34], relying on a-priori understanding of the asymptotic free
energy and structure of the Gibbs measure [32, 47].
Likewise, while mean-field characterizations
of the ground state energy in convex landscapes may be established
by certifying optimality of optimization algorithms through a
first-order condition [7, 25, 36], certifying global optimality of
such algorithms in non-convex landscapes remains challenging. In this work, we
take an approach of analyzing the standard overdamped Langevin dynamics, which
has a more complex dynamical mean-field limit than AMP-type algorithms, but
whose convergence to the Gibbs measure may be certified through
entropy-decay arguments external to the mean-field theory.
As a benefit of our dynamical approach to analyzing the free energy, our results inherit the aforementioned universality over semi-random and deterministic matrices \mathbf{X} [26, 71, 38], which has been shown for algorithm dynamics but not yet for static properties of the Gibbs measure. Our results confirm that disordered-systems characterizations of the Gibbs measure can hold for systems without random disorder, as originally anticipated by [52].
1.2. Proof ideas
We describe briefly the main ideas of our analyses.
As discussed in the preceding section, (1.4) is obtained by
passing a characterization of a discrete-time AMP algorithm in
[55, 35] to
continuous time. An important distinction between these discrete-time
and continuous-time characterizations is that the correlation/response kernels
of the former are defined iteratively/inductively over time. The first contribution of our work is to formalize a sense in which the continuous-time kernels
C_{\theta},R_{\theta},C_{g},R_{g} may instead be understood as the fixed points of a
contractive map.
An obstacle to this formalization is that the convolutional
equations mapping
(1.8)
(C_{\theta},R_{\theta})\mapsto(C_{g},R_{g})
do not, in general, ensure that C_{g} remains a positive-semidefinite (p.s.d.)
kernel, which is needed to define the process (1.4); thus, it
is a bit unclear on what domain such a contractive map should be defined.
A related issue is that even when C_{g} is p.s.d., it seems challenging to
analyze contractivity of (1.8) under a Wasserstein-coupling
metric for C_{\theta},C_{g} as used in the arguments of
[13, 30, 33]. We resolve these issues by
formalizing the fixed-point interpretation of the dynamical mean-field limit
via a sequence of mappings
(C_{\theta},R_{\theta})\mapsto(C_{g},R_{g})\mapsto\mathcal{P}(C_{g},R_{g})\mapsto(C_{\theta},R_{\theta}),
where \mathcal{P} projects C_{g} under an alternative weighted L^{2} metric onto a subset of the p.s.d. cone. We then
develop different arguments to
establish contractivity in this metric, and leverage results of [35] to show that at the fixed point of these mappings, C_{g} is in fact p.s.d., and thus is also a fixed point without projection by \mathcal{P} .
Turning to the analysis of the overdamped
Langevin equation, from the
assumed convergence condition in Assumption 2.5 and an
identification of (C_{\theta},R_{\theta}) as the limits of
coordinate-wise correlation and response functions of
\{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} , one may deduce the existence of
time-translation-invariant limits c_{\theta},r_{\theta} for these kernels at
large times, together with their fluctuation-dissipation relation
(1.9)
r_{\theta}(t)={-}c_{\theta}^{\prime}(t)
(Lemma 4.1).
These arguments are similar to [31] which analyzed a statistical model with Gaussian disorder.
Interestingly, we are able to verify that (1.9)
implies also the fluctuation-dissipation relation
r_{g}(t)={-}c_{g}^{\prime}(t) corresponding to the kernels
C_{g},R_{g} appearing in the generalized Langevin
equation (1.4). This verification is a short
calculation in the Fourier domain (Lemma 4.2).
We show that c_{g}(\cdot) may be interpreted as
the large- n limit of the correlation function of coordinates of
\mathbf{g}^{t}=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}-\int_{-\infty}^{t}r_{g}(t-s)\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}\mathrm{d}s
at equilibrium, which are observables of the full path history
\boldsymbol{\xi}^{t}:=\{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}\}_{s:s\leq t} .
As this “lifted” process \{\boldsymbol{\xi}^{t}\}_{t\in\mathbb{R}} remains Markovian over this
space of path histories, writing \nu for its stationary measure
and \{P_{t}\}_{t\geq 0} for its
L^{2}(\nu) -semigroup, this implies a representation
c_{g}(t)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\,\mathbb{E}_{\nu}[f^{\top}P_{t}f]
where f is the function for which \mathbf{g}^{t}=f(\boldsymbol{\xi}^{t}) .
An important distinction with the setting of Gaussian disorder is that here
\{P_{t}\}_{t\geq 0} is irreversible, and its infinitesimal generator is not
self-adjoint on L^{2}(\nu) . Thus, we do not obtain from this representation a
mixture-of-exponentials form for c_{g}(\cdot) , and in general, we do not expect
such a form to hold true. Instead, we establish an approximation
c_{g}(t)\approx u_{m}^{\top}e^{-tA_{m}}u_{m}
where {-}A_{m}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m} is a (non-diagonal, asymmetric)
matrix that constitutes a finite-dimensional
approximation for the generator of \{P_{t}\}_{t\geq 0} .
Together with the fluctuation-dissipation
relation (1.5), this leads to the previously stated Markov
approximation (1.6) for (1.4).
Finally, we show convergence of (1.4) to an equilibrium law
characterized by replica-symmetric fixed point equations, by analyzing
convergence of the Markovian system (1.6) together with
its approximation error for (1.4). The primary technical
challenge is that the generator {-}A for the above semigroup
\{P_{t}\}_{t\geq 0} has non-trivial (in fact, dense)
null space in L^{2}(\nu) , and thus the spectral gap of its approximant {-}A_{m} must vanish with the
approximation error. Thus, it seems challenging to prove convergence to
equilibrium of the Markovian
system (1.6) over a fixed time horizon that is
independent of this error and the dimension m ; on the other hand,
the accumulated approximation error over a m -dependent time horizon may not be
small under a naive coupling and Grönwall argument.
We circumvent this issue by using a careful
construction of {-}A_{m} that instead approximates a slightly damped version of
{-}A , and that allows for a stable coupling of
(1.4) and (1.6) over an arbitrarily long
time horizon on which (1.6) is guaranteed to converge
(Corollary 5.2, Lemma 5.3).
This implies the replica-symmetric characterization of the Gibbs measure
(1.2) under Assumption 2.5, for
laws \nu having a smooth potential. The concrete implication for the Ising
model is then deduced by verifying Assumption 2.5 using the
log-Sobolev inequality of [6] for a
sequence of double-well potentials that converge to the Ising law.
2. Main results
2.1. Dynamical mean-field limit
Let \{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} be a diffusion process on \mathbb{R}^{n} taking the form
(2.1)
\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}=[f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t})+\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}]\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{b}^{t}
where \mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} is a symmetric matrix, f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} is a
Lipschitz-continuous function applied coordinate-wise, and \{\mathbf{b}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0}
is a standard Brownian motion on \mathbb{R}^{n} . The case \gamma=0 corresponds to gradient flow.
Our first main result establishes a deterministic limit, as n\to\infty ,
of the empirical distribution of coordinate sample paths
\{(\theta_{i}^{t})_{t\in[0,T]}\}_{i=1}^{n}
for any fixed time horizon T>0 independent of n . For expositional clarity, let us first state
this result for the following class of random disorder matrices \mathbf{X} that
are orthogonally invariant in law; we discuss universality over the disorder in
Section 2.3.
Assumption 2.1.
\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{O}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{O}^{\top} , where \mathbf{O}\sim\operatorname{Haar}(\mathbb{O}(n)) is a Haar-uniform
random matrix on the orthogonal group, and
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{n}) is a (deterministic or random)
diagonal matrix independent of \mathbf{O} . There exists a constant \Lambda_{\max}>0
such that almost surely for all large n ,
\|\mathbf{X}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\Lambda_{\max}.
Furthermore, there exists a random variable \Lambda (supported on
[-\Lambda_{\max},\Lambda_{\max}] ) with \mathbb{E}[\Lambda]=0 and \operatorname{Var}[\Lambda]>0
such that almost surely as n\to\infty ,
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\delta_{\lambda_{i}}\to\operatorname{Law}(\Lambda)\text{ weakly.}
Throughout, we denote by
\{\kappa_{p}\}_{p\geq 2} the free cumulants of this random variable \Lambda .
We impose, in addition, the following assumptions on the
dynamics (2.1).
Assumption 2.2.
(a)
f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} is fixed for all n , and three-times continuously-differentiable
with uniformly bounded first, second, and third derivatives.
(b)
\gamma\geq 0 is a fixed scalar parameter, and
the Brownian motion \{\mathbf{b}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} is independent of \mathbf{X} .
(c)
The initial state
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0}=(\theta_{1}^{0},\ldots,\theta_{n}^{0}) is independent of \mathbf{X} and
\{\mathbf{b}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} . There exists a random variable \theta^{0} with
\operatorname{Var}[\theta^{0}]>0 and finite moments of all orders,
such that for each fixed p\geq 1 , almost surely as n\to\infty ,
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\delta_{\theta_{i}^{0}}\to\operatorname{Law}(\theta^{0})\text{ weakly
and in Wasserstein-$p$.}
Under these assumptions, we will show that the limit as n\to\infty of
the dynamics (2.1) admits the following mean-field
characterization:
Definition 2.3.
Let \theta^{0} , \{b^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} , and \{g^{t}\}_{t\geq 0}
be mutually independent scalar variables/processes on a filtered
probability space (\Omega,\mathcal{F},\{\mathcal{F}_{t}\}_{t\geq 0},\mathbb{P}) , where
\operatorname{Law}(\theta^{0}) is given by Assumption 2.2(c),
\{b^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} is a standard \mathcal{F}_{t} -adapted Brownian motion, and
\{g^{t}\}_{t\geq 0}\sim\operatorname{GP}(0,C_{g})
is a continuous, mean-zero, \mathcal{F}_{t} -adapted Gaussian process with a symmetric
positive-semidefinite covariance kernel C_{g}:[0,\infty)\times[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R} . Let \{\theta^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} be the solution of the SDE
(2.2)
\mathrm{d}\theta^{t}=\left[f(\theta^{t})+\int_{0}^{t}R_{g}(t,s)\theta^{s}ds+g^{t}\right]\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\mathrm{d}b^{t},\qquad\theta^{t}|_{t=0}=\theta^{0},
where R_{g}:[0,\infty)\times[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}
is a response kernel satisfying R_{g}(t,s)=0 for s>t . Let
\{\frac{\mathrm{d}\theta^{t}}{\mathrm{d}g^{s}}\}_{t\geq s\geq 0} be the solution of the
response equation
(2.3)
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\frac{\mathrm{d}\theta^{t}}{\mathrm{d}g^{s}}=\left[f^{\prime}(\theta^{t})\frac{\mathrm{d}\theta^{t}}{\mathrm{d}g^{s}}+\int_{s}^{t}R_{g}(t,r)\frac{\mathrm{d}\theta^{r}}{\mathrm{d}g^{s}}\mathrm{d}r\right],\qquad\frac{\mathrm{d}\theta^{t}}{\mathrm{d}g^{s}}\bigg|_{t=s}=1.
These kernels C_{g},R_{g} , in conjunction with a pair of auxiliary kernels
C_{\theta},R_{\theta}:[0,\infty)\times[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R} ,
are self-consistently defined from the laws of the above processes by the
fixed point conditions
(2.4)
\displaystyle C_{\theta}(t,s)
\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\theta^{t}\theta^{s}]
(2.5)
\displaystyle R_{\theta}(t,s)
\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\mathrm{d}\theta^{t}}{\mathrm{d}g^{s}}\right]\text{ for }s\in[0,t],\quad R_{\theta}(t,s)=0\text{ for }s>t,
(2.6)
\displaystyle C_{g}(t,s)
\displaystyle=\sum_{p,q\geq 0}\kappa_{p+q+2}\,R_{\theta}^{\ast p}*C_{\theta}*\bar{R}_{\theta}^{\ast q}(t,s),\quad\text{ where }\bar{R}_{\theta}(t,s)=R_{\theta}(s,t)\text{ for all }s,t\geq 0,
(2.7)
\displaystyle R_{g}(t,s)
\displaystyle=\sum_{p\geq 1}\kappa_{p+1}\,R_{\theta}^{\ast p}(t,s).
Here, A*B denotes the standard convolution for kernels defined over
[0,\infty) ,
[A\ast B](t,s)=\int_{0}^{\infty}A(t,r)B(r,s)\mathrm{d}r,\quad A^{\ast p}=\underbrace{A\ast\ldots\ast A}_{p\text{
times}},\quad A^{\ast 0}*B=B*A^{\ast 0}=B.
Theorem 2.4.
Suppose Assumptions 2.1 and 2.2 hold. Then:
(a)
There exist domains \mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{+} for (C_{\theta},R_{\theta}) and
\mathcal{S}_{g}^{+} for (C_{g},R_{g}) for which the kernels and processes of
Definition 2.3 are well-defined and unique.
That is, (2.2–2.3) have unique
\mathcal{F}_{t} -adapted solutions for any (C_{g},R_{g})\in\mathcal{S}_{g}^{+} ,
the series (2.6–2.7) are absolutely convergent for
any (C_{\theta},R_{\theta})\in\mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{+} , and there exists a
unique fixed point (C_{\theta},R_{\theta},C_{g},R_{g})\in\mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{+}\times\mathcal{S}_{g}^{+} satisfying (2.4–2.7).
(b)
Fix any T>0 not depending on n . Define
\mathbf{g}^{t}=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}-\int_{0}^{t}R_{g}(t,s)\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}\mathrm{d}s.
Let \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\delta_{\{(\theta_{i}^{t},g_{i}^{t},b_{i}^{t})\}_{t\in[0,T]}} be the empirical measure of sample paths
(\theta_{i}^{t},g_{i}^{t},b_{i}^{t})_{t\in[0,T]} and let
\operatorname{Law}(\{(\theta^{t},g^{t},b^{t})\}_{t\in[0,T]}) be the joint law of these
processes in Definition 2.3, as probability measures on
C([0,T],\mathbb{R}^{3}) . Then almost surely
as n\to\infty ,
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\delta_{\{(\theta_{i}^{t},g_{i}^{t},b_{i}^{t})\}_{t\in[0,T]}}\to\operatorname{Law}(\{(\theta^{t},g^{t},b^{t})\}_{t\in[0,T]})\text{ weakly and in
Wasserstein-2.}
(c)
Write \langle\cdot\rangle for the expectation over \{\mathbf{b}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} , conditional on \mathbf{X} and \boldsymbol{\theta}^{0} . Then for any fixed s,t\geq 0
with s\leq t , almost surely as n\to\infty ,
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\langle\theta_{i}^{t}\theta_{i}^{s}\rangle\to C_{\theta}(t,s),\,\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\langle g_{i}^{t}g_{i}^{s}\rangle\to C_{g}(t,s),\,\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\langle\theta_{i}^{t}b_{i}^{s}\rangle\to\sqrt{2\gamma}\int_{0}^{s}R_{\theta}(t,\tau)\mathrm{d}\tau.
An explicit definition of the domains \mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{+},\mathcal{S}_{g}^{+} may be found in Appendix 3 of the Supplementary Appendices. We remark that the third claim of Theorem 2.4(c) will lead to an interpretation of R_{\theta} as an averaged coordinate-wise response function for the dynamics \{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} (cf. (4.26) and (4.28) in Section 4).
2.2. Langevin dynamics and replica-symmetric free energy
Now let U:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} be a scalar confining potential, and consider the Gibbs
measure having Lebesgue density on \mathbb{R}^{n} given by
(2.8)
\mu_{\mathrm{Gibbs}}(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\frac{1}{\mathcal{Z}}\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}U(\theta_{i})\right)
where \mathcal{Z} is the partition function
(2.9)
\mathcal{Z}=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}U(\theta_{i})\right)\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}.
We will assume
(2.10)
\liminf_{|x|\to\infty}U^{\prime\prime}(x)\geq\alpha
for a sufficiently large constant \alpha>0 so that \mathcal{Z}<\infty .
We write
\langle f(\boldsymbol{\theta})\rangle=\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}\sim\mu_{\mathrm{Gibbs}}}[f(\boldsymbol{\theta})\mid\mathbf{X}],\qquad\langle f(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime})\rangle=\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}\overset{iid}{\sim}\mu_{\mathrm{Gibbs}}}[f(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime})\mid\mathbf{X}]
for the average over independent replicas from this Gibbs measure.
We will analyze the preceding dynamical mean-field limit for the overdamped
Langevin diffusion
(2.11)
\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}=\big[\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}-U^{\prime}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t})\big]\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{b}^{t}
having \mu_{\mathrm{Gibbs}} as stationary law. We carry out this analysis under
a condition that these dynamics
(2.11) exhibit dimension-free convergence in the following sense,
both from the given initial state \boldsymbol{\theta}^{0} (independent of \mathbf{X} ) satisfying
Assumption 2.2 as well as from an equilibrium initialization.
Assumption 2.5.
Let \{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} be the solution of (2.11)
with the given initial state \boldsymbol{\theta}^{0} . Let \{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{t}\}_{t\in\mathbb{R}}
denote a stationary process also satisfying (2.11) with
equilibrium initial state
\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0}\sim\mu_{\mathrm{Gibbs}}.
Let
\operatorname{Law}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}) denote the law of \boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}
conditional on (\mathbf{X},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}) , and define similarly \operatorname{Law}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{t}\mid\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{s}) .
Then for some constants C,c>0 , almost surely (over (\mathbf{X},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0}) )
for all large n ,
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{n}W_{2}(\operatorname{Law}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}),\,\mu_{\mathrm{Gibbs}})^{2}\;\bigg|\;\mathbf{X},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0}\right]
\displaystyle\leq Ce^{-c(t-s)}\text{ for all }t\geq s\geq 0,
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{n}W_{2}(\operatorname{Law}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{\tau}\mid\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0}),\,\mu_{\mathrm{Gibbs}})^{2}\;\bigg|\;\mathbf{X}\right]
\displaystyle\leq Ce^{-c\tau}\text{ for all }\tau\geq 0.
Under this condition, assuming that the potential U(\cdot) is
suitably confining, our second main result is the following theorem establishing
deterministic limits for the free energy and
replica overlaps of the above Gibbs measure.
Theorem 2.6.
Suppose there exists a (deterministic or random) initial state \boldsymbol{\theta}^{0} for
which Assumptions 2.1 and 2.2 hold with f=-U^{\prime} .
Suppose that the bound \alpha>0 in
(2.10) satisfies
(2.12)
\alpha>\Lambda_{\max},\qquad\alpha>\sum_{p\geq 1}|\kappa_{p+1}|\left(\frac{1}{n}\langle\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_{2}^{2}\rangle-\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}\rangle+\varepsilon\right)^{p}
almost surely for all large n and some constant \varepsilon>0 .
Suppose that Assumption 2.5 holds for this initial state
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0} .
For any v\geq q\geq 0 such that the R-transform series
(2.13)
\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(x)=\sum_{p\geq 1}\kappa_{p+1}x^{p}
is absolutely convergent in a neighborhood of v-q and q\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(v-q)\geq 0 , define
the probability density on \mathbb{R}
(2.14)
\mu(\theta\mid v,q,\xi)\propto\exp\left(-U(\theta)+\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(v-q)\theta^{2}+\sqrt{q\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(v-q)}\,\xi\theta\right).
Then:
(a)
There exist deterministic almost-sure limits
(2.15)
v_{*}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\langle\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_{2}^{2}\rangle,\qquad q_{*}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}\rangle
satisfying the above conditions.
These solve the fixed-point equations
(2.16)
v_{*}=\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}\langle\theta^{2}\rangle_{v_{*},q_{*},\xi},\qquad q_{*}=\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}\langle\theta\rangle_{v_{*},q_{*},\xi}^{2}
where \langle\cdot\rangle_{v,q,\xi} denotes the expectation under
\mu(\cdot\mid v,q,\xi) . Furthermore, almost surely
(2.17)
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}\rangle=v_{*}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(v_{*}-q_{*})+q_{*}(v_{*}-q_{*})\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(v_{*}-q_{*}).
For any function f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} satisfying
|f(x)-f(y)|\leq C(1+|x|+|y|)|x-y| for some C>0 , almost surely
(2.18)
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\langle f(\theta_{i})\rangle=\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}\langle f(\theta)\rangle_{v_{*},q_{*},\xi}.
(b)
Suppose, in addition, that almost surely over (\mathbf{X},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0}) for all
large n , for every \beta\in[0,1] ,
the condition (2.12) and Assumption
2.5 hold for the Gibbs measure, dynamics, and free
cumulants associated to \beta\mathbf{X} , with some constants C,c,\varepsilon>0
that are uniform over \beta\in[0,1] .
Let \mathcal{Z} be
the partition function (2.9) (for \beta=1 ). Then almost surely
\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\log\mathcal{Z}
\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}\log\int\exp\Big({-}U(\theta)+\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(v_{*}-q_{*})\theta^{2}+\sqrt{q_{*}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(v_{*}-q_{*})}\,\xi\theta\Big)
(2.19)
\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{v_{*}-q_{*}}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(s)\mathrm{d}s-\frac{1}{2}(v_{*}-q_{*})\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(v_{*}-q_{*})-\frac{1}{2}q_{*}(v_{*}-q_{*})\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(v_{*}-q_{*}).
It may be checked that the free energy limit (2.19) coincides with the formula predicted by the replica method under an ansatz of replica symmetry, and that (2.16) are the fixed-point equations arising from this replica calculation. We note that the first condition of (2.12) ensures that the Gibbs measure (2.8) is well-defined, and the second condition of (2.12) ensures that U^{\prime\prime}(x)\geq\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(v_{*}-q_{*}) for all large |x| , hence the scalar law (2.14) is well-defined at (v_{*},q_{*}) .
All conditions of Theorem 2.6 may be checked in a
“high-temperature” regime of sufficiently small \Lambda_{\max} depending on
U(\cdot) , where Assumption 2.5 (in a stronger form,
uniformly over all deterministic initial states \boldsymbol{\theta}^{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} ) is
implied by a log-Sobolev inequality for \mu_{\mathrm{Gibbs}}
[6]. The following corollary gives a concrete
statement of such a result with explicit bounds for \Lambda_{\max} ,
restricting to a class of potentials U(x) where e^{-U(x)}
is a convolution of a Gaussian law with a compactly supported probability
measure.
Corollary 2.7.
Suppose U:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} is any potential taking the form
e^{-U(x)}=\int_{-M}^{M}\sqrt{\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{\alpha}{2}(x-y)^{2}}\mathrm{d}\nu(y)
for some \alpha,M>0 and probability measure \nu supported
on [-M,M] . Suppose \mathbf{X} satisfies Assumption 2.1 where,
for some \varepsilon>0 ,
(2.20)
\begin{gathered}\Lambda_{\max}<\alpha,\qquad 2\Lambda_{\max}\left(M^{2}+\frac{1}{\alpha+\Lambda_{\max}}\right)<1,\\
\sum_{p\geq 1}|\kappa_{p+1}|\left[\frac{1}{\alpha-\Lambda_{\max}}+\frac{\alpha^{2}M^{2}}{(\alpha-\Lambda_{\max})^{2}}+\varepsilon\right]^{p}<\alpha.\end{gathered}
Then all conclusions of Theorem 2.6 hold.
Specializing to \nu supported on \{\pm 1\} , applying a growth estimate
\limsup_{p\to\infty}|\kappa_{p}|^{1/p}\leq 2\Lambda_{\max} for the free
cumulants (Proposition A.1),
and taking the limit \alpha\to\infty ,
we obtain the following consequence for the classical Ising model
of [52] with an external field.
Corollary 2.8.
Fix a constant h\in\mathbb{R} , and consider the Gibbs measure
(2.21)
\mu_{\mathrm{Ising}}=\frac{1}{\mathcal{Z}}\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}+h\sum_{i=1}^{n}\theta_{i}\right)\text{ for }\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\{\pm 1\}^{n},
with partition function
\mathcal{Z}_{\mathrm{Ising}}=\sum_{\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\{\pm 1\}^{n}}\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}+h\sum_{i=1}^{n}\theta_{i}\right)
and associated Gibbs average \langle\cdot\rangle_{\mathrm{Ising}} .
Suppose \mathbf{X} satisfies Assumption 2.1 with
\Lambda_{\max}<1/2 . Then there exists a deterministic almost sure limit
q_{*}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}\rangle_{\mathrm{Ising}},
which satisfies the fixed point equation
q_{*}=\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}\tanh\left(h+\sqrt{q_{*}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(1-q_{*})}\,\xi\right)^{2}.
Furthermore,
\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\log\mathcal{Z}_{\mathrm{Ising}}=\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}\log 2\cosh\Big(h+\sqrt{q_{*}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(1-q_{*})}\,\xi\Big)
(2.22)
\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1-q_{*}}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(s)\mathrm{d}s+\frac{1}{2}q_{*}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(1-q_{*})-\frac{1}{2}q_{*}(1-q_{*})\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(1-q_{*}).
This limit (2.22) coincides with the replica formula computed in [56, 15], and proved previously under a less explicit high temperature assumption in [34].
2.3. Universality over the disorder
Orthogonal invariance of the disorder matrix \mathbf{X} in Assumption
2.1 underlies a mean-field characterization of a discrete-time
AMP algorithm in
[35], from which the dynamical mean-field limit in
Theorem 2.4 and results for the Gibbs measure in Theorem
2.6 and Corollaries 2.7 and 2.8
are derived.
It has been shown, in increasing generality in
[26, 71, 38], that
this characterization holds more broadly over universality classes of
(possibly deterministic) matrices \mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} .
This implies, as a consequence, that our preceding results carry over to such
universality classes.
We provide here a concrete statement of universality for one such class of
deterministic disorder matrices \mathbf{X} studied in
[26, 71].
Assumption 2.9.
Let \mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} be a deterministic symmetric matrix such that
\|\mathbf{X}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\Lambda_{\max}
for a constant \Lambda_{\max}>0 , and
there exists a random variable \Lambda with \mathbb{E}[\Lambda]=0 and \operatorname{Var}[\Lambda]>0
such that as n\to\infty , the empirical eigenvalue distribution of \mathbf{X}
satisfies
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\delta_{\lambda_{i}(\mathbf{X})}\to\operatorname{Law}(\Lambda)\text{ weakly}.
Furthermore, for each fixed integer k\geq 1 , any
constant \varepsilon>0 , and all large n\geq n_{0}(\varepsilon,k) ,
\max_{i=1}^{n}\left|(\mathbf{X}^{k})_{ii}-\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{Tr}\mathbf{X}^{k}\right|<n^{-1/2+\varepsilon},\qquad\max_{i\neq j}\left|(\mathbf{X}^{k})_{ij}\right|<n^{-1/2+\varepsilon}.
For example, one may take \mathbf{X}=\beta\mathbf{M} where \beta\in\mathbb{R} and \mathbf{M}
is a Hadamard matrix (with n a power of 2) or the sine transform
\mathbf{M}=\left(\sqrt{\frac{2}{n+1}}\sin\frac{\pi ij}{n+1}\right)_{i,j=1}^{n}.
In either case, \mathbf{M} is orthogonal, and Assumption 2.9
holds with \Lambda_{\max}=|\beta| and
\Lambda=\frac{1}{2}\delta_{\beta}+\frac{1}{2}\delta_{-\beta} .
Corollary 2.10.
Suppose \mathbf{X} satisfies Assumption 2.9.
(a)
If Assumption 2.2 holds,
f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} is odd, and \theta^{0} is
sign invariant in law (i.e. f(x)={-}f(-x) for all x\in\mathbb{R} , and
\operatorname{Law}(\theta^{0})=\operatorname{Law}({-}\theta^{0}) ),
then Theorem 2.4 holds for the dynamics
\{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} .
(b)
If U(\cdot) and \Lambda satisfy all conditions of
Corollary 2.7, and U:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} is even
(i.e. U(x)=U(-x) for all x\in\mathbb{R} ),
then all statements of Theorem 2.6 hold for \mu_{\mathrm{Gibbs}} .
(c)
If h=0 in the Ising model (2.21) and \Lambda_{\max}<1/2 ,
then all statements of Corollary 2.8 hold.
(d)
If f(\cdot) is not odd, \theta^{0} is not sign-invariant in law,
U(\cdot) is not even, or h\neq 0 , then the
same conclusions hold for the dynamics and Gibbs measures defined with
\mathbf{S}\mathbf{X}\mathbf{S} in place of \mathbf{X} , where \mathbf{S} is a
diagonal matrix of i.i.d. Rademacher \pm 1 signs
independent of \boldsymbol{\theta}^{0} and \{\mathbf{b}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} .
Remark 2.11.
Let \mathbf{X}=(\mathrm{Id}-\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top})\mathbf{H}(\mathrm{Id}-\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}) be a
“puncturing” of a deterministic matrix \mathbf{H} satisfying the conditions of
Assumption 2.9, and let
\tilde{\mathbf{X}}=(\mathrm{Id}-\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top})\tilde{\mathbf{H}}(\mathrm{Id}-\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top})
be a similar puncturing of an orthogonally-invariant random matrix \tilde{\mathbf{H}}
satisfying Assumption 2.1 with the same spectral limit \operatorname{Law}(\Lambda) .
One may also verify using [71, Proposition 2.7, Lemma
B.1] and the recent result of
[38, Theorem 5.3] that, even if
f(\cdot) is not odd / U(\cdot) is not even,
the mean-field limits for the dynamics
\{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} and Gibbs measure \mu_{\mathrm{Gibbs}} coincide for
\mathbf{X} and \tilde{\mathbf{X}} .
However, without further assumptions for f(\cdot) / U(\cdot)
such as the sign symmetry conditions in Corollary 2.10 above,
these limits would, in general, be different from
those stated in Theorems 2.4 and 2.6
for the unpunctured orthogonally-invariant matrix \tilde{\mathbf{H}} . It is possible to derive analogues of
our results for this puncturing of \tilde{\mathbf{H}} , but for brevity we will not do
so in the current work.
The remainder of this paper proves the preceding results. Section 3 proves Theorem 2.4 on the dynamical mean-field limit, Section 4 analyzes the kernels C_{\theta},R_{\theta},C_{g},R_{g} for the overdamped Langevin diffusion at equilibrium, Section 5 proves Theorem 2.6 and Corollaries 2.7 and 2.8 on the Gibbs measure, and Section 6 proves Corollary 2.10 on universality over the disorder.
3. Dynamical mean-field limit
In this section, we prove Theorem 2.4. We will omit arguments
that are similar to ones in [30] for brevity, and focus on
the differences in our setting of a non-Gaussian disorder matrix \mathbf{X} .
3.1. Kernel spaces and kernel mappings
Fixing two constants K_{0},K_{1}>0 , we define “envelope” functions
\Phi_{R_{\theta}},\Phi_{R_{g}},\Phi_{C_{\theta}},\Phi_{C_{g}} on [0,\infty) via
(3.1)
\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\Phi_{R_{\theta}}(t)
\displaystyle=K_{0}\left(\Phi_{R_{\theta}}(t)+\int_{0}^{t}\Phi_{R_{g}}(t-s)\Phi_{R_{\theta}}(s)\mathrm{d}s\right),\qquad\Phi_{R_{\theta}}(0)=K_{0},
(3.2)
\displaystyle\Phi_{R_{g}}(t)
\displaystyle=\sum_{p\geq 1}K_{1}^{p+1}\Phi_{R_{\theta}}^{\ast p}(t),
(3.3)
\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\Phi_{C_{\theta}}(t)
\displaystyle=K_{0}\left(\Phi_{C_{\theta}}(t)+\int_{0}^{t}\Phi_{R_{g}}(t-s)[\Phi_{C_{\theta}}(s)+\Phi_{C_{\theta}}(t)]\mathrm{d}s+\Phi_{C_{g}}(t)+1\right),\qquad\Phi_{C_{\theta}}(0)=K_{0},
(3.4)
\displaystyle\sqrt{\Phi_{C_{g}}(t)}
\displaystyle=\sum_{p\geq 0}K_{1}^{p+1}\Phi_{R_{\theta}}^{\ast p}\ast\sqrt{\Phi_{C_{\theta}}}(t),
where, for a,b:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R} , [a*b](t)=\int_{0}^{t}a(t-s)b(s)\mathrm{d}s .
It may be verified through a Laplace transform argument that
this system has a unique solution, satisfying
\Phi_{R_{\theta}},\allowbreak\Phi_{R_{g}},\allowbreak\Phi_{C_{\theta}},\allowbreak\Phi_{C_{g}}\in S(\lambda)
for all sufficiently large \lambda>0 where
S(\lambda)=\left\{\Phi:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R},\;\Phi(t),\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\Phi(t)\geq 0\text{ for all }t\geq 0,\;\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\lambda t}\Phi(t)\mathrm{d}t<\infty\right\}.
We omit details of this verification, and refer to
[30, Lemma 3.1] for an analogous argument.
We define from these envelope functions the following kernel spaces.
Definition 3.1.
Let T>0 , let D=\{d_{1},\ldots,d_{m}\}\subset[0,T] be a finite subset,
and call
[0,d_{1}),[d_{1},d_{2}),\ldots,[d_{m-1},d_{m}),[d_{m},T]
the maximal intervals of [0,T]\setminus D .
Fixing T -dependent
constants K_{0},K_{1},K_{2},K_{3}>0 where K_{0},K_{1} define the above envelopes,
let \mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{+}(T,D) be the space of all
pairs (C_{\theta},R_{\theta}) such that:
(1)
C_{\theta}:[0,T]\times[0,T]\to\mathbb{R} is a positive-semidefinite
covariance kernel satisfying
C_{\theta}(t,t)\leq\Phi_{C_{\theta}}(t)\text{ for all }0\leq t\leq T,
and for any maximal interval I of [0,T]\setminus D ,
(3.5)
|C_{\theta}(t,t)+C_{\theta}(s,s)-2C_{\theta}(t,s)|\leq K_{2}|t-s|\text{ for all }t,s\in I.
(2)
R_{\theta}:[0,T]\times[0,T]\to\mathbb{R} is a function satisfying
|R_{\theta}(t,s)|\leq\Phi_{R_{\theta}}(t-s)\text{ for all }0\leq s\leq t\leq T,\qquad R_{\theta}(t,s)=0\text{ for all }s>t,
and for any two maximal intervals I,I^{\prime} of [0,T]\setminus D ,
(3.6)
\displaystyle|R_{\theta}(t,s)-R_{\theta}(t^{\prime},s^{\prime})|
\displaystyle\leq K_{2}(|t-t^{\prime}|+|s-s^{\prime}|)
\displaystyle\text{ for all }t,t^{\prime}\in I,~s,s^{\prime}\in I^{\prime}\text{ with }s\leq t\text{ and }s^{\prime}\leq t^{\prime}.
Let \mathcal{S}_{g}(T,D) be the space of all pairs
(C_{g},R_{g}) such that:
(1)
C_{g}:[0,T]\times[0,T]\to\mathbb{R} is a symmetric function (not necessarily
positive-semidefinite) satisfying
C_{g}(t,t)\leq\Phi_{C_{g}}(t)\text{ for all }0\leq t\leq T,
and for any two maximal intervals I,I^{\prime} of [0,T]\setminus D ,
(3.7)
|C_{g}(t,t)+C_{g}(s,s)-2C_{g}(t,s)|\leq K_{2}K_{3}|t-s|\text{ for all }t,s\in I,
(3.8)
|C_{g}(t,s)-C_{g}(t^{\prime},s^{\prime})|\leq K_{2}K_{3}(\sqrt{|t-t^{\prime}|}+\sqrt{|s-s^{\prime}|})\text{ for all }t,t^{\prime}\in I,~s,s^{\prime}\in I^{\prime}.
(2)
R_{g}:[0,T]\times[0,T]\to\mathbb{R} is a function satisfying
|R_{g}(t,s)|\leq\Phi_{R_{g}}(t-s)\text{ for all }0\leq s\leq t\leq T,\qquad R_{g}(t,s)=0\text{ for all }s>t,
and for any two maximal intervals I,I^{\prime} of [0,T]\setminus D ,
(3.9)
\displaystyle|R_{g}(t,s)-R_{g}(t^{\prime},s^{\prime})|
\displaystyle\leq K_{2}K_{3}(|t-t^{\prime}|+|s-s^{\prime}|)
\displaystyle\text{ for all }t,t^{\prime}\in I,~s,s^{\prime}\in I^{\prime}\text{ with }s\leq t\text{ and }s^{\prime}\leq t^{\prime}.
We denote by \mathcal{S}_{g}^{+}(T,D)\subset\mathcal{S}_{g}(T,D)
the subset of pairs (C_{g},R_{g}) where C_{g} is positive-semidefinite.
These spaces depend on the constants K_{0},K_{1},K_{2},K_{3}>0 , although we make this
dependence implicit in the notation. The final spaces \mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{+},\mathcal{S}_{g}^{+} in
Theorem 2.4(a) will be the spaces of kernels
C_{\theta},R_{\theta},C_{g},R_{g} on [0,\infty)\times[0,\infty) whose restrictions
to [0,T]\times[0,T]
belong to \mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{+}(T,\emptyset) and \mathcal{S}_{g}^{+}(T,\emptyset) with
D=\emptyset for every T>0 .
We define a mapping
\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}:\mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{+}(T,D)\to\mathcal{S}_{g}(T,D),\qquad(C_{\theta},R_{\theta})\mapsto(C_{g},R_{g})
by (2.6–2.7):
C_{g}=\sum_{p,q\geq 0}\kappa_{p+q+2}\,R_{\theta}^{\ast p}*C_{\theta}*\bar{R}_{\theta}^{\ast q},\qquad R_{g}=\sum_{p\geq 1}\kappa_{p+1}\,R_{\theta}^{\ast p}.
Note that C_{g} is not necessarily positive-semidefinite.
Restricting to positive-semidefinite C_{g} , we define a reverse mapping
\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}:\mathcal{S}_{g}^{+}(T,D)\to\mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{+}(T,\emptyset),\qquad(C_{g},R_{g})\mapsto(C_{\theta},R_{\theta})
by (2.4–2.5):
C_{\theta}(t,s)=\mathbb{E}[\theta^{t}\theta^{s}],\qquad R_{\theta}(t,s)=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\mathrm{d}\theta^{t}}{\mathrm{d}g^{s}}\right]
where \{\theta^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} and \{\frac{\partial\theta^{t}}{\partial g^{s}}\}_{t\geq s\geq 0} solve (2.2–2.3)
with R_{g} and \{g^{t}\}_{t\geq 0}\sim\operatorname{GP}(0,C_{g}) . The following lemma
verifies that these mappings are well-defined.
Lemma 3.2.
Fix any T>0 . Then for all sufficiently large ( T -dependent)
constants K_{0},K_{1},K_{2},K_{3}>0 defining the spaces of Definition 3.1,
the following holds:
For any finite subset D\subset[0,T] , given any (C_{g},R_{g})\in\mathcal{S}_{g}^{+}(T,D) , the system (2.2–2.3) has a
unique solution, and \mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}(C_{g},R_{g})\in\mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{+}(T,\emptyset) .
Given any (C_{\theta},R_{\theta})\in\mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{+}(T,D) ,
the series (2.6–2.7) are pointwise convergent, and
\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}(C_{\theta},R_{\theta})\in\mathcal{S}_{g}(T,D) .
Proof.
Given (C_{g},\allowbreak R_{g})\in\mathcal{S}_{g}^{+}(T,\allowbreak D) , existence and uniqueness of \{\theta^{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]} and \{\frac{\partial\theta^{t}}{\partial g^{s}}\}_{0\leq s\leq t\leq T} solving (2.2–2.3) follows from the
same argument as [30, Lemma 3.3], which we omit here for brevity.
Therefore, \mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta} is well-defined.
Let (C_{\theta},R_{\theta})=\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}(C_{g},R_{g}) .
We check that (C_{\theta},R_{\theta})\in\mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{+}(T,\emptyset) :
First, according to (2.3),
\displaystyle\left|\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\frac{\partial\theta^{t}}{\partial g^{s}}\right|\leq\|f\|_{\mathrm{Lip}}\left|\frac{\partial\theta^{t}}{\partial g^{s}}\right|+\int_{s}^{t}\Phi_{R_{g}}(t-r)\left|\frac{\partial\theta^{r}}{\partial g^{s}}\right|\mathrm{d}r
where \|f\|_{\mathrm{Lip}}<\infty is the Lipschitz constant of f .
Noting that \frac{\partial\theta^{s}}{\partial g^{s}}=1 and
comparing with (3.1), this implies for K_{0}>0 large enough
that
(3.10)
\displaystyle\left|\frac{\partial\theta^{t}}{\partial g^{s}}\right|\leq\Phi_{R_{\theta}}(t-s).
Then by definition of R_{\theta} in (2.5),
|R_{\theta}(t,s)|\leq\Phi_{R_{\theta}}(t-s) for all 0\leq s\leq t\leq T .
Similarly, for any 0\leq s,t,t^{\prime}\leq T with s\leq t^{\prime}\leq t , we have
\displaystyle|R_{\theta}(t,s)-R_{\theta}(t^{\prime},s)|
\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\left|\frac{\partial\theta^{t}}{\partial g^{s}}-\frac{\partial\theta^{t^{\prime}}}{\partial g^{s}}\right|\leq\mathbb{E}\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t}\left|\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}r}\frac{\partial\theta^{r}}{\partial g^{s}}\right|\mathrm{d}r
(3.11)
\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\int_{t^{\prime}}^{t}\left(\|f\|_{\mathrm{Lip}}\left|\frac{\partial\theta^{r}}{\partial g^{s}}\right|+\int_{s}^{r}\Phi_{R_{g}}(r-r^{\prime})\left|\frac{\partial\theta^{r^{\prime}}}{\partial g^{s}}\right|\mathrm{d}r^{\prime}\right)\mathrm{d}r\leq K_{2}|t-t^{\prime}|,
the last inequality holding by (3.10) for some
large enough ( T -dependent) K_{2}>0 .
For continuity in s , by the response equation (2.3), for
t\geq s ,
\frac{\partial\theta^{t}}{\partial g^{s}}=1+\int_{s}^{t}\left[f^{\prime}(\theta^{u})\frac{\partial\theta^{u}}{\partial g^{s}}+\int_{s}^{u}R_{g}(u,r)\frac{\partial\theta^{r}}{\partial g^{s}}\,\mathrm{d}r\right]\mathrm{d}u.
Consider any t\geq s^{\prime}\geq s . Then
\displaystyle\left|\frac{\partial\theta^{s^{\prime}}}{\partial g^{s}}-1\right|
\displaystyle\leq\int_{s}^{s^{\prime}}\|f\|_{\mathrm{Lip}}\left|\frac{\partial\theta^{u}}{\partial g^{s}}\right|\,\mathrm{d}u+\int_{s}^{s^{\prime}}\int_{s}^{u}|R_{g}(u,r)|\left|\frac{\partial\theta^{r}}{\partial g^{s}}\right|\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}u\leq C|s^{\prime}-s|,
the last holding by
(3.10) and |R_{g}(u,r)|\leq\Phi_{R_{g}}(T)
for some large enough ( T -dependent) constant C>0 .
Then subtracting the two response equations for
\frac{\partial\theta^{t}}{\partial g^{s}} and
\frac{\partial\theta^{t}}{\partial g^{s^{\prime}}} gives
\displaystyle\left|\frac{\partial\theta^{t}}{\partial g^{s}}-\frac{\partial\theta^{t}}{\partial g^{s^{\prime}}}\right|\leq\left|\frac{\partial\theta^{s^{\prime}}}{\partial g^{s}}-1\right|+\int_{s^{\prime}}^{t}\|f\|_{\mathrm{Lip}}\left|\frac{\partial\theta^{u}}{\partial g^{s}}-\frac{\partial\theta^{u}}{\partial g^{s^{\prime}}}\right|\,\mathrm{d}u
\displaystyle\quad+\int_{s^{\prime}}^{t}\int_{s^{\prime}}^{u}|R_{g}(u,r)|\left|\frac{\partial\theta^{r}}{\partial g^{s}}-\frac{\partial\theta^{r}}{\partial g^{s^{\prime}}}\right|\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}u+\int_{s^{\prime}}^{t}\int_{s}^{s^{\prime}}|R_{g}(u,r)|\left|\frac{\partial\theta^{r}}{\partial g^{s}}\right|\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}u.
The first and last terms are bounded by C|s^{\prime}-s| for some C>0 , and the
second and third terms by C\sup_{u\in[s^{\prime},t]}|\frac{\partial\theta^{u}}{\partial g^{s}}-\frac{\partial\theta^{u}}{\partial g^{s^{\prime}}}| .
Then by Grönwall’s inequality,
\left|\frac{\partial\theta^{t}}{\partial g^{s}}-\frac{\partial\theta^{t}}{\partial g^{s^{\prime}}}\right|\leq K_{2}|s^{\prime}-s|
for some sufficiently large K_{2}>0 . Taking expectations gives
(3.12)
\left|R_{\theta}(t,s)-R_{\theta}(t,s^{\prime})\right|\leq K_{2}|s^{\prime}-s|.
Combining (3.11) and (3.12) shows the continuity property (3.6).
This verifies all properties for R_{\theta} in Definition 3.1.
For the covariance kernel C_{\theta} , applying Itô’s formula to
the equation (2.2) gives
\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathbb{E}(\theta^{t})^{2}
\displaystyle=2\mathbb{E}[\theta^{t}f(\theta^{t})]+2\int_{0}^{t}R_{g}(t,s)\mathbb{E}[\theta^{t}\theta^{s}]\mathrm{d}s+2\mathbb{E}[\theta^{t}g^{t}]+2\gamma
\displaystyle\leq K_{0}\left(\mathbb{E}(\theta^{t})^{2}+\int_{0}^{t}\Phi_{R_{g}}(t-s)[\mathbb{E}(\theta^{s})^{2}+\mathbb{E}(\theta^{t})^{2}]\mathrm{d}s+C_{g}(t,t)+1\right),
the second inequality holding for large enough K_{0}>0
since \{g^{t}\}_{t\geq 0}\sim\operatorname{GP}(0,C_{g}) , f is Lipschitz, and |R_{g}(s,r)|\leq\Phi_{R_{g}}(s-r) .
Comparing with (3.3), this implies
C_{\theta}(t,t)=\mathbb{E}(\theta^{t})^{2}\leq\Phi_{C_{\theta}}(t) .
Similarly, for all s,s^{\prime},t,t^{\prime}\in[0,T] , one can show
|C_{\theta}(t,t)+C_{\theta}(s,s)-2C_{\theta}(t,s)|=\mathbb{E}(\theta^{t}-\theta^{s})^{2}\leq K_{2}|t-s|
for large enough K_{2}>0 . This verifies all properties for C_{\theta} in
Definition 3.1 with D=\emptyset , so (C_{\theta},R_{\theta})\in\mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{+}(T,\emptyset) .
For the map \mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g} , given (C_{\theta},R_{\theta})\in\mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{+}(T,D) , note that Proposition A.1
implies |\kappa_{p}|\leq K_{1}^{p} for any sufficiently large K_{1}>0 and all
p\geq 1 , and |R_{\theta}(t,s)|\leq\Phi_{R_{\theta}}(t-s) . Then
\left|\sum_{p\geq 1}\kappa_{p+1}R_{\theta}^{*p}(t,s)\right|\leq\sum_{p\geq 1}K_{1}^{p+1}\Phi_{R_{\theta}}^{*p}(t-s)\leq\sum_{p\geq 1}K_{1}^{p+1}\Phi_{R_{\theta}}(T)^{p}\frac{(t-s)^{p-1}}{(p-1)!}<\infty,
so the series (2.7) is pointwise convergent. Similarly
(2.6) is pointwise convergent, so
\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g} is well-defined.
Let (C_{g},R_{g})=\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}(C_{\theta},R_{\theta}) .
Applying |\kappa_{p}|\leq K_{1}^{p} , |R_{\theta}(t,s)|\leq\Phi_{R_{\theta}}(t-s) ,
and
|C_{\theta}(t,s)|\leq\sqrt{C_{\theta}(t,t)}\sqrt{C_{\theta}(s,s)}\leq\sqrt{\Phi_{C_{\theta}}(t)}\sqrt{\Phi_{C_{\theta}}(s)},
we can verify that
\displaystyle|R_{g}(t,s)|
\displaystyle\leq\sum_{p\geq 1}K_{1}^{p+1}\,\Phi_{R_{\theta}}^{\ast p}(t-s)=\Phi_{R_{g}}(t-s),
\displaystyle|C_{g}(t,t)|
\displaystyle\leq\sum_{p,q\geq 0}K_{1}^{p+q+2}\,(\Phi_{R_{\theta}}^{\ast p}\ast\sqrt{\Phi_{C_{\theta}}})(t)(\Phi_{R_{\theta}}^{\ast q}\ast\sqrt{\Phi_{C_{\theta}}})(t)
\displaystyle=\left(\sum_{p\geq 0}K_{1}^{p+1}\,(\Phi_{R_{\theta}}^{\ast p}\ast\sqrt{\Phi_{C_{\theta}}})(t)\right)^{2}=\Phi_{C_{g}}(t).
For any maximal interval I of [0,T]\setminus D and any s,t\in I
with t\geq s , note that
\displaystyle|C_{g}(t,t)+C_{g}(s,s)-2C_{g}(t,s)|
\displaystyle=\Bigg|\kappa_{2}\Big(C_{\theta}(t,t)+C_{\theta}(s,s)-2C_{\theta}(t,s)\Big)+\sum_{p\geq 1}\kappa_{p+2}\int_{0}^{t}(R_{\theta}^{\ast p}(t,r)-R_{\theta}^{\ast p}(s,r))(C_{\theta}(r,t)-C_{\theta}(r,s))\mathrm{d}r
\displaystyle\hskip 36.135pt+\sum_{q\geq 1}\kappa_{q+2}\int_{0}^{t}\mathrm{d}u\,(C_{\theta}(t,u)-C_{\theta}(s,u))(R_{\theta}^{\ast q}(t,u)-R_{\theta}^{\ast q}(s,u))
(3.13)
\displaystyle\hskip 36.135pt+\sum_{p,q\geq 1}\kappa_{p+q+2}\int_{0}^{t}\mathrm{d}r\int_{0}^{t}\mathrm{d}u\,(R_{\theta}^{\ast p}(t,r)-R_{\theta}^{\ast p}(s,r))C_{\theta}(r,u)(R_{\theta}^{\ast q}(t,u)-R_{\theta}^{\ast q}(s,u))\Bigg|.
For any p\geq 1 and t\geq s\geq r ,
\displaystyle R_{\theta}^{\ast p}(t,r)-R_{\theta}^{\ast p}(s,r)
\displaystyle=\int_{r}^{s}\bigl(R_{\theta}(t,u)-R_{\theta}(s,u)\bigr)R_{\theta}^{\ast(p-1)}(u,r)\,\mathrm{d}u+\int_{s}^{t}R_{\theta}(t,u)R_{\theta}^{\ast(p-1)}(u,r)\,\mathrm{d}u.
Therefore, combined with
\displaystyle|R_{\theta}(t,u)-R_{\theta}(s,u)|
\displaystyle\leq K_{2}|t-s|,
\displaystyle|R_{\theta}^{\ast p}(t,s)|
\displaystyle\leq\Phi_{R_{\theta}}^{\ast p}(t-s)\leq\frac{\Phi_{R_{\theta}}(T)^{p}(t-s)^{p-1}}{(p-1)!},
we have that
\displaystyle|R_{\theta}^{\ast p}(t,r)-R_{\theta}^{\ast p}(s,r)|
\displaystyle\leq\int_{r}^{s}K_{2}|t-s|\Phi_{R_{\theta}}^{\ast(p-1)}(u-r)\,\mathrm{d}u+\int_{s}^{t}\Phi_{R_{\theta}}(t-u)\Phi_{R_{\theta}}^{\ast(p-1)}(u-r)\mathrm{d}u
\displaystyle\leq(K_{2}T+\Phi_{R_{\theta}}(T))\frac{\Phi_{R_{\theta}}(T)^{p-1}T^{p-1}}{(p-1)!}|t-s|.
This bound holds also for r\in[s,t] , noting in this case that
R_{\theta}^{\ast p}(t,r)-R_{\theta}^{\ast p}(s,r)=R_{\theta}^{\ast p}(t,r)=\int_{r}^{t}R_{\theta}(t,u)R_{\theta}^{*(p-1)}(u,r)\,\mathrm{d}u
and applying the same argument. Applying this bound for summands of
(3.13) where either p\geq 1 or q\geq 1 , and applying
|C_{\theta}(t,t)+C_{\theta}(s,s)-2C_{\theta}(t,s)|\leq K_{2}|t-s|
for p=q=0 , we obtain
|C_{g}(t,t)+C_{g}(s,s)-2C_{g}(t,s)|\leq K_{2}K_{3}|t-s|
for all large enough K_{2},K_{3}>0 , which is the continuity property
(3.7).
Since C_{\theta} is positive-semidefinite, writing u\sim\operatorname{GP}(0,C_{\theta}) ,
for any two maximal intervals I,I^{\prime} of [0,T]\setminus D and any
t,t^{\prime}\in I and s,s^{\prime}\in I^{\prime} , we have also
\displaystyle|C_{\theta}(t,s)-C_{\theta}(t^{\prime},s^{\prime})|
\displaystyle\leq|\mathbb{E}[(u^{t}-u^{t^{\prime}})u^{s}]|+|\mathbb{E}[u^{t^{\prime}}(u^{s}-u^{s^{\prime}})]|
\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{\Phi_{C_{\theta}}(T)}\cdot K_{2}(\sqrt{|t-t^{\prime}|}+\sqrt{|s-s^{\prime}|}),
by Cauchy-Schwarz. Then applying a similar argument as above shows
|C_{g}(t,s)-C_{g}(t^{\prime},s^{\prime})|\leq K_{2}K_{3}(\sqrt{|t-t^{\prime}|}+\sqrt{|s-s^{\prime}|})
for all large enough K_{2},K_{3}>0 ,
which is the continuity property (3.8).
Finally, for any maximal intervals I,I^{\prime} of
[0,T]\setminus D and s,s^{\prime}\in I , t,t^{\prime}\in I^{\prime} with s\leq t and s^{\prime}\leq t^{\prime} , a similar argument as above using |R_{\theta}(t,s)-R_{\theta}(t^{\prime},s^{\prime})|\leq K_{2}(|t-t^{\prime}|+|s-s^{\prime}|) checks that
|R_{g}(t,s)-R_{g}(t^{\prime},s^{\prime})|\leq K_{2}K_{3}(|t-t^{\prime}|+|s-s^{\prime}|)
for large enough K_{2},K_{3}>0 , which is (3.9).
Thus (C_{g},R_{g})\in\mathcal{S}_{g}(T,D) .
∎
Henceforth, given T>0 , we will fix T -dependent constants
K_{0},K_{1},K_{2},K_{3}>0 large enough such that Lemma 3.2
holds.
3.2. Contractivity and uniqueness of fixed point with projection
Next, we define a metric on \mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{+} and \mathcal{S}_{g} . Fix \lambda>0 .
For a pair of response kernels (R_{1},R_{2})\equiv(R_{\theta,1},R_{\theta,2})
or (R_{1},R_{2})\equiv(R_{g,1},R_{g,2}) satisfying the conditions of
Definition 3.1, we define
(3.14)
\displaystyle d_{\lambda}(R_{1},R_{2})=\sup_{0\leq s\leq t\leq T}e^{-\lambda t}|R_{1}(t,s)-R_{2}(t,s)|.
For a pair of (not necessarily positive-semidefinite) correlation kernels
(C_{1},\allowbreak C_{2})\equiv(C_{\theta,1},\allowbreak C_{\theta,2})
or (C_{1},\allowbreak C_{2})\equiv(C_{g,1},\allowbreak C_{g,2}) satisfying the conditions of
\mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{+} / \mathcal{S}_{g} in Definition 3.1, we define
(3.15)
\displaystyle\langle C_{1},C_{2}\rangle_{\lambda}=\int_{0}^{T}\int_{0}^{T}e^{-2\lambda(t\vee s)}C_{1}(t,s)C_{2}(t,s)\,\mathrm{d}t\,\mathrm{d}s,\qquad\|C\|_{\lambda}=\langle C,C\rangle_{\lambda}^{1/2}
and the metric
(3.16)
\displaystyle d_{\lambda}(C_{1},C_{2})=\|C_{1}-C_{2}\|_{\lambda}=\sqrt{\int_{0}^{T}\int_{0}^{T}e^{-2\lambda(t\vee s)}(C_{1}(t,s)-C_{2}(t,s))^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t\,\mathrm{d}s}.
Finally, for either
(C,R)\equiv(C_{\theta},R_{\theta}) or (C,R)\equiv(C_{g},R_{g}) , we set
d_{\lambda}((C_{1},R_{1}),(C_{2},R_{2}))=d_{\lambda}(R_{1},R_{2})+d_{\lambda}(C_{1},C_{2}).
By the uniform continuity properties of the kernels on [0,T]\setminus D
in Definition 3.1,
this defines a valid metric d_{\lambda} on both \mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{+} and
\mathcal{S}_{g} .
Lemma 3.3 (Contractivity of \mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta} ).
Let X_{i}=(C_{g,i},R_{g,i})\in\mathcal{S}_{g}^{+}(T,D) for i=1,2 , and let
Y_{i}=(C_{\theta,i},R_{\theta,i})=\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}(C_{g,i},R_{g,i}) .
Then for any fixed 0<\alpha<1 and all sufficiently large \lambda>0
(depending on \alpha,T ),
(3.17)
\displaystyle d_{\lambda}(Y_{1},Y_{2})\leq\alpha\cdot d_{\lambda}(X_{1},X_{2}).
Proof.
We first consider C_{g,1}=C_{g,2}\equiv C_{g} and different R_{g,1},R_{g,2} .
Coupling the processes \{\theta_{i}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0}
and \{\frac{\partial\theta_{i}^{t}}{\partial g^{s}}\}_{t\geq s\geq 0}
solving (2.2–2.3) with R_{g,i}
by the same realizations of \{g^{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]}\sim\operatorname{GP}(0,C_{g}) and
\{b^{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]} , a Grönwall
argument (c.f. [30, Lemma 3.7]) shows,
for all sufficiently large \lambda>0 and a constant C>0 not depending on
\lambda ,
\displaystyle\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}e^{-2\lambda t}\mathbb{E}(\theta_{1}^{t}-\theta_{2}^{t})^{2}\leq\frac{C}{\lambda}\,d_{\lambda}(R_{g,1},R_{g,2})^{2},
\displaystyle\sup_{0\leq s\leq t\leq T}e^{-\lambda t}\mathbb{E}\left|\frac{\partial\theta_{1}^{t}}{\partial g^{s}}-\frac{\partial\theta_{2}^{t}}{\partial g^{s}}\right|\leq\frac{C}{\lambda}\,d_{\lambda}(R_{g,1},R_{g,2}).
The second inequality implies
d_{\lambda}(R_{\theta,1},R_{\theta,2})\leq\frac{C}{\lambda}d_{\lambda}(R_{g,1},R_{g,2}) . By Cauchy-Schwarz,
\displaystyle|C_{\theta,1}(t,s)-C_{\theta,2}(t,s)|^{2}
\displaystyle\leq 2\mathbb{E}(\theta_{1}^{t}-\theta_{2}^{t})^{2}\mathbb{E}(\theta_{1}^{s})^{2}+2\mathbb{E}(\theta_{2}^{t})^{2}\mathbb{E}(\theta_{1}^{s}-\theta_{2}^{s})^{2}
\displaystyle\leq 2\Phi_{C_{\theta}}(T)\left(\mathbb{E}(\theta_{1}^{t}-\theta_{2}^{t})^{2}+\mathbb{E}(\theta_{1}^{s}-\theta_{2}^{s})^{2}\right).
Integrating both sides, we have
\displaystyle d_{\lambda}(C_{\theta,1},C_{\theta,2})^{2}
\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{T}\int_{0}^{T}e^{-2\lambda(t\vee s)}|C_{\theta,1}(t,s)-C_{\theta,2}(t,s)|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t\,\mathrm{d}s
\displaystyle\leq 4\Phi_{C_{\theta}}(T)T^{2}\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}e^{-2\lambda t}\mathbb{E}(\theta_{1}^{t}-\theta_{2}^{t})^{2},
so the first inequality implies
d_{\lambda}(C_{\theta,1},C_{\theta,2})\leq\frac{C^{\prime}}{\sqrt{\lambda}}d_{\lambda}(R_{g,1},R_{g,2}) . Thus, for any \alpha\in(0,1) and all large
enough \lambda>0 ,
(3.18)
d_{\lambda}(Y_{1},Y_{2})\leq\alpha\cdot d_{\lambda}(R_{g,1},R_{g,2}).
We next consider R_{g,1}=R_{g,2}\equiv R_{g} and different C_{g,1},C_{g,2} .
For u\in[0,1] , define the interpolation C_{u}=(1-u)C_{g,1}+uC_{g,2} ,
and let g_{u}\sim\operatorname{GP}(0,C_{u}) .
Note that C_{u} induces a positive-semidefinite, trace-class covariance operator
Q_{u} on \mathcal{H}:=L^{2}([0,T]) , given by
(Q_{u}\varphi)(r):=\int_{0}^{T}C_{u}(r,r^{\prime})\varphi(r^{\prime})\,\mathrm{d}r^{\prime},\qquad\varphi\in\mathcal{H}.
Let \{e_{k}\}_{k\geq 1} be an orthonormal basis of
\mathcal{H} , and let \{\xi_{k}\}_{k\geq 1} be i.i.d. standard Gaussian random
variables. Then we may realize g_{u}\sim\operatorname{GP}(0,C_{u}) as
g_{u}=\sum_{k\geq 1}Q_{u}^{1/2}e_{k}\cdot\xi_{k} .
Fixing an integer N\geq 1 , define \Pi_{N}:{\mathcal{H}}\to{\operatorname{span}(e_{1},\ldots,e_{N})} as the orthogonal projection onto the subspace spanned by e_{1},\ldots,e_{N} . Consider the truncation
g_{u,N}:=\Pi_{N}g_{u} ,
and define \theta_{g_{u,N}} by
\mathrm{d}\theta_{g_{u,N}}^{t}=\left[f(\theta_{g_{u,N}}^{t})+\int_{0}^{t}R_{g}(t,s)\theta_{g_{u,N}}^{s}\mathrm{d}s+g_{u,N}^{t}\right]\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\mathrm{d}b^{t},\qquad\theta_{g_{u,N}}^{0}=\theta^{0}.
Let us compute
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}u}\mathbb{E}[\theta_{g_{u,N}}^{t}\theta_{g_{u,N}}^{s}] :
For any h\in\mathcal{H} , define \{\theta_{h}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} by
\theta_{h}^{t}=\theta^{0}+\int_{0}^{t}\left[f(\theta_{h}^{s})+\int_{0}^{s}R_{g}(s,r)\theta_{h}^{r}\mathrm{d}r+{h}^{s}\right]\mathrm{d}s+\sqrt{2\gamma}\,b^{t}.
By [72, Theorem 2.5], for any h,k,l\in\mathcal{H} ,
the above equation has a unique solution \{\theta_{h}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} , and
there exist directional derivative processes
D_{k}\theta_{h} and D_{kl}^{2}\theta_{h} on [0,T]
for which
\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\mathbb{E}_{\{b^{t}\}}\left(\frac{\theta_{h+\varepsilon k}^{t}-\theta_{h}^{t}}{\varepsilon}-D_{k}\theta_{h}^{t}\right)^{2}=0,\qquad\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\mathbb{E}_{\{b^{t}\}}\left(\frac{D_{k}\theta_{h+\varepsilon l}^{t}-D_{k}\theta_{h}^{t}}{\varepsilon}-D_{kl}^{2}\theta_{h}^{t}\right)^{2}=0
where \mathbb{E}_{\{b^{t}\}} is the expectation over the Brownian motion
\{b^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} . Then
\mathbb{E}_{\{b^{t}\}}[\theta_{h+\varepsilon k+\varepsilon^{\prime}l}^{t}\allowbreak\theta_{h+\varepsilon k+\varepsilon^{\prime}l}^{s}] is twice continuously-differentiable in
(\varepsilon,\varepsilon^{\prime}) , and
(3.19)
\displaystyle\partial_{\varepsilon}\partial_{\varepsilon^{\prime}}\mathbb{E}_{\{b^{t}\}}[\theta_{h+\varepsilon k+\varepsilon^{\prime}l}^{t}\theta_{h+\varepsilon k+\varepsilon^{\prime}l}^{s}]\big|_{\varepsilon=\varepsilon^{\prime}=0}
\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\{b^{t}\}}\Big[(D_{kl}^{2}\theta_{h}^{t})\theta_{h}^{s}+\theta_{h}^{t}(D_{kl}^{2}\theta_{h}^{s})+(D_{k}\theta_{h}^{t})(D_{l}\theta_{h}^{s})
\displaystyle+(D_{l}\theta_{h}^{t})(D_{k}\theta_{h}^{s})\Big].
Furthermore by [72, Theorem 2.5], D_{k}\theta_{h} and
D_{kl}^{2}\theta_{h} are the unique solutions of
\displaystyle D_{k}\theta_{h}^{t}
\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{t}\left[f^{\prime}(\theta_{h}^{s})D_{k}\theta_{h}^{s}+\int_{0}^{s}R_{g}(s,r)D_{k}\theta_{h}^{r}\mathrm{d}r+k^{s}\right]\mathrm{d}s,
\displaystyle D_{kl}^{2}\theta^{t}
\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{t}\left[f^{\prime\prime}(\theta_{h}^{s})(D_{k}\theta_{h}^{s})(D_{l}\theta_{h}^{s})+f^{\prime}(\theta_{h}^{s})D_{kl}^{2}\theta_{h}^{s}+\int_{0}^{s}R_{g}(s,r)D_{kl}^{2}\theta_{h}^{r}\mathrm{d}r\right]\mathrm{d}s.
Equivalently, define first-order and second-order response kernels J_{h},K_{h} by
\displaystyle J_{h}(t,r)
\displaystyle=1+\int_{r}^{t}\bigg[f^{\prime}(\theta_{h}^{s})J_{h}(s,r)+\int_{r}^{s}R_{g}(s,r^{\prime})J_{h}(r^{\prime},r)\mathrm{d}r\bigg]\mathrm{d}s
\displaystyle K_{h}(t,r,r^{\prime})
\displaystyle=\int_{r\vee r^{\prime}}^{t}\bigg[f^{\prime\prime}(\theta_{h}^{s})J_{h}(s,r)J_{h}(s,r^{\prime})+f^{\prime}(\theta_{h}^{s})K_{h}(s,r,r^{\prime})+\int_{r\vee r^{\prime}}^{s}R_{g}(s,s^{\prime})K_{h}(s^{\prime},r,r^{\prime})\mathrm{d}s^{\prime}\bigg]\mathrm{d}s
for t\geq\max(r,r^{\prime}) , and J_{h}(t,r)=0 and K_{h}(t,r,r^{\prime})=0 if t<r and/or
t<r^{\prime} . Then it may be checked that the above solutions are given by
(3.20)
D_{k}\theta_{h}^{t}=\int_{0}^{T}J_{h}(t,r)k^{r}\,\mathrm{d}r,\qquad D_{kl}^{2}\theta_{h}^{t}=\int_{0}^{T}\int_{0}^{T}K_{h}(t,r,r^{\prime})k^{r}l^{r^{\prime}}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}r^{\prime}.
Hence (3.19) takes the form
\displaystyle\partial_{\varepsilon}\partial_{\varepsilon^{\prime}}\mathbb{E}_{\{b^{t}\}}[\theta_{h+\varepsilon k+\varepsilon^{\prime}l}^{t}\theta_{h+\varepsilon k+\varepsilon^{\prime}l}^{s}]\big|_{\varepsilon=\varepsilon^{\prime}=0}
\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{T}\int_{0}^{T}H_{h}(t,s;r,r^{\prime})k^{r}l^{r^{\prime}}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}r^{\prime},
where
\displaystyle H_{h}(t,s;r,r^{\prime})
\displaystyle:=K_{h}(t,r,r^{\prime})\theta_{h}^{s}+K_{h}(s,r,r^{\prime})\theta_{h}^{t}+J_{h}(t,r)J_{h}(s,r^{\prime})+J_{h}(t,r^{\prime})J_{h}(s,r).
Then, by the finite-dimensional Gaussian interpolation formula
(see e.g. [70, Lemma 7.2.7]),
\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}u}\mathbb{E}[\theta_{g_{u,N}}^{t}\theta_{g_{u,N}}^{s}]
\displaystyle=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}u}\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}_{\{b^{t}\}}[\theta_{g_{u,N}}^{t}\theta_{g_{u,N}}^{s}]]
\displaystyle=\hskip-2.0pt\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j=1}^{N}\bigl\langle(Q_{1}-Q_{0})e_{i},e_{j}\bigr\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\,\mathbb{E}\left[\partial_{\varepsilon}\partial_{\varepsilon^{\prime}}\mathbb{E}_{\{b^{t}\}}[\theta_{g_{u,N}+\varepsilon e_{i}+\varepsilon^{\prime}e_{j}}^{t}\theta_{g_{u,N}+\varepsilon e_{i}+\varepsilon^{\prime}e_{j}}^{s}]\big|_{\varepsilon=\varepsilon^{\prime}=0}\right]
(3.21)
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j=1}^{N}\bigl\langle(Q_{1}-Q_{0})e_{i},e_{j}\bigr\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\,\mathbb{E}\left[\int_{0}^{T}\int_{0}^{T}H_{g_{u,N}}(t,s;r,r^{\prime})e_{i}^{r}e_{j}^{r^{\prime}}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}r^{\prime}\right].
By the Parseval identity, as N\to\infty ,
\sum_{i,j=1}^{N}\bigl\langle(Q_{1}-Q_{0})e_{i},e_{j}\bigr\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}e_{i}^{r}e_{j}^{r^{\prime}}\to(C_{g,2}-C_{g,1})(r,r^{\prime})
in L^{2}([0,T]\times[0,T]) .
Also as N\to\infty , g_{u,N}\to g_{u} in L^{2}([0,T]) . Then
applying a Grönwall argument to the definitions of the above processes
shows that \theta_{g_{u,N}}\to\theta_{g_{u}} and
J_{g_{u,N}}(t,\cdot)\to J_{g_{u}}(t,\cdot)
in L^{2}([0,T]) , and K_{g_{u,N}}(t,\cdot,\cdot)\to K_{g_{u}}(t,\cdot,\cdot) and
H_{g_{u,N}}(t,s;\cdot,\cdot)\to H_{g_{u}}(t,s;\cdot,\cdot)
in L^{2}([0,T]\times[0,T]) . Then,
integrating (3.21) over u\in[0,1] and taking the limit N\to\infty ,
\displaystyle(C_{\theta,2}-C_{\theta,1})(t,s)
\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\theta_{g_{1}}^{t}\theta_{g_{1}}^{s}]-\mathbb{E}[\theta_{g_{0}}^{t}\theta_{g_{0}}^{s}]
\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{1}\mathrm{d}u\left(\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{0}^{T}(C_{g,2}-C_{g,1})(r,r^{\prime})\mathbb{E}\left[H_{g_{u}}(t,s;r,r^{\prime})\right]\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}r^{\prime}\right).
As f^{\prime},f^{\prime\prime} are bounded and R_{g} is bounded on [0,T] ,
a Grönwall argument checks that J_{h}(t,r) and K_{h}(t,r,r^{\prime}) are both uniformly
bounded over t,r,r^{\prime}\in[0,T] and h=g_{u} for all u\in[0,1] . Then
\mathbb{E}[H_{g_{u}}(t,s;r,r^{\prime})] is also uniformly bounded over t,s,r,r^{\prime}\in[0,T]
and u\in[0,1] . Furthermore, we have \mathbb{E}[H_{g_{u}}(t,s;r,r^{\prime})]=0 unless r,r^{\prime}\leq\max(t,s) . Thus, there exists a T -dependent constant C>0 for which
\displaystyle|(C_{\theta,2}-C_{\theta,1})(t,s)|
\displaystyle\leq C\int_{0}^{t\vee s}\int_{0}^{t\vee s}|(C_{g,2}-C_{g,1})(r,r^{\prime})|\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}r^{\prime}
Then by Cauchy-Schwarz, for T -dependent constants C^{\prime},C^{\prime\prime}>0 (not depending on
\lambda ),
\displaystyle d_{\lambda}(C_{\theta,1},C_{\theta,2})^{2}=\int_{0}^{T}\int_{0}^{T}e^{-2\lambda(t\vee s)}(C_{\theta,2}(t,s)-C_{\theta,1}(t,s))^{2}\mathrm{d}t\,\mathrm{d}s
\displaystyle\leq C^{\prime}\int_{0}^{T}\mathrm{d}t\int_{0}^{T}\mathrm{d}s\,e^{-2\lambda(t\vee s)}\int_{0}^{t\vee s}\mathrm{d}r\int_{0}^{t\vee s}\mathrm{d}r^{\prime}(C_{g,2}(r,r^{\prime})-C_{g,1}(r,r^{\prime}))^{2}
\displaystyle=C^{\prime}\int_{0}^{T}\mathrm{d}r\int_{0}^{T}\mathrm{d}r^{\prime}e^{-2\lambda(r\vee r^{\prime})}(C_{g,2}(r,r^{\prime})-C_{g,1}(r,r^{\prime}))^{2}\mathop{\int_{0}^{T}\mathrm{d}t\int_{0}^{T}\mathrm{d}s}\mathbf{1}_{t\vee s\geq r\vee r^{\prime}}e^{-2\lambda(t\vee s)+2\lambda(r\vee r^{\prime})}
\displaystyle\leq\frac{C^{\prime\prime}}{\lambda}\int_{0}^{T}\mathrm{d}r\int_{0}^{T}\mathrm{d}r^{\prime}e^{-2\lambda(r\vee r^{\prime})}(C_{g,2}(r,r^{\prime})-C_{g,1}(r,r^{\prime}))^{2}=\frac{C^{\prime\prime}}{\lambda}d_{\lambda}(C_{g,1},C_{g,2})^{2}.
Thus for any \alpha\in(0,1) and all sufficiently large \lambda ,
d_{\lambda}(C_{\theta,1},C_{\theta,2})\leq\alpha\cdot d_{\lambda}(C_{g,1},C_{g,2}) .
The analysis of the response R_{\theta} is similar: Fixing s\in[0,T] ,
there exist directional derivative processes
D_{k}J_{h}(\cdot,s)
and D_{kl}^{2}J_{h}(\cdot,s) over t\in[s,T] for which
\displaystyle\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\mathbb{E}_{\{b^{t}\}}\left(\frac{J_{h+\varepsilon k}(t,s)-J_{h}(t,s)}{\varepsilon}-D_{k}J_{h}(t,s)\right)^{2}
\displaystyle=0,
\displaystyle\qquad\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\mathbb{E}_{\{b^{t}\}}\left(\frac{D_{k}J_{h+\varepsilon l}(t,s)-D_{k}J_{h}(t,s)}{\varepsilon}-D_{kl}^{2}J_{h}(t,s)\right)^{2}
\displaystyle=0.
These are the unique solutions of the equations
\displaystyle D_{k}J_{h}(t,s)
\displaystyle=\int_{s}^{t}\bigg[f^{\prime\prime}(\theta_{h}^{a})(D_{k}\theta_{h}^{a})J_{h}(a,s)+f^{\prime}(\theta_{h}^{a})D_{k}J_{h}(a,s)+\int_{s}^{a}R_{g}(a,b)D_{k}J_{h}(b,s)\mathrm{d}b\bigg]\mathrm{d}a,
\displaystyle D_{kl}^{2}J_{h}(t,s)
\displaystyle=\int_{s}^{t}\bigg[\Bigl(f^{\prime\prime\prime}(\theta_{h}^{a})(D_{k}\theta_{h}^{a})(D_{l}\theta_{h}^{a})+f^{\prime\prime}(\theta_{h}^{a})D_{kl}^{2}\theta_{h}^{a}\Bigr)J_{h}(a,s)+f^{\prime\prime}(\theta_{h}^{a})(D_{k}\theta_{h}^{a})D_{l}J_{h}(a,s)
\displaystyle\qquad+f^{\prime\prime}(\theta_{h}^{a})(D_{l}\theta_{h}^{a})D_{k}J_{h}(a,s)+f^{\prime}(\theta_{h}^{a})D_{kl}^{2}J_{h}(a,s)+\int_{s}^{a}R_{g}(a,b)D_{kl}^{2}J_{h}(b,s)\mathrm{d}b\bigg]\mathrm{d}a.
Analogously to (3.20),
we may represent these solutions as
D_{k}J_{h}(t,s)=\int_{0}^{T}M_{h}(t,s;r)k^{r}\,\mathrm{d}r,\qquad D_{kl}^{2}J_{h}(t,s)=\int_{0}^{T}\int_{0}^{T}L_{h}(t,s;r,r^{\prime})k^{r}l^{r^{\prime}}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}r^{\prime},
where M_{h},L_{h} are the response processes
\displaystyle M_{h}(t,s;r)
\displaystyle=\int_{s}^{t}\bigg[f^{\prime\prime}(\theta_{h}^{a})J_{h}(a,r)J_{h}(a,s)+f^{\prime}(\theta_{h}^{a})M_{h}(a,s;r)+\int_{s}^{a}R_{g}(a,b)M_{h}(b,s;r)\mathrm{d}b\bigg]\mathrm{d}a,
\displaystyle L_{h}(t,s;r,r^{\prime})
\displaystyle=\int_{s}^{t}\bigg[\Bigl(f^{\prime\prime\prime}(\theta_{h}^{a})J_{h}(a,r)J_{h}(a,r^{\prime})+f^{\prime\prime}(\theta_{h}^{a})K_{h}(a,r,r^{\prime})\Bigr)J_{h}(a,s)+f^{\prime\prime}(\theta_{h}^{a})J_{h}(a,r)M_{h}(a,s;r^{\prime})
\displaystyle\hskip 28.90755pt+f^{\prime\prime}(\theta_{h}^{a})J_{h}(a,r^{\prime})M_{h}(a,s;r)+f^{\prime}(\theta_{h}^{a})L_{h}(a,s;r,r^{\prime})+\int_{s}^{a}R_{g}(a,b)L_{h}(b,s;r,r^{\prime})\mathrm{d}b\bigg]\mathrm{d}a.
Applying the finite-dimensional Gaussian interpolation formula, we have
\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}u}\mathbb{E}J_{g_{u,N}}(t,s)
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j=1}^{N}\bigl\langle(Q_{1}-Q_{0})e_{i},e_{j}\bigr\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\,\mathbb{E}\left[\partial_{\varepsilon}\partial_{\varepsilon^{\prime}}J_{g_{u,N}+\varepsilon e_{i}+\varepsilon^{\prime}e_{j}}(t,s)\big|_{\varepsilon=\varepsilon^{\prime}=0}\right]
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j=1}^{N}\bigl\langle(Q_{1}-Q_{0})e_{i},e_{j}\bigr\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\,\mathbb{E}\left[\int_{0}^{T}\int_{0}^{T}L_{g_{u,N}}(t,s;r,r^{\prime})e_{i}^{r}e_{j}^{r^{\prime}}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}r^{\prime}\right].
Integrating over u\in[0,1] , taking the limit N\to\infty , and applying
that L_{g_{u}}(t,s;r,r^{\prime}) is uniformly bounded and is equal to 0 unless
r,r^{\prime}\leq t , we get
\displaystyle|(R_{\theta,2}-R_{\theta,1})(t,s)|
\displaystyle=\left|\lim_{N\to\infty}\mathbb{E}J_{g_{1,N}}(t,s)-\mathbb{E}J_{g_{0,N}}(t,s)\right|
\displaystyle\leq C\int_{0}^{t}\int_{0}^{t}|(C_{g,2}-C_{g,1})(r,r^{\prime})|\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}r^{\prime}.
Then, for constants C,C^{\prime}>0 depending on T but not \lambda ,
\displaystyle d_{\lambda}(R_{\theta,1},R_{\theta,2})
\displaystyle=\sup_{0\leq s\leq t\leq T}e^{-\lambda t}|R_{\theta,1}(t,s)-R_{\theta,2}(t,s)|
\displaystyle\leq C\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\int_{0}^{t}\int_{0}^{t}e^{-\lambda t+\lambda(r\vee r^{\prime})}e^{-\lambda(r\vee r^{\prime})}|C_{g,2}(r,r^{\prime})-C_{g,1}(r,r^{\prime})|\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}r^{\prime}
\displaystyle\leq C\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\left(\int_{0}^{t}\int_{0}^{t}e^{-2\lambda t+2\lambda(r\vee r^{\prime})}\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}r^{\prime}\right)^{1/2}d_{\lambda}(C_{g,1},C_{g,2})\leq\frac{C^{\prime}}{\sqrt{\lambda}}d_{\lambda}(C_{g,1},C_{g,2}).
Combining these bounds for C_{\theta} and R_{\theta} ,
for any \alpha\in(0,1) and all large enough \lambda>0 ,
(3.22)
d_{\lambda}(Y_{1},Y_{2})\leq\alpha\cdot d_{\lambda}(C_{g,1},C_{g,2})
The lemma then follows from applying (3.18) to bound
d_{\lambda}(\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}(C_{g,1},R_{g,1}),\allowbreak\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}(C_{g,1},R_{g,2})) , and then
(3.22) to bound
d_{\lambda}(\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}(C_{g,1},R_{g,2}),\allowbreak\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}(C_{g,2},R_{g,2})) .
∎
Lemma 3.4 (Lipschitz continuity of \mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g} ).
Let Y_{i}=(C_{\theta,i},R_{\theta,i})\in\mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{+}(T,D) for i=1,2 , and
let X_{i}=(C_{g,i},R_{g,i})=\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}(Y_{i}) . Then there exists a constant
C>0 not depending on \lambda such that for all sufficiently large
\lambda>0 ,
d_{\lambda}(X_{1},X_{2})\leq C\cdot d_{\lambda}(Y_{1},Y_{2}).
Proof.
We have
\displaystyle C_{g,1}(t,s)-C_{g,2}(t,s)
\displaystyle=\sum_{p,q\geq 0}\kappa_{p+q+2}\bigl(R_{\theta,1}^{\ast p}\ast(C_{\theta,1}-C_{\theta,2})\ast\bar{R}_{\theta,1}^{\ast q}\bigr)(t,s)
\displaystyle+\sum_{p,q\geq 0}\kappa_{p+q+2}\bigl[\bigl(R_{\theta,1}^{\ast p}\ast C_{\theta,2}\ast\bar{R}_{\theta,1}^{\ast q}\bigr)(t,s)-\bigl(R_{\theta,2}^{\ast p}\ast C_{\theta,2}\ast\bar{R}_{\theta,2}^{\ast q}\bigr)(t,s)\bigr].
Consequently,
d_{\lambda}(C_{g,1},C_{g,2})\leq I_{C}+I_{R},
where
\displaystyle I_{C}
\displaystyle:=\sum_{p,q\geq 0}|\kappa_{p+q+2}|\cdot\big\|R_{\theta,1}^{\ast p}\ast(C_{\theta,1}-C_{\theta,2})\ast\bar{R}_{\theta,1}^{\ast q}\big\|_{\lambda},
\displaystyle I_{R}
\displaystyle:=\sum_{p,q\geq 0}|\kappa_{p+q+2}|\cdot\big\|\bigl(R_{\theta,1}^{\ast p}\ast C_{\theta,2}\ast\bar{R}_{\theta,1}^{\ast q}\bigr)(t,s)-\bigl(R_{\theta,2}^{\ast p}\ast C_{\theta,2}\ast\bar{R}_{\theta,2}^{\ast q}\bigr)\big\|_{\lambda}.
We first bound I_{C} . Note that
|R_{\theta,1}(t,s)|\leq\Phi_{R_{\theta}}(t-s) for all 0\leq s\leq t\leq T , and
\|\Phi_{R_{\theta}}^{\ast p}\|_{L^{1}([0,T])}\leq\frac{(\Phi_{R_{\theta}}(T)T)^{p}}{p!}.
For p,q\geq 1 ,
\displaystyle\big\|R_{\theta,1}^{\ast p}\ast(C_{\theta,1}-C_{\theta,2})\ast\bar{R}_{\theta,1}^{\ast q}\big\|_{\lambda}^{2}
\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{T}\int_{0}^{T}e^{-2\lambda(t\vee s)}\left(\int_{0}^{t}\mathrm{d}t^{\prime}\int_{0}^{s}\mathrm{d}s^{\prime}R_{\theta,1}^{*p}(t,t^{\prime})(C_{\theta,1}-C_{\theta,2})(t^{\prime},s^{\prime})R_{\theta,1}^{*q}(s,s^{\prime})\right)^{2}\mathrm{d}t\,\mathrm{d}s
\displaystyle\leq C\int_{0}^{T}\int_{0}^{T}e^{-2\lambda(t\vee s)}\int_{0}^{t}\mathrm{d}t^{\prime}\int_{0}^{s}\mathrm{d}s^{\prime}R_{\theta,1}^{*p}(t,t^{\prime})^{2}(C_{\theta,1}-C_{\theta,2})(t^{\prime},s^{\prime})^{2}R_{\theta,1}^{*q}(s,s^{\prime})^{2}\mathrm{d}t\,\mathrm{d}s
