\displaystyle\leq C\int_{0}^{T}\mathrm{d}t^{\prime}\int_{0}^{T}\mathrm{d}s^{\prime}e^{-2\lambda(t^{\prime}\vee s^{\prime})}(C_{\theta,1}-C_{\theta,2})(t^{\prime},s^{\prime})^{2}\int_{t^{\prime}}^{T}\mathrm{d}t\int_{s^{\prime}}^{T}\mathrm{d}sR_{\theta,1}^{*p}(t,t^{\prime})^{2}R_{\theta,1}^{*q}(s,s^{\prime})^{2}
\displaystyle\leq C^{\prime}\|C_{\theta,1}-C_{\theta,2}\|_{\lambda}^{2}\|\Phi_{R_{\theta}}^{*p}\|_{L^{1}([0,T])}^{2}\|\Phi_{R_{\theta}}^{*q}\|_{L^{1}([0,T])}^{2},
where C,C^{\prime}>0 are T -dependent constants independent of p,q . The same bound holds for p=0 and/or q=0 . Thus
\displaystyle I_{C}
\displaystyle\leq C\sum_{p,q\geq 0}|\kappa_{p+q+2}|\frac{(\Phi_{R_{\theta}}(T)T)^{p}}{p!}\frac{(\Phi_{R_{\theta}}(T)T)^{q}}{q!}\|C_{\theta,1}-C_{\theta,2}\|_{\lambda}\leq C^{\prime}d_{\lambda}(C_{\theta,1},C_{\theta,2})
for constant C,C^{\prime}>0 not depending on \lambda .
We now bound I_{R} . First,
we have |C_{\theta,2}(t,s)|\leq C_{\theta,2}(t,t)^{1/2}C_{\theta,2}(s,s)^{1/2}\leq\Phi_{C_{\theta}}(T) .
Next, for the product of response kernels, writing t_{0}=t and s_{0}=s ,
\displaystyle\left|\prod_{a=0}^{p-1}R_{\theta,1}(t_{a},t_{a+1})\prod_{b=0}^{q-1}R_{\theta,1}(s_{b},s_{b+1})-\prod_{a=0}^{p-1}R_{\theta,2}(t_{a},t_{a+1})\prod_{b=0}^{q-1}R_{\theta,2}(s_{b},s_{b+1})\right|
\displaystyle\leq e^{\lambda(t\vee s)}\left(\sup_{0\leq r\leq q\leq T}e^{-\lambda q}|R_{\theta,1}(q,r)-R_{\theta,2}(q,r)|\right)\sum_{\ell=1}^{p+q}\prod_{m\neq\ell}\Phi_{R_{\theta}}(\xi_{m}),
where \{\xi_{m}\}_{m=1}^{p+q} denotes the collection of increments
t_{0}-t_{1},\allowbreak\ldots,\allowbreak t_{p-1}-t_{p},\allowbreak s_{0}-s_{1},\allowbreak\ldots,\allowbreak s_{q-1}-s_{q} .
(The empty product is interpreted as 1 .)
Hence, integrating over t_{1},\ldots,t_{p} and s_{1},\ldots,s_{q} ,
I_{R}\leq Cd_{\lambda}(R_{\theta,1},R_{\theta,2})\int_{0}^{T}\int_{0}^{T}\sum_{p,q\geq 0}|\kappa_{p+q+2}|(p+q)\Phi_{R_{\theta}}(T)^{p+q-1}\frac{t^{p}}{p!}\frac{s^{q}}{q!}\,\mathrm{d}t\mathrm{d}s.
This shows
I_{R}\leq Cd_{\lambda}(R_{\theta,1},R_{\theta,2}) for a constant C>0 not
depending on \lambda . Therefore,
\displaystyle d_{\lambda}(C_{g,1},C_{g,2})\leq Cd_{\lambda}(Y_{1},Y_{2}).
By (2.7) and a similar argument omitted for brevity,
d_{\lambda}(R_{g,1},R_{g,2})\leq Cd_{\lambda}(R_{\theta,1},R_{\theta,2}) .
Thus
d_{\lambda}(X_{1},X_{2})\leq Cd_{\lambda}(Y_{1},Y_{2}) .
∎
Fixing T>0 , define the projection
\mathcal{P}_{D}:\mathcal{S}_{g}(T,D)\to\mathcal{S}_{g}^{+}(T,D),\qquad(C_{g},R_{g})\mapsto(C_{g}^{+},R_{g})
that preserves R_{g} and projects C_{g} onto the subset \mathcal{S}_{g}^{+}(T,D) of the positive-semidefinite cone
(3.23)
C_{g}^{+}=\operatorname{arg\,min}_{C\in\mathcal{S}_{g}^{+}(T,D)}\|C-C_{g}\|_{\lambda}
in the weighted L^{2} -metric d_{\lambda} . We note that if (C_{g}^{(m)},R_{g}^{(m)})\in\mathcal{S}_{g}^{+}(T,D)
for m=1,2,\ldots is a Cauchy sequence under d_{\lambda} ,
then by completeness of the weighted L^{\infty} -metric
d_{\lambda}(R_{g,1},R_{g,2}) , there exists R_{g}:[0,T]\times[0,T]\to\mathbb{R} for
which
(3.24)
\lim_{m\to\infty}\sup_{s,t\in[0,T]}|R_{g}^{(m)}(t,s)-R_{g}(t,s)|=0.
By completeness of the weighted L^{2} -metric d_{\lambda}(C_{g,1},C_{g,2}) ,
there also exists C_{g}:[0,T]\times[0,T]\to\mathbb{R} for which
\|C_{g}\|_{\lambda}<\infty
and \lim_{m\to\infty}d_{\lambda}(C_{g}^{(m)},C_{g})=0 .
Then the continuity condition (3.8) for each kernel C_{g}^{(m)}
implies there exists
a modification \tilde{C}_{g}:[0,T]\times[0,T]\to\mathbb{R} of C_{g} (equal to C_{g}
Lebesgue-a.e.) for which
(3.25)
\lim_{m\to\infty}\sup_{s,t\in[0,T]}|C_{g}^{(m)}(t,s)-\tilde{C}_{g}(t,s)|=0.
The statements (3.24) and (3.25) imply that R_{g} and \tilde{C}_{g} satisfy all conditions of
\mathcal{S}_{g}^{+}(T,D) , so (\tilde{C}_{g},R_{g})\in\mathcal{S}_{g}^{+}(T,D) ,
and d_{\lambda}((C_{g}^{(m)},R_{g}^{(m)}),(\tilde{C}_{g},R_{g}))\to 0 .
Then \mathcal{S}_{g}^{+}(T,D) is a
closed, convex subset of \mathcal{S}_{g}(T,D) under d_{\lambda} , so the
projection (3.23) is well-defined. Furthermore, by the
non-expansive property of projections in a Hilbert space,
(3.26)
d_{\lambda}(C_{g,1}^{+},C_{g,2}^{+})\leq d_{\lambda}(C_{g,1},C_{g,2}).
Lemma 3.2 then implies that
\mathcal{T}_{g\to g}^{D}:=\mathcal{P}_{D}\circ\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}\circ\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}
is a well-defined mapping from \mathcal{S}_{g}^{+}(T,D) to itself. The following corollary
collects the preceding results to show that this mapping is contractive in
d_{\lambda} and has a unique fixed point in \mathcal{S}_{g}^{+}(T,D) .
Corollary 3.5.
Fix any T>0 and finite subset D\subset[0,T] . Then
\mathcal{T}_{g\to g}^{D}:=\mathcal{P}_{D}\circ\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}\circ\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}
has a unique fixed point in \mathcal{S}_{g}^{+}(T,D) .
Proof.
The preceding argument verifies that
\mathcal{S}_{g}^{+}(T,D) is complete under the metric d_{\lambda} . Lemmas
3.3 and 3.4, together with
(3.26), show that
\mathcal{T}_{g\to g}^{D} is a contraction on \mathcal{S}_{g}^{+}(T,D) with respect to d_{\lambda} ,
for any sufficiently large \lambda>0 . Thus it has a unique fixed point by the
Banach fixed point theorem.
∎
3.3. Discrete-time dynamical mean-field limit
We next prove a dynamical mean-field limit for a discretized version of the
dynamics, and identify continuous-time embeddings of its correlation and response
kernels as fixed points of a discretized version of the preceding mappings.
Fix a discretization step size \eta>0 . Given \mathbf{X} , \boldsymbol{\theta}^{0} , and the
Brownian motion \{\mathbf{b}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} defining (2.1),
set \mathbf{b}_{\eta}^{k}=\mathbf{b}^{k\eta} and define the discretized dynamics
(3.27)
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{k+1}_{\eta}-\boldsymbol{\theta}^{k}_{\eta}=\eta[f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{k}_{\eta})+\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{k}_{\eta}]+\sqrt{2\gamma}(\mathbf{b}^{k+1}_{\eta}-\mathbf{b}^{k}_{\eta}),\qquad\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\eta}^{0}=\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0}.
For its mean-field limit, let \theta^{0} and \{b^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} be as in
Definition 2.3, and set
\theta_{\eta}^{0}=\theta^{0},\qquad b_{\eta}^{k}=b^{k\eta}.
Given the processes \{\theta_{\eta}^{i}\}_{0\leq i\leq k}
and \{\frac{\partial\theta_{\eta}^{i}}{\partial g_{\eta}^{j}}\}_{0\leq j<i\leq k}
up to step k , define correlation and response matrices
\mathbf{C}_{\theta},\mathbf{R}_{\theta},\mathbf{C}_{g},\mathbf{R}_{g}\in\mathbb{R}^{(k+1)\times(k+1)} by
(3.28)
\begin{gathered}\mathbf{C}_{\theta}=\Big(\mathbb{E}[\theta^{i}_{\eta}\theta^{j}_{\eta}]\Big)_{0\leq i,j\leq k},\qquad\mathbf{R}_{\theta}=\Big(\mathbf{1}_{i>j}\mathbb{E}\Big[\frac{\partial\theta^{i}_{\eta}}{\partial g^{j}_{\eta}}\Big]\Big)_{0\leq i,j\leq k},\\
\mathbf{C}_{g}=\sum_{p,q\geq 0}\kappa_{p+q+2}\mathbf{R}_{\theta}^{p}\mathbf{C}_{\theta}\mathbf{R}_{\theta}^{q\top},\qquad\mathbf{R}_{g}=\sum_{p\geq 1}\kappa_{p+1}\mathbf{R}_{\theta}^{p}.\end{gathered}
Here, the matrices \mathbf{R}_{\theta},\mathbf{R}_{g} are strictly lower-triangular.
We will verify in Theorem 3.6 below that
\mathbf{C}_{g} is positive-semidefinite. Then, letting
(3.29)
(g^{0}_{\eta},\ldots,g^{k}_{\eta})\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{C}_{g})
be independent of \theta^{0} and \{b^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} , and writing
\mathbf{R}_{g}=(r_{ij})_{0\leq i,j\leq k} for the entries of \mathbf{R}_{g} , define
the processes up to step k+1 by
(3.30)
\displaystyle\theta^{k+1}_{\eta}
\displaystyle=\theta^{k}_{\eta}+\eta\Big[f(\theta^{k}_{\eta})+\sum_{q=0}^{k}r_{kq}\theta^{q}_{\eta}+g^{k}_{\eta}\Big]+\sqrt{2\gamma}(b^{k+1}_{\eta}-b^{k}_{\eta}),
(3.31)
\displaystyle\frac{\partial\theta^{k+1}_{\eta}}{\partial g^{j}_{\eta}}
\displaystyle=\frac{\partial\theta^{k}_{\eta}}{\partial g^{j}_{\eta}}+\eta\Big[f^{\prime}(\theta^{k}_{\eta})\frac{\partial\theta^{k}_{\eta}}{\partial g^{j}_{\eta}}+\sum_{q=j+1}^{k}r_{kq}\frac{\partial\theta^{q}_{\eta}}{\partial g^{j}_{\eta}}\Big]\text{ for }0\leq j<k,\qquad\frac{\partial\theta^{k+1}_{\eta}}{\partial g^{k}_{\eta}}=\eta.
These definitions (3.28–3.31)
are understood iteratively in time for k=0,1,2,\ldots , and
(3.31) is the usual derivative
of (3.30) in g_{\eta}^{j} (by the chain rule).
Note that \mathbf{C}_{\theta},\mathbf{R}_{\theta},\mathbf{C}_{g},\mathbf{R}_{g} up to each step k\geq 0
are the upper-left corners of those up to step k+1 ; thus we may write
unambiguously (\mathbf{C}_{\theta})_{ij},(\mathbf{R}_{\theta})_{ij} etc. for their entries.
We denote also
(3.32)
\mathbf{g}^{k}_{\eta}=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{k}_{\eta}-\sum_{q=0}^{k}r_{kq}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{q}_{\eta}.
Theorem 3.6.
The matrix \mathbf{C}_{g} is positive-semidefinite.
For any fixed integer K\geq 0 , almost surely as n\to\infty ,
(3.33)
\displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\delta_{(\theta^{0}_{\eta,i},\ldots,\theta^{K}_{\eta,i},g^{0}_{\eta,i},\ldots,g^{K}_{\eta,i},b^{0}_{\eta,i},\ldots,b^{K}_{\eta,i})}\to\operatorname{Law}(\theta^{0}_{\eta},\ldots,\theta^{K}_{\eta},g^{0}_{\eta},\ldots,g^{K}_{\eta},b^{0}_{\eta},\ldots,b^{K}_{\eta})
weakly and in Wasserstein-2, where the right side denotes the joint law under
(3.29–3.30). Furthermore,
for any fixed 0\leq j\leq k , almost surely
(3.34)
\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\eta}^{k\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\eta}^{j}\rangle\to(\mathbf{C}_{\theta})_{k,j},\quad\frac{1}{n}\langle\mathbf{g}_{\eta}^{k\top}\mathbf{g}_{\eta}^{j}\rangle\to(\mathbf{C}_{g})_{k,j},\quad\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\eta}^{k\top}\mathbf{b}_{\eta}^{j}\rangle\to\sqrt{2\gamma}\sum_{q=0}^{j-1}(\mathbf{R}_{\theta})_{k,q}.
Proof.
Set \mathbf{v}^{0}=\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0} and \mathbf{v}^{k}=\boldsymbol{\theta}^{k}_{\eta}-\boldsymbol{\theta}^{k-1}_{\eta} , so that
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{k}_{\eta}=\mathbf{v}^{0}+\ldots+\mathbf{v}^{k} .
It is readily checked that for any deterministic scalar
values \{a_{jk}\}_{0\leq j\leq k} ,
the dynamics (3.27) may be equivalently written as
(3.35)
\displaystyle\mathbf{z}^{k}
\displaystyle=\mathbf{X}\mathbf{v}^{k}-\sum_{j=0}^{k}a_{jk}\mathbf{v}^{j},
\displaystyle\mathbf{v}^{k+1}
\displaystyle=\underbrace{\eta\left[f\Big(\sum_{j=0}^{k}\mathbf{v}^{j}\Big)+\sum_{j=0}^{k}\Big(\sum_{i=0}^{j}a_{ij}\mathbf{v}^{i}+\mathbf{z}^{j}\Big)\right]+\sqrt{2\gamma}(\mathbf{b}_{\eta}^{k+1}-\mathbf{b}_{\eta}^{k})}_{:=v_{k+1}(\mathbf{z}^{0},\ldots,\mathbf{z}^{k},\mathbf{v}^{0},\mathbf{b}_{\eta}^{1},\ldots,\mathbf{b}_{\eta}^{k+1})},
where v_{k+1}:\mathbb{R}^{2k+3}\to\mathbb{R} is a scalar function defined recursively for
k=0,1,2,\ldots so that
\mathbf{v}^{k+1}=v_{k+1}(\mathbf{z}^{0},\ldots,\mathbf{z}^{k},\mathbf{v}^{0},\mathbf{b}_{\eta}^{1},\ldots,\mathbf{b}_{\eta}^{k+1}) holds.
Since f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} is Lipschitz and continuously-differentiable,
each function v_{k+1} is also Lipschitz and continuously-differentiable
in all arguments.
We define iteratively in time a corresponding AMP state evolution:
Let v^{0}=\theta^{0} . Given the law of Gaussian variables (z^{0},\ldots,z^{k-1})
independent of \theta^{0} and \{b^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} , define
\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\Phi}
\displaystyle=\Big(\mathbf{1}_{i<j}\mathbb{E}\Big[\frac{\partial}{\partial z^{i}}v_{j}(z^{0},\ldots,z^{j-1},v^{0},b_{\eta}^{1},\ldots,b_{\eta}^{j})\Big]\Big)_{0\leq i,j\leq k},
\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\Delta}
\displaystyle=\Big(\mathbb{E}[v_{i}(z^{0},\ldots,z^{i-1},v^{0},b_{\eta}^{1},\ldots,b_{\eta}^{i})v_{j}(z^{0},\ldots,z^{j-1},v^{0},b_{\eta}^{1},\ldots,b_{\eta}^{j})]\Big)_{0\leq i,j\leq k}
where v_{i}(z^{0},\ldots,z^{i-1},v^{0},b_{\eta}^{1},\ldots,b_{\eta}^{i})\equiv v^{0} for
i=0 . Then define the AMP Onsager matrix and state evolution covariance by
\mathbf{A}=\sum_{p\geq 1}\kappa_{p+1}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{p},\qquad\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\sum_{p,q\geq 0}\kappa_{p+q+2}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{p\top}\boldsymbol{\Delta}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^{q},
let (z^{0},\ldots,z^{k})\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) (independent of \theta^{0} and
\{b^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} ), and let
(3.36)
v^{k}=v_{k}(z^{0},\ldots,z^{k-1},v^{0},b_{\eta}^{1},\ldots,b_{\eta}^{k}).
Note that \mathbf{A} is strictly upper-triangular, and the matrices
\boldsymbol{\Phi},\boldsymbol{\Delta},\mathbf{A},\boldsymbol{\Sigma} up to step k are the upper-left corners of those up
to step k+1 .
Writing \mathbf{A}=(a_{ij})_{0\leq i,j\leq k} and choosing the
coefficients a_{ij} in (3.35) to be the entries of \mathbf{A} ,
[35, Theorem 4.3] then implies that \boldsymbol{\Sigma}
above is positive-semidefinite (hence the above law of (z^{0},\ldots,z^{k})
is well-defined), and for any fixed K , almost surely in Wasserstein-2,
(3.37)
\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\delta_{(v_{i}^{0},\ldots,v_{i}^{K},z_{i}^{0},\ldots,z_{i}^{K},b_{\eta,i}^{0},\ldots,b_{\eta,i}^{K})}\to\operatorname{Law}\left(v^{0},\ldots,v^{K},z^{0},\ldots,z^{K},b_{\eta}^{0},\ldots,b_{\eta}^{K}\right).
To check that this implies (3.33),
recall \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\eta}^{k}=\mathbf{v}^{0}+\ldots+\mathbf{v}^{k} , define
\mathbf{g}_{\eta}^{k}=\mathbf{z}^{0}+\ldots+\mathbf{z}^{k} , and define also
from the above AMP state evolution variables
\displaystyle\theta^{j}_{\eta}:=v^{0}+\ldots+v^{j},\qquad g^{j}_{\eta}:=z^{0}+\cdots+z^{j}.
Denote the upper-triangular
matrix \mathbf{E}=(\mathbf{1}_{i\leq j})_{0\leq i,j\leq k} . Comparing the above definitions
of \boldsymbol{\Phi},\boldsymbol{\Delta},\mathbf{A},\boldsymbol{\Sigma} with the
definitions (3.28), we then have
\mathbf{R}_{\theta}^{\top}=\mathbf{E}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\mathbf{E},\qquad\mathbf{C}_{\theta}=\mathbf{E}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Delta}\mathbf{E},\qquad\mathbf{R}_{g}^{\top}=\mathbf{E}^{-1}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{E},\qquad\mathbf{C}_{g}=\mathbf{E}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{E}
and (g_{\eta}^{0},\ldots,g_{\eta}^{k})\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{C}_{g}) . In particular, \mathbf{C}_{g} is
positive-semidefinite as claimed. Noting that \mathbf{A}\mathbf{E}=\mathbf{E}\mathbf{R}_{g}^{\top}
and writing \mathbf{R}_{g}=(r_{ij})_{0\leq i,j\leq k} ,
the recursions for \mathbf{z}^{k} and \mathbf{v}^{k+1} in (3.35) then imply
\displaystyle\mathbf{g}_{\eta}^{k}
\displaystyle=\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{v}^{0}+\ldots+\mathbf{v}^{k})-\sum_{j=0}^{k}r_{kj}(\mathbf{v}^{0}+\ldots+\mathbf{v}^{j})=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\eta}^{k}-\sum_{j=0}^{k}r_{kj}\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\eta}^{j},
\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\eta}^{k+1}-\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\eta}^{k}=\mathbf{v}^{k+1}
\displaystyle=\eta\Big[f(\mathbf{v}^{0}+\cdots+\mathbf{v}^{k})+\sum_{j=0}^{k}r_{kj}(\mathbf{v}^{0}+\cdots+\mathbf{v}^{j})+\mathbf{g}_{\eta}^{k}\Big]+\sqrt{2\gamma}(\mathbf{b}_{\eta}^{k+1}-\mathbf{b}_{\eta}^{k})
\displaystyle=\eta\Big[f(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\eta}^{k})+\sum_{j=0}^{k}r_{kj}\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\eta}^{j}+\mathbf{g}_{\eta}^{k}\Big]+\sqrt{2\gamma}(\mathbf{b}_{\eta}^{k+1}-\mathbf{b}_{\eta}^{k}).
Thus \mathbf{g}_{\eta}^{k} coincides with the definition (3.32), and we
have analogously from the definition of v^{k+1} in (3.36) that
\displaystyle\theta_{\eta}^{k+1}-\theta_{\eta}^{k}=v^{k+1}=\eta\Bigg[f(\theta_{\eta}^{k})+\sum_{j=0}^{k}r_{kj}\theta_{\eta}^{j}+g_{\eta}^{k}\Bigg]+\sqrt{2\gamma}(b_{\eta}^{k+1}-b_{\eta}^{k}),
coinciding with (3.30). Thus
\{\theta_{\eta}^{k},g_{\eta}^{k},b_{\eta}^{k}\}_{k\geq 0} have the same joint law as defined in
(3.29–3.30), and the Wasserstein-2
convergence (3.37) implies (3.33) as desired.
The first two statements of (3.34) follow
immediately from (3.33) and dominated convergence to take
the expectation over \{\mathbf{b}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} . Also from (3.33) and
dominated convergence, for any j\leq k ,
\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\eta}^{k\top}\mathbf{b}_{\eta}^{j}\rangle\to\mathbb{E}[\theta^{k}_{\eta}b^{j}_{\eta}].
Denoting w^{q}=b_{\eta}^{q+1}-b_{\eta}^{q}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\eta) ,
Gaussian integration-by-parts gives
\mathbb{E}[\theta^{k}_{\eta}(b^{q+1}_{\eta}-b^{q}_{\eta})]=\mathbb{E}[\theta^{k}_{\eta}w^{q}]=\eta\,\mathbb{E}\Big[\frac{\partial\theta^{k}_{\eta}}{\partial w^{q}}\Big]=\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\mathbb{E}\Big[\frac{\partial\theta^{k}_{\eta}}{\partial g^{q}_{\eta}}\Big]
where the last step holds by the form of the equation (3.30).
Noting that \mathbb{E}[\theta_{\eta}^{k}b_{\eta}^{0}]=0 and summing over q=0,\ldots,j-1
shows the last statement of (3.34).
∎
We next identify piecewise-constant continuous-time embeddings of the
discrete-time mean-field limit as fixed points of a discretized system of
mappings. Still fixing the discretization step size \eta>0 ,
for t\geq 0 , define
\displaystyle\lfloor t\rfloor=\max\{k\eta:k\in\mathbb{Z},\ k\eta\leq t\},\qquad\lceil t\rceil=\lfloor t\rfloor+\eta,\qquad[t]=\lfloor t\rfloor/\eta\in\mathbb{Z}.
We use the convention that \int_{s}^{t}f(r)\mathrm{d}r=0 if t<s .
Fixing T>0 , define the discontinuity set
D_{\eta}=[0,T]\cap\eta\mathbb{Z}.
Let \mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{\eta,+}\subset\mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{+}(T,D_{\eta}) and \mathcal{S}_{g}^{\eta}\subset\mathcal{S}_{g}(T,D_{\eta}) be the subsets of the spaces
\mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{+}(T,D_{\eta}) , \mathcal{S}_{g}(T,D_{\eta}) defined in Section 3.1,
for which the kernels have the piecewise-constant structure
(3.38)
C(t,s)=C(\lfloor t\rfloor,\lfloor s\rfloor),\qquad R(t,s)=\mathbf{1}_{t\geq s}\,R(\lfloor t\rfloor,\lfloor s\rfloor)
for (C,R)=(C_{\theta},R_{\theta}) or (C,R)=(C_{g},R_{g}) , respectively. We define a map
(3.39)
\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}^{\eta}:\mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{\eta,+}\to\mathcal{S}_{g}^{\eta},\qquad(C_{\theta},R_{\theta})\mapsto(C_{g},R_{g})
by
\displaystyle R_{g}(t,s)
\displaystyle=\kappa_{2}R_{\theta}(t,s)+\sum_{p\geq 2}\kappa_{p+1}\int_{\lceil s\rceil}^{\lfloor t\rfloor}\mathrm{d}t_{1}\int_{\lceil s\rceil}^{\lfloor t_{1}\rfloor}\mathrm{d}t_{2}\ldots\int_{\lceil s\rceil}^{\lfloor t_{p-2}\rfloor}\mathrm{d}t_{p-1}
\displaystyle\hskip 144.54ptR_{\theta}(t,t_{1})R_{\theta}(t_{1},t_{2})\ldots R_{\theta}(t_{p-1},s),
\displaystyle C_{g}(t,s)
\displaystyle=\sum_{p,q\geq 0}\kappa_{p+q+2}\int_{0}^{\lfloor t\rfloor}\mathrm{d}t_{1}\ldots\int_{0}^{\lfloor t_{p-1}\rfloor}\mathrm{d}t_{p}\int_{0}^{\lfloor s\rfloor}\mathrm{d}s_{1}\ldots\int_{0}^{\lfloor s_{q-1}\rfloor}\mathrm{d}s_{q}
\displaystyle\hskip 144.54ptR_{\theta}(t,t_{1})\ldots R_{\theta}(t_{p-1},t_{p})R_{\theta}(s,s_{1})\ldots R_{\theta}(s_{q-1},s_{q})C_{\theta}(t_{p},s_{q}),
where t_{0}=t and s_{0}=s . Let
\mathcal{S}_{g}^{\eta,+}=\big\{\mathcal{P}_{D_{\eta}}(C_{g},R_{g}):(C_{g},R_{g})\in\mathcal{S}_{g}^{\eta}\big\}\subset\mathcal{S}_{g}^{+}(T,D_{\eta})
be the image of \mathcal{S}_{g}^{\eta} under the preceding projection \mathcal{P}_{D_{\eta}} .
We denote
\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}^{\eta,+}:\mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{\eta,+}\to\mathcal{S}_{g}^{\eta,+},\qquad\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}^{\eta,+}=\mathcal{P}_{D_{\eta}}\circ\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}^{\eta}.
Next, we define a map
(3.40)
\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}^{\eta}:\mathcal{S}_{g}^{\eta,+}\to\mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{\eta,+},\qquad(C_{g},R_{g})\mapsto(C_{\theta},R_{\theta})
by
C_{\theta}(t,s)=\mathbb{E}[\bar{\theta}^{t}\bar{\theta}^{s}],\qquad R_{\theta}(t,s)=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial\bar{\theta}^{t}}{\partial g^{s}}\right]
where \{\bar{\theta}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} and \{\frac{\partial\bar{\theta}^{t}}{\partial g^{s}}\}_{t\geq s\geq 0} solve
(3.41)
\displaystyle\bar{\theta}^{t}
\displaystyle=\bar{\theta}^{0}+\int_{0}^{\lfloor t\rfloor}\bigg[f(\bar{\theta}^{r})+\int_{0}^{\lfloor r\rfloor}R_{g}(r,q)\bar{\theta}^{q}\,\mathrm{d}q+g^{\lfloor r\rfloor}\bigg]\mathrm{d}r+\sqrt{2\gamma}\,b^{\lfloor t\rfloor},\qquad\bar{\theta}^{0}=\theta^{0},
(3.42)
\displaystyle\frac{\partial\bar{\theta}^{t}}{\partial g^{s}}
\displaystyle=1+\int_{\lceil s\rceil}^{\lfloor t\rfloor}\bigg[f^{\prime}(\bar{\theta}^{r})\frac{\partial\bar{\theta}^{r}}{\partial g^{s}}+\int_{\lceil s\rceil}^{\lfloor r\rfloor}R_{g}(r,q)\frac{\partial\bar{\theta}^{q}}{\partial g^{s}}\,\mathrm{d}q\bigg]\mathrm{d}r\text{ for }t\geq s,\quad\frac{\partial\bar{\theta}^{t}}{\partial g^{s}}=0\text{ for }t<s,
and \{g^{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]}\sim\operatorname{GP}(0,C_{g}) in
(3.41) which is independent of \theta^{0} and
\{b^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} .
Lemma 3.7.
For any fixed T>0 and all sufficiently small \eta>0 , the following hold:
(a)
For any (C_{g},R_{g})\in\mathcal{S}_{g}^{\eta,+} , we have \mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}^{\eta}(C_{g},R_{g})\in\mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{\eta,+} .
(b)
For any (C_{\theta},R_{\theta})\in\mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{\eta,+} , we have \mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}^{\eta}(C_{\theta},R_{\theta})\in\mathcal{S}_{g}^{\eta}
and \mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}^{\eta,+}(C_{\theta},R_{\theta})\in\mathcal{S}_{g}^{\eta,+} .
(c)
Let \mathbf{C}_{\theta},\mathbf{R}_{\theta},\mathbf{C}_{g},\mathbf{R}_{g} be the matrices
(3.28) defined up to a step
k>T/\eta , and define their continuous-time embeddings
C_{\theta}^{\eta}(t,s)=(\mathbf{C}_{\theta})_{[t],[s]},\qquad C_{g}^{\eta}(t,s)=(\mathbf{C}_{g})_{[t],[s]},
\displaystyle R_{\theta}^{\eta}(t,s)
\displaystyle=\begin{cases}0&\text{ if }s>t\\
1&\text{ if }s\leq t,\,[s]=[t]\\
\frac{1}{\eta}\,(\mathbf{R}_{\theta})_{[t],[s]}&\text{ if }[s]<[t]\end{cases},
\displaystyle R_{g}^{\eta}(t,s)
\displaystyle=\begin{cases}0&\text{ if }s>t\\
\kappa_{2}&\text{ if }s\leq t,\,[s]=[t]\\
\frac{1}{\eta}\,(\mathbf{R}_{g})_{[t],[s]}&\text{ if }[s]<[t].\end{cases}
Then (C_{g}^{\eta},R_{g}^{\eta})\in\mathcal{S}_{g}^{\eta,+}\cap\mathcal{S}_{g}^{\eta} and
(C_{\theta}^{\eta},R_{\theta}^{\eta})\in\mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{\eta,+} . Furthermore,
\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}^{\eta}(C_{g}^{\eta},R_{g}^{\eta})=(C_{\theta}^{\eta},R_{\theta}^{\eta})
and \mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}^{\eta}(C_{\theta}^{\eta},R_{\theta}^{\eta})=\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}^{\eta,+}(C_{\theta}^{\eta},R_{\theta}^{\eta})=(C_{g}^{\eta},R_{g}^{\eta}) .
Proof.
The proof is similar to [30, Lemma 4.3], so we will omit
some details.
Similar arguments as in Lemma 3.2
show that (C_{g},R_{g})\in\mathcal{S}_{g}^{\eta,+}
implies \mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}^{\eta}(C_{g},R_{g})\in\mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{\eta}(T,D_{\eta}) ,
and (C_{\theta},R_{\theta})\in\mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{\eta,+} implies
\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}^{\eta}(C_{\theta},R_{\theta})\in\mathcal{S}_{g}(T,D_{\eta}) .
An induction in time checks that the processes solving
(3.41)
and (3.42) must satisfy
(3.43)
\theta^{t}=\theta^{\lfloor t\rfloor},\qquad\frac{\partial\theta^{t}}{\partial g^{s}}=\mathbf{1}_{t\geq s}\frac{\partial\theta^{\lfloor t\rfloor}}{\partial g^{\lfloor s\rfloor}}.
Then \mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}^{\eta}(C_{g},R_{g}) satisfies (3.38),
so \mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}^{\eta}(C_{g},R_{g})\in\mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{\eta,+} . If (C_{\theta},R_{\theta})\in\mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{\eta,+}
satisfies (3.38), then the definition of
(3.39) also implies that
\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}^{\eta}(C_{\theta},R_{\theta}) satisfies
(3.38), so
\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}^{\eta}(C_{\theta},R_{\theta})\in\mathcal{S}_{g}^{\eta}
and hence (by definition) \mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}^{\eta,+}(C_{\theta},R_{\theta})\in\mathcal{S}_{g}^{\eta,+} .
Thus parts (a) and (b) hold.
Letting (C_{\theta}^{\eta},R_{\theta}^{\eta},C_{g}^{\eta},R_{g}^{\eta}) be the embeddings of part (c),
an induction in time using the piecewise-constant properties
(3.38) and
(3.43) also checks that
\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}^{\eta}(C_{g}^{\eta},R_{g}^{\eta})=(C_{\theta}^{\eta},R_{\theta}^{\eta})
and \mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}^{\eta}(C_{\theta}^{\eta},R_{\theta}^{\eta})=(C_{g}^{\eta},R_{g}^{\eta}) .
Theorem 3.6 shows that \mathbf{C}_{g} is
positive-semidefinite; hence C_{g}^{\eta} is also a
positive-semidefinite kernel on [0,T]\times[0,T] , so
\mathcal{P}_{D_{\eta}}(C_{g}^{\eta})=C_{g}^{\eta} . Then also
\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}^{\eta,+}(C_{\theta}^{\eta},R_{\theta}^{\eta})=(C_{g}^{\eta},R_{g}^{\eta}) .
Finally, similar arguments as in Lemmas 3.3
and 3.4 show that
\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}^{\eta}\circ\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}^{\eta,+}:\mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{\eta,+}\to\mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{\eta,+} is contractive in
the metric d_{\lambda} for all sufficiently large \lambda . Then, since
\mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{\eta,+} is also closed under d_{\lambda} ,
this map has a unique fixed point (\bar{C}_{\theta}^{\eta},\bar{R}_{\theta}^{\eta})\in\mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{\eta,+} . Letting (\bar{C}_{g}^{\eta},\bar{R}_{g}^{\eta})=\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}^{\eta,+}(\bar{C}_{\theta}^{\eta},\bar{R}_{\theta}^{\eta})\in\mathcal{S}_{g}^{\eta,+} , an induction in time using (3.39) and
(3.40) shows that we must have
(\bar{C}_{\theta}^{\eta},\bar{R}_{\theta}^{\eta})=(C_{\theta}^{\eta},R_{\theta}^{\eta})
and (\bar{C}_{g}^{\eta},\bar{R}_{g}^{\eta})=(C_{g}^{\eta},R_{g}^{\eta}) . Thus
(C_{\theta}^{\eta},R_{\theta}^{\eta})\in\mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{\eta,+} and
(C_{g}^{\eta},R_{g}^{\eta})\in\mathcal{S}_{g}^{\eta,+}\cap\mathcal{S}_{g}^{\eta} ,
showing part (c).
∎
3.4. Proof of Theorem 2.4
We proceed to show Theorem 2.4. The following lemma bounding
the difference between the continuous-time and discretized mappings will be
used to show part (a).
Lemma 3.8.
There exists a constant C>0 depending on T but not on \lambda,\eta
such that for all sufficiently large \lambda>0 and
sufficiently small \eta>0 ,
(a)
For any (C_{g},R_{g})\in\mathcal{S}_{g}^{\eta,+} ,
d_{\lambda}\big(\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}(C_{g},R_{g}),\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}^{\eta}(C_{g},R_{g})\big)\leq C\sqrt{\eta}.
(b)
For any (C_{\theta},R_{\theta})\in\mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{\eta,+} ,
d_{\lambda}\big(\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}(C_{\theta},R_{\theta}),\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}^{\eta}(C_{\theta},R_{\theta})\big)\leq C\eta.
Proof.
Given (C_{g},\allowbreak R_{g})\in\mathcal{S}_{g}^{\eta,+} , let
(C_{\theta},\allowbreak R_{\theta})=\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}(C_{g},R_{g}) and (\bar{C}_{\theta},\bar{R}_{\theta})=\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}^{\eta}(C_{g},R_{g}) .
By arguments similar to [30, Lemma 4.4], there exists a
coupling of (\{\theta^{t}\}_{t\geq 0},\allowbreak\{\frac{\partial\theta^{t}}{\partial g^{s}}\}_{t\geq s\geq 0}) solving (2.2–2.3)
and (\{\bar{\theta}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0},\allowbreak\{\frac{\partial\bar{\theta}^{t}}{\partial g^{s}}\}_{t\geq s\geq 0}) solving
(3.41–3.42)
for which, for all large \lambda>0 and small \eta>0 ,
\sup_{t\in[0,T]}e^{-\lambda t}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}(\theta^{t}-\bar{\theta}^{t})^{2}}\leq C\sqrt{\eta},\qquad\sup_{0\leq s\leq t\leq T}e^{-\lambda t}\mathbb{E}\left|\frac{\partial\theta^{t}}{\partial g^{s}}-\frac{\partial\bar{\theta}^{t}}{\partial g^{s}}\right|\leq C\sqrt{\eta}.
The second inequality implies d_{\lambda}(R_{\theta},\bar{R}_{\theta})\leq C\sqrt{\eta} , while the first inequality and \mathbb{E}(\theta^{t})^{2}\leq\Phi_{C_{\theta}}(T)
imply
\displaystyle\sup_{s,t\in[0,T]}e^{-\lambda(s\vee t)}|C_{\theta}(s,t)-\bar{C}_{\theta}(s,t)|=\sup_{s,t\in[0,T]}e^{-\lambda(s\vee t)}|\mathbb{E}(\theta^{s}\theta^{t})-\mathbb{E}(\bar{\theta}^{s}\bar{\theta}^{t})|
\displaystyle\leq\sup_{s,t\in[0,T]}e^{-\lambda s}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}(\theta^{s}-\bar{\theta}^{s})^{2}}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}(\theta^{t})^{2}}+e^{-\lambda t}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}(\theta^{t}-\bar{\theta}^{t})^{2}}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}(\bar{\theta}^{s})^{2}}\leq C^{\prime}\sqrt{\eta}.
Thus part (a) follows.
For part (b), given (C_{\theta},R_{\theta})\in\mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{\eta,+} , let
(C_{g},R_{g})=\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}(C_{\theta},R_{\theta})
and (\bar{C}_{g},\bar{R}_{g})=\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}^{\eta}(C_{\theta},R_{\theta}) . According
to (2.7) and (3.39), we know that
R_{g}-\bar{R}_{g}=\sum_{p\geq 2}\kappa_{p+1}\Big[R_{\theta}^{\ast p}-R_{\theta}^{\lfloor\ast\rfloor p}\Big]
where, denoting t=s_{0} and s=s_{p} , we have
\displaystyle R^{\ast p}(t,s)
\displaystyle=\int_{D_{p}(t,s)}\prod_{a=0}^{p-1}R(s_{a},s_{a+1})\,\mathrm{d}s_{1}\cdots\mathrm{d}s_{p-1},
\displaystyle\hskip 72.26999ptD_{p}(t,s)=\left\{(s_{1},\ldots,s_{p-1}):s\leq s_{p-1}\leq\cdots\leq s_{1}\leq t\right\},
\displaystyle R^{\lfloor\ast\rfloor p}(t,s)
\displaystyle=\int_{D_{p,\eta}(t,s)}\prod_{a=0}^{p-1}R(s_{a},s_{a+1})\,\mathrm{d}s_{1}\cdots\mathrm{d}s_{p-1},\hskip 21.68121ptD_{p,\eta}(t,s)=\left\{\begin{aligned} &(s_{1},\ldots,s_{p-1}):s_{a+1}\leq\lfloor s_{a}\rfloor\\
&\text{ for }a=0,\ldots,p-1\end{aligned}\right\}.
Since D_{p,\eta}(t,s)\subseteq D_{p}(t,s) and
|R_{\theta}(t,s)|\leq\Phi_{R_{\theta}}(T) , we have the entrywise bound
\left|R_{\theta}^{\ast p}(t,s)-R_{\theta}^{\lfloor\ast\rfloor p}(t,s)\right|\leq\Phi_{R_{\theta}}(T)^{p}\,\left|D_{p}(t,s)\setminus D_{p,\eta}(t,s)\right|.
If a point belongs to D_{p}(t,s)\setminus D_{p,\eta}(t,s) , then for at least one a\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\} ,
s_{a+1}>\lfloor s_{a}\rfloor ,
and therefore
0\leq s_{a}-s_{a+1}<\eta .
Using a union bound over the p possible gaps gives
\left|D_{p}(t,s)\setminus D_{p,\eta}(t,s)\right|\leq\frac{p(t-s)^{p-2}\eta}{(p-2)!}.
Therefore,
\displaystyle d_{\lambda}(R_{g},\bar{R}_{g})\leq\sup_{0\leq s\leq t\leq T}|R_{g}(t,s)-\bar{R}_{g}(t,s)|\leq\sum_{p\geq 2}|\kappa_{p+1}|\frac{p\Phi_{R_{\theta}}(T)^{p}T^{p-2}}{(p-2)!}\eta\leq C\eta.
A similar argument shows d_{\lambda}(C_{g},\bar{C}_{g})\leq C\eta .
∎
Proof of Theorem 2.4(a).
Fix any \eta>0 small enough.
Let X^{\eta}\in\mathcal{S}_{g}^{+}(T,D_{\eta}) be the unique fixed
point of the projected continuous-time mapping
\mathcal{T}_{g\to g}^{\eta}:=\mathcal{P}_{D_{\eta}}\circ\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}\circ\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta},
as guaranteed by Corollary
3.5.
This definition depends on \eta
through \mathcal{P}_{D_{\eta}} .
Let \bar{X}^{\eta} be the fixed point of the projected
discrete-time mapping
\bar{\mathcal{T}}_{g\to g}^{\eta}:=\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}^{\eta,+}\circ\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}^{\eta}=\mathcal{P}_{D_{\eta}}\circ\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}^{\eta}\circ\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}^{\eta}
that is constructed in Lemma 3.7.
By the triangle inequality, we have
\displaystyle d_{\lambda}(X^{\eta},\bar{X}^{\eta})
\displaystyle=d_{\lambda}(\mathcal{T}_{g\to g}^{\eta}(X^{\eta}),\bar{\mathcal{T}}_{g\to g}^{\eta}(\bar{X}^{\eta}))
\displaystyle\leq d_{\lambda}(\mathcal{T}_{g\to g}^{\eta}(X^{\eta}),\mathcal{T}_{g\to g}^{\eta}(\bar{X}^{\eta}))+d_{\lambda}(\mathcal{T}_{g\to g}^{\eta}(\bar{X}^{\eta}),\bar{\mathcal{T}}^{\eta}_{g\to g}(\bar{X}^{\eta})).
Lemmas
3.3 and
3.4
ensure for the first term that
d_{\lambda}(\mathcal{T}_{g\to g}^{\eta}(X^{\eta}),\allowbreak\mathcal{T}_{g\to g}^{\eta}(\bar{X}^{\eta}))<\frac{1}{2}d_{\lambda}(X^{\eta},\bar{X}^{\eta}) , for sufficiently large \lambda>0 .
Applying contractivity of \mathcal{P}_{D_{\eta}} with respect to d_{\lambda}(\cdot) ,
the triangle inequality, and Lemmas
3.4 and
3.8, the second term is bounded as
\displaystyle d_{\lambda}(\mathcal{T}^{\eta}_{g\to g}(\bar{X}^{\eta}),\bar{\mathcal{T}}_{g\to g}^{\eta}(\bar{X}^{\eta}))
\displaystyle\leq d_{\lambda}(\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}\circ\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}(\bar{X}^{\eta}),\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}^{\eta}\circ\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}^{\eta}(\bar{X}^{\eta}))
\displaystyle\leq d_{\lambda}(\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}\circ\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}(\bar{X}^{\eta}),\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}\circ\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}^{\eta}(\bar{X}^{\eta}))+d_{\lambda}(\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}\circ\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}^{\eta}(\bar{X}^{\eta}),\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}^{\eta}\circ\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}^{\eta}(\bar{X}^{\eta}))
(3.44)
\displaystyle\leq C\sqrt{\eta}+C\eta\leq C^{\prime}\sqrt{\eta}.
Thus, rearranging the above shows, for some C>0 not depending on \eta ,
(3.45)
d_{\lambda}(X^{\eta},\bar{X}^{\eta})\leq C\sqrt{\eta}.
By (3.45) and Lemmas 3.3 and 3.4,
\displaystyle d_{\lambda}(X^{\eta},\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}\circ\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}(X^{\eta}))
\displaystyle\leq d_{\lambda}(X^{\eta},\bar{X}^{\eta})+d_{\lambda}(\bar{X}^{\eta},\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}\circ\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}(\bar{X}^{\eta}))+d_{\lambda}(\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}\circ\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}(\bar{X}^{\eta}),\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}\circ\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}(X^{\eta}))
\displaystyle\leq C^{\prime\prime}\sqrt{\eta}+d_{\lambda}(\bar{X}^{\eta},\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}\circ\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}(\bar{X}^{\eta}))
Also by the identity \bar{X}^{\eta}=\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}^{\eta}\circ\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}^{\eta}(\bar{X}^{\eta}) (without projection) from
Lemma 3.7 and the bound for the second line of
(3.44),
d_{\lambda}(\bar{X}^{\eta},\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}\circ\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}(\bar{X}^{\eta}))=d_{\lambda}(\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}^{\eta}\circ\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}^{\eta}(\bar{X}^{\eta}),\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}\circ\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}(\bar{X}^{\eta}))\leq C^{\prime}\sqrt{\eta}.
So for some C>0 not depending on \eta ,
(3.46)
d_{\lambda}(X^{\eta},\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}\circ\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}(X^{\eta}))\leq C\sqrt{\eta}.
For any \delta>0 , let D_{\eta\cup\delta}=D_{\eta}\cup D_{\delta} , and define X^{\delta}\in\mathcal{S}^{+}(T,D_{\delta}) analogously to X^{\eta} . Then X^{\eta},X^{\delta}\in\mathcal{S}_{g}^{+}(T,D_{\eta\cup\delta}) , and
\displaystyle d_{\lambda}(X^{\eta},X^{\delta})
\displaystyle\leq d_{\lambda}(X^{\eta},\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}\circ\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}(X^{\eta}))+d_{\lambda}(\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}\circ\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}(X^{\delta}),X^{\delta})
\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad+d_{\lambda}(\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}\circ\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}(X^{\eta}),\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}\circ\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}(X^{\delta}))
\displaystyle\leq C(\sqrt{\eta}+\sqrt{\delta})+\frac{1}{2}d_{\lambda}(X^{\eta},X^{\delta}).
Consequently, d_{\lambda}(X^{\eta},X^{\delta})\leq C^{\prime}(\sqrt{\eta}+\sqrt{\delta}) . This shows along any sequence of values \eta>0 converging to 0 that
\{X^{\eta}\} is a Cauchy sequence under d_{\lambda} . Then by completeness of the ambient weighted L^{\infty} and L^{2} spaces over [0,T]\times[0,T] as in (3.24) and (3.25), there
exist R_{g},C_{g}:[0,T]\times[0,T]\to\mathbb{R} such that X=(C_{g},R_{g}) satisfies d_{\lambda}(X,X^{\eta})\leq C\sqrt{\eta} . Together with (3.46), we have d_{\lambda}(X,\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}\circ\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}(X^{\eta}))\leq C\sqrt{\eta}. By Lemma 3.2,
the image of \mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}\circ\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta} is contained in
\mathcal{S}_{g}(T,\emptyset) with discontinuity set D=\emptyset . Then as in (3.25), there exists a continuous modification of C_{g} so that X=(C_{g},R_{g})\in\mathcal{S}_{g}(T,\emptyset) . Writing X^{\eta}=(C_{g}^{\eta},R_{g}^{\eta}) , since also \lim_{\eta\to 0}d_{\lambda}(X,X^{\eta})=0 and C_{g}^{\eta} is positive-semidefinite, we have that C_{g} is positive-semidefinite, so X\in\mathcal{S}_{g}^{+}(T,\emptyset) .
Finally,
\displaystyle d_{\lambda}(X,\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}\circ\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}(X))
\displaystyle\leq d_{\lambda}(X,X^{\eta})+d_{\lambda}(X^{\eta},\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}\circ\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}(X^{\eta}))+d_{\lambda}(\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}\circ\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}(X^{\eta}),\mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}\circ\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}(X))\leq C\sqrt{\eta}.
Since \eta>0 is arbitrary, this shows that X\in\mathcal{S}_{g}^{+}(T,\emptyset) is a fixed point of \mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}\circ\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta} . Uniqueness of such a fixed point in \mathcal{S}_{g}^{+}(T,\emptyset) is immediate as \mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}\circ\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta} is contractive under d_{\lambda} .
This shows that the components of Theorem 2.4(a) are
well-defined up to any fixed time T>0 , where the fixed points
(C_{\theta},R_{\theta}) and (C_{g},R_{g}) are unique in
\mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{+}(T,\emptyset) and
\mathcal{S}_{g}^{+}(T,\emptyset) . Then Theorem 2.4(a) holds upon setting
\mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{+} as the space of kernels
(C_{\theta},R_{\theta}) on [0,\infty)\times[0,\infty) whose
restrictions to [0,T]\times[0,T] belong to \mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{+}(T,\emptyset) for
each T>0 , and similarly for \mathcal{S}_{g}^{+} .
∎
In the remainder of the proof, we fix T>0 ,
X=(C_{g},R_{g})\in\mathcal{S}_{g}^{+}(T,\emptyset) as
the preceding unique fixed point of \mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}\circ\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta} , and \bar{X}^{\eta}=(C_{g}^{\eta},R_{g}^{\eta})\in\mathcal{S}_{g}^{+}(T,D_{\eta}) as the
fixed point of \mathcal{T}_{\theta\to g}^{\eta}\circ\mathcal{T}_{g\to\theta}^{\eta} . To show Theorem 2.4(b), we record the following
continuity properties of C_{g},C_{g}^{\eta} .
Lemma 3.9.
For all sufficiently small \eta>0 ,
there is a constant C>0 depending on T but not \eta , such that
(3.47)
\displaystyle|C_{g}(t,s)-C_{g}(t^{\prime},s^{\prime})|
\displaystyle\leq C\left(\sqrt{|t-t^{\prime}|}+\sqrt{|s-s^{\prime}|}\right),
(3.48)
\displaystyle|C_{g}^{\eta}(t,s)-C_{g}^{\eta}(t^{\prime},s^{\prime})|
\displaystyle\leq C\left(\sqrt{|t-t^{\prime}|+\eta}+\sqrt{|s-s^{\prime}|+\eta}\right)
for all s,t,s^{\prime},t^{\prime}\in[0,T] .
Proof.
Since (C_{g},R_{g})\in\mathcal{S}_{g}^{+}(T,\emptyset) , we have from (3.8) that
|C_{g}(t,s)-C_{g}(t^{\prime},s^{\prime})|\leq C\left(\sqrt{|t-t^{\prime}|}+\sqrt{|s-s^{\prime}|}\right).
For (3.48), let \{\bar{\theta}^{t},\frac{\partial\bar{\theta}^{t}}{\partial g^{s}}\} be the processes solving the discretized
equations
(3.41–3.42)
for the kernels (C_{g}^{\eta},R_{g}^{\eta}) . By arguments analogous to those of
Lemma 3.2,
for some C>0 depending on T but not \eta , we have
\displaystyle|C_{\theta}^{\eta}(t,s)-C_{\theta}^{\eta}(t^{\prime},s^{\prime})|
\displaystyle\leq C(\sqrt{|t-t^{\prime}|+\eta}+\sqrt{|s-s^{\prime}|+\eta})\text{ for all }s,t\in[0,T],
\displaystyle|R_{\theta}^{\eta}(t,s)-R_{\theta}^{\eta}(t^{\prime},s)|
\displaystyle\leq C(|t-t^{\prime}|+\eta)\text{ for all }s\leq t,t^{\prime}\leq T,
and hence also
|C_{g}^{\eta}(t,s)-C_{g}^{\eta}(t^{\prime},s^{\prime})|\leq C\left(\sqrt{|t-t^{\prime}|+\eta}+\sqrt{|s-s^{\prime}|+\eta}\right).
∎
Proof of Theorem 2.4(b).
Fix \eta>0 , and consider a piecewise-constant embedding
of the discretized Langevin process
(3.27) defined as \bar{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{t}=\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\eta}^{[t]} .
An induction in time checks that this solves
(3.49)
\bar{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{t}=\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0}+\int_{0}^{\lfloor{t}\rfloor}[f(\bar{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{s})+\mathbf{X}\bar{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{s}]\mathrm{d}s+\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\mathbf{b}^{\lfloor{t}\rfloor}
where \{\mathbf{b}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} is the same Brownian motion as defining the
continuous process \{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} .
Define also a piecewise constant embedding \bar{\mathbf{g}}^{t}=\mathbf{g}_{\eta}^{[t]} of
(3.32), and \bar{\mathbf{b}}^{t}=\mathbf{b}_{\eta}^{[t]}=\mathbf{b}^{[t]\eta} .
By [30, Lemma 4.7], for a constant C>0 independent of
\eta , a.s. for all large n ,
\displaystyle\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\|\mathbf{b}^{t}\|_{2}
\displaystyle\leq C,
\displaystyle\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\big(\|{\mathbf{b}^{t}-\mathbf{b}^{\lfloor{t}\rfloor}}\|_{2}+\|{\mathbf{b}^{t}-\mathbf{b}^{\lceil{t}\rceil}}\|_{2}\big)
\displaystyle\leq C\sqrt{\eta\max(\log(1/\eta),1)}.
Then by a Grönwall argument (see [30, Lemma 4.8]), a.s. for
all large n ,
(3.50)
\displaystyle\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\|{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}}\|_{2}\leq C,\qquad\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\|{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}-\bar{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{t}}\|_{2}\leq C\sqrt{\eta\max(\log(1/\eta),1)}
For \bar{\mathbf{g}}^{t} , we have
\displaystyle\|\mathbf{g}^{t}-\bar{\mathbf{g}}^{t}\|_{2}
\displaystyle=\left\|\mathbf{X}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}-\bar{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{t})-\left(\int_{0}^{t}R_{g}(t,s)\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}\mathrm{d}s-\int_{0}^{\lfloor t\rfloor}R_{g}(t,s)\bar{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{s}\mathrm{d}s\right)\right\|_{2}
\displaystyle\leq\|\mathbf{X}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}-\bar{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{t}\|_{2}+\Phi_{R_{g}}(T)\int_{0}^{\lfloor t\rfloor}\|\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}-\bar{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{s}\|_{2}\mathrm{d}s+\Phi_{R_{g}}(T)\int_{\lfloor t\rfloor}^{t}\|\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}\|_{2}\mathrm{d}s,
so also a.s. for all large n ,
\displaystyle\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\|{\mathbf{g}^{t}-\bar{\mathbf{g}}^{t}}\|_{2}\leq C^{\prime}\sqrt{\eta\max(\log(1/\eta),1)}.
This implies that for any fixed m\geq 1 and t_{1},\ldots,t_{m}\in[0,T] ,
\displaystyle\limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty}W_{2}\Bigg(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\delta_{\left(\theta^{t_{1}}_{j},\ldots,\theta^{t_{m}}_{j},g^{t_{1}}_{j},\ldots,g^{t_{m}}_{j},b^{t_{1}}_{j},\ldots,b^{t_{m}}_{j}\right)},
(3.51)
\displaystyle\hskip 96.73918pt\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\delta_{\left(\bar{\theta}^{t_{1}}_{j},\ldots,\bar{\theta}_{j}^{t_{m}},\bar{g}^{t_{1}}_{j},\ldots,\bar{g}_{j}^{t_{m}},\bar{b}^{t_{1}}_{j},\ldots,\bar{b}_{j}^{t_{m}}\right)}\Bigg)<C\sqrt{\eta\max(\log(1/\eta),1)}\text{ a.s.}
Now let \{\theta^{t},g^{t},b^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} be the components of the
continuous-time dynamical mean-field limit in Definition
2.3, defined from the fixed point X=(C_{g},R_{g}) .
Let \{\bar{\theta}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} be the solution of
(3.41) with the same Brownian motion
\{b^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} , defined from the discrete-time fixed
point \bar{X}^{\eta}=(C_{g}^{\eta},R_{g}^{\eta}) and \{\bar{g}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0}\sim\operatorname{GP}(0,C_{g}^{\eta}) . Let \bar{b}^{t}=b^{\lfloor t\rfloor} . The bound
(3.45) implies that for any sufficiently large \lambda>0 ,
\displaystyle\lim_{\eta\to 0}\sup_{0\leq s\leq t\leq T}|R_{g}(t,s)-R_{g}^{\eta}(t,s)|
\displaystyle\leq\lim_{\eta\to 0}e^{\lambda T}d_{\lambda}(R_{g},R_{g}^{\eta})=0,
\displaystyle\lim_{\eta\to 0}\int_{0}^{T}\mathrm{d}t\int_{0}^{T}\mathrm{d}s\,|C_{g}(t,s)-C_{g}^{\eta}(t,s)|^{2}
\displaystyle\leq\lim_{\eta\to 0}e^{2\lambda T}d_{\lambda}(C_{g},C_{g}^{\eta})=0.
The continuity properties for C_{g},C_{g}^{\eta} in Lemma
3.9 then imply that also
\lim_{\eta\to 0}\sup_{s,t\in[0,T]}|C_{g}(t,s)-C_{g}^{\eta}(t,s)|=0.
Then (c.f. [31, Lemma D.1]) there exists a coupling of
\{g^{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]} and \{\bar{g}^{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]} for which
\lim_{\eta\to 0}\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\mathbb{E}(g^{t}-\bar{g}^{t})^{2}=0.
Under this coupling of \{g^{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]} and \{\bar{g}^{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]} ,
a Grönwall argument (see [30, Eq. (100)])
shows that the resulting coupling
of \{\theta^{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]} and \{\bar{\theta}^{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]} satisfies
\lim_{\eta\to 0}\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\mathbb{E}(\theta^{t}-\bar{\theta}^{t})^{2}=0.
Hence, for any fixed m\geq 1 and t_{1},\ldots,t_{m}\in[0,T] ,
\displaystyle\lim_{\eta\to 0}W_{2}\Big(\operatorname{Law}(\theta^{t_{1}},\ldots,\theta^{t_{m}},g^{t_{1}},\ldots,g^{t_{m}},b^{t_{1}},\ldots,b^{t_{m}}),
(3.52)
\displaystyle\hskip 72.26999pt\operatorname{Law}(\bar{\theta}^{t_{1}},\ldots,\bar{\theta}^{t_{m}},\bar{g}^{t_{1}},\ldots,\bar{g}^{t_{m}},\bar{b}^{t_{1}},\ldots,\bar{b}^{t_{m}})\Big)=0.
Combining (3.51), (3.52), and Theorem
3.6 which shows
\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}W_{2}\Bigg(
\displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\delta_{\left(\bar{\theta}^{t_{1}}_{j},\ldots,\bar{\theta}_{j}^{t_{m}},\bar{g}^{t_{1}}_{j},\ldots,\bar{g}_{j}^{t_{m}},\bar{b}^{t_{1}}_{j},\ldots,\bar{b}_{j}^{t_{m}}\right)},\operatorname{Law}(\bar{\theta}^{t_{1}},\ldots,\bar{\theta}^{t_{m}},\bar{g}^{t_{1}},\ldots,\bar{g}^{t_{m}},\bar{b}^{t_{1}},\ldots,\bar{b}^{t_{m}})\Bigg)=0\text{ a.s.},
and taking \eta\to 0 , we have that for any fixed m\geq 1
and t_{1},\ldots,t_{m}\in[0,T] ,
(3.53)
\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \lim_{n\to\infty}W_{2}\Bigg(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\delta_{\left(\theta^{t_{1}}_{j},\ldots,\theta^{t_{m}}_{j},g^{t_{1}}_{j},\ldots,g^{t_{m}}_{j},b^{t_{1}}_{j},\ldots,b^{t_{m}}_{j}\right)},\,\operatorname{Law}(\theta^{t_{1}},\ldots,\theta^{t_{m}},g^{t_{1}},\ldots,g^{t_{m}},b^{t_{1}},\ldots,b^{t_{m}})\Bigg)=0\text{ a.s.}\end{aligned}
We may strengthen this to Wasserstein-2 convergence over C([0,T],\mathbb{R}^{3}) using
a similar tightness argument as in [30, Theorem 2.5(b)]:
Let
\mathbf{x}=\{\mathbf{x}^{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]}=\{(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t},\mathbf{g}^{t},\mathbf{b}^{t})\}_{t\in[0,T]},\qquad x=\{x^{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]}=\{(\theta^{t},g^{t},b^{t})\}_{t\in[0,T]}.
Denote
\|x\|_{\infty}=\sup_{t\in[0,T]}|\theta^{t}|+\sup_{t\in[0,T]}|g^{t}|+\sup_{t\in[0,T]}|b^{t}|,
and write the coordinates of \mathbf{x} as x_{j}=(\theta_{j},g_{j},b_{j})\in C([0,T],\mathbb{R}^{3}) for j=1,\ldots,n .
Fix any test function F:C([0,T],\mathbb{R}^{3})\to\mathbb{R} satisfying
(3.54)
\big|F(x)-F(x^{\prime})\big|\leq C\|x-x^{\prime}\|_{\infty}(1+\|x\|_{\infty}+\|x^{\prime}\|_{\infty}).
Fix any \eta>0 , and let \{\tilde{\mathbf{x}}^{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]} and \{\tilde{x}^{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]} be the piecewise-linear
interpolations of \{\tilde{\mathbf{x}}^{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]\cap\eta\mathbb{Z}}
and \{\tilde{x}^{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]\cap\eta\mathbb{Z}} , respectively, with
knots at [0,T]\cap\eta\mathbb{Z} . Then
(3.53) implies
(3.55)
\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}F(\{\tilde{x}_{j}^{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]})=\mathbb{E}F(\{\tilde{x}^{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]})\text{ a.s.}
By the property (3.54) and Cauchy-Schwarz, we have
\displaystyle\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}F(\{x_{j}^{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]})-F(\{\tilde{x}_{j}^{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]})\right|\leq C\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\|x_{j}-\tilde{x}_{j}\|_{\infty}^{2}\right)^{1/2}\left(1+\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\|x_{j}\|_{\infty}^{2}\right)^{1/2}.
By a modulus-of-continuity bound for Brownian motion,
the bound (3.50), and a Grönwall argument
(see [30, Theorem 2.5(b)]), for some C>0 and
\alpha\in(0,1/2) , a.s. for all large n ,
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\|b_{j}\|_{\infty}^{2}\leq C,\quad\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\|\theta_{j}\|_{\infty}^{2}\leq C,\quad\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\|g_{j}\|_{\infty}^{2}\leq C,
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\|b_{j}-\tilde{b}_{j}\|_{\infty}^{2}\leq C\eta^{2\alpha},\quad\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\|\theta_{j}-\tilde{\theta}_{j}\|_{\infty}^{2}\leq C\eta^{2\alpha},\quad\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\|g_{j}-\tilde{g}_{j}\|_{\infty}^{2}\leq C\eta^{2\alpha}.
Applying this above and taking \eta\to 0 ,
(3.56)
\lim_{\eta\to 0}\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}F(\{x_{j}^{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]})-F(\{\tilde{x}_{j}^{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]})\right|=0\text{ a.s.}
For the components of the dynamical mean-field limit,
by standard Gaussian process bounds and a Grönwall argument, also
\mathbb{E}\|b\|_{\infty}^{2}\leq C,\quad\mathbb{E}\|g\|_{\infty}^{2}\leq C,\quad\mathbb{E}\|\theta\|_{\infty}^{2}\leq C,
\mathbb{E}\|b-\tilde{b}\|_{\infty}^{2}\leq C\eta^{2\alpha},\quad\mathbb{E}\|g-\tilde{g}\|_{\infty}^{2}\leq C\eta^{2\alpha},\quad\mathbb{E}\|\theta-\tilde{\theta}\|_{\infty}^{2}\leq C\eta^{2\alpha},
and hence
(3.57)
\lim_{\eta\to 0}\big|\mathbb{E}F(\{x^{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]})-\mathbb{E}F(\{\tilde{x}^{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]})\big|=0.
Combining (3.55), (3.56),
and (3.57) and taking \eta\to 0
shows
(3.58)
\displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}F(\{x_{j}^{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]})\rightarrow\mathbb{E}F(\{x^{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]})\text{ a.s.}
This holds for any function F:C([0,T],\mathbb{R}^{3})\to\mathbb{R}
satisfying (3.54), implying the claimed Wasserstein-2
convergence in Theorem 2.4(b).
∎
Proof of Theorem 2.4(c).
Theorem 2.4(b) implies, almost surely as n\to\infty ,
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\theta_{i}^{t}\theta_{i}^{s}\to\mathbb{E}[\theta^{t}\theta^{s}]=C_{\theta}(t,s),\quad\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}g_{i}^{t}g_{i}^{s}\to\mathbb{E}[g^{t}g^{s}]=C_{g}(t,s).
The first two claims of Theorem 2.4(c) follow from this and
dominated convergence to take an expectation over \{\mathbf{b}^{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]} . For
the third claim, (3.51) implies
\lim_{\eta\to 0}\limsup_{n\to\infty}\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\theta_{i}^{t}b_{i}^{s}-\bar{\theta}_{i}^{t}\bar{b}_{i}^{s}\right|=0\text{ a.s.}
Theorem 3.6 shows
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bar{\theta}_{i}^{t}\bar{b}_{i}^{s}\to\sqrt{2\gamma}\int_{0}^{\lfloor s\rfloor}R_{\theta}^{\eta}(t,s)\mathrm{d}s\text{ a.s.}
The bound (3.45) and |R_{\theta}^{\eta}(t,s)|\leq\Phi_{R_{\theta}}(T) imply
\lim_{\eta\to 0}\left|\int_{0}^{s}R_{\theta}(t,s)\mathrm{d}s-\int_{0}^{\lfloor s\rfloor}R_{\theta}^{\eta}(t,s)\mathrm{d}s\right|=0.
Then the third claim of Theorem 2.4(c) follows from combining
these three statements, taking \eta\to 0 , and again applying dominated
convergence to take an expectation over \{\mathbf{b}^{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]} .
∎
4. Analyses of correlation and response
In this section, we specialize the dynamical mean-field limit of Theorem 2.4 to the overdamped
Langevin equation (2.11). Our analysis relies on several
important structural
properties of the kernels C_{\theta},R_{\theta},C_{g},R_{g} at large times.
We collect these properties in the following two lemmas.
First, under Assumption 2.5, we have the following
properties for C_{\theta},R_{\theta} , including the existence of
time-translation-invariant limits c_{\theta},r_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} for these
kernels as t\to\infty , and a fluctuation-dissipation relation between
these limits.
Lemma 4.1.
Suppose Assumptions 2.1 and 2.2 hold with f=-U^{\prime} ,
the lower bound \alpha>0 in (2.10) satisfies
\alpha>\Lambda_{\max} , and Assumption 2.5 holds. Then:
(a)
The Gibbs measure \mu_{\mathrm{Gibbs}} is well-defined, and there exist deterministic almost sure limits
(4.1)
v_{*}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\langle\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_{2}^{2}\rangle,\qquad q_{*}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}\rangle.
(b)
For each fixed \tau\in\mathbb{R} , there exists a limit
c_{\theta}(\tau)=\lim_{s\to\infty}C_{\theta}(s+\tau,s) . This defines a
symmetric positive-semidefinite function
c_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} satisfying, for some C,c>0 and
all s,t\geq 0 and \tau\in\mathbb{R} ,
(4.2)
\begin{gathered}c_{\theta}(0)=v_{*},\qquad\lim_{\tau\to\infty}c_{\theta}(\tau)=q_{*},\\
|C_{\theta}(t,s)-c_{\theta}(t-s)|\leq Ce^{-c\min(s,t)},\qquad|c_{\theta}(\tau)-q_{*}|\leq Ce^{-c|\tau|}.\end{gathered}
(c)
For each fixed \tau\geq 0 , there exists a limit
r_{\theta}(\tau)=\lim_{s\to\infty}R_{\theta}(s+\tau,s) . This defines a
function r_{\theta}:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R} satisfying, for some C,c>0
and all t\geq s\geq 0 and \tau\geq 0 ,
(4.3)
\begin{gathered}|R_{\theta}(t,s)|\leq Ce^{-c(t-s)},\qquad|r_{\theta}(\tau)|\leq Ce^{-c\tau},\\
|R_{\theta}(t,s)-r_{\theta}(t-s)|\leq Ce^{-cs},\qquad\int_{0}^{t}|R_{\theta}(t,s)-r_{\theta}(t-s)|\mathrm{d}s\leq Ce^{-ct}.\end{gathered}
(d)
c_{\theta} is continuous on \mathbb{R} , smooth on (0,\infty) ,
and has a right derivative c_{\theta}^{\prime}(0^{+})=\lim_{\tau\to 0^{+}}c_{\theta}^{\prime}(\tau)
at \tau=0 . We have the fluctuation-dissipation relation
(4.4)
r_{\theta}(\tau)={-}c_{\theta}^{\prime}(\tau)\text{ for }\tau>0,\qquad r_{\theta}(0)={-}c_{\theta}^{\prime}(0^{+})=1.
Furthermore, for all \tau>0 , we have
c_{\theta}(\tau)\geq 0,\qquad r_{\theta}(\tau)\geq 0,\qquad r_{\theta}^{\prime}(\tau)\leq 0.
We may then define time-translation-invariant limits for C_{g},R_{g} as t\to\infty by
\displaystyle r_{g}(\tau)
\displaystyle=\sum_{p\geq 1}\kappa_{p+1}\,r_{\theta}^{\ast p}(\tau)\text{ for }\tau\geq 0,\qquad\text{ where }r_{\theta}(\tau)=0\text{ for }\tau<0,
\displaystyle c_{g}(\tau)
\displaystyle=\sum_{p,q\geq 0}\kappa_{p+q+2}\,r_{\theta}^{\ast p}*c_{\theta}*\bar{r}_{\theta}^{\ast q},\qquad\text{ where }\bar{r}_{\theta}(\tau)=r_{\theta}(-\tau)\text{ for all }\tau\in\mathbb{R}.
Here, for integrable functions a,b:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} , we use the convolution notation
[a*b](\tau)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}a(\tau-s)b(s)\mathrm{d}s,\qquad a^{*p}=\underbrace{a*\ldots*a}_{p\text{ times}},\qquad a^{*0}*b=b*a^{*0}=b.
These definitions of r_{g},c_{g} are alternatively expressed in the Fourier
domain (c.f. (4.51)) as
(4.5)
\mathcal{F}[r_{g}](\omega)=\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(\mathcal{F}[r_{\theta}](\omega)),\,\mathcal{F}[c_{g}^{0}](\omega)=\mathcal{F}[c_{\theta}^{0}](\omega)\frac{\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(\mathcal{F}[r_{\theta}](\omega))-\overline{\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(\mathcal{F}[r_{\theta}](\omega))}}{\mathcal{F}[r_{\theta}](\omega)-\overline{\mathcal{F}[r_{\theta}](\omega)}},
where \mathcal{F}[f](\omega)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}f(\tau)e^{-i\omega\tau}\mathrm{d}\tau is the Fourier
transform of f , \mathcal{R}_{\Lambda} is the R-transform (2.13), and c_{\theta}^{0}(\tau)=c_{\theta}(\tau)-\lim_{s\to\infty}c_{\theta}(s) and c_{g}^{0}(\tau)=c_{g}(\tau)-\lim_{s\to\infty}c_{g}(s) .
When v_{*}-q_{*} of Lemma 4.1
is within the radius of convergence of (2.13),
we have the following properties for C_{g},R_{g} , including
importantly a fluctuation-dissipation relation between c_{g} and r_{g} .
Lemma 4.2.
In addition to the conditions of Lemma 4.1, suppose that
(4.6)
\sum_{p\geq 1}|\kappa_{p+1}|(v_{*}-q_{*}+\varepsilon)^{p}<\alpha
for some constant \varepsilon>0 and the limits v_{*},q_{*} defined in Lemma
4.1. Then:
(a)
r_{g}:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R} is continuous on [0,\infty) and
continuously-differentiable on (0,\infty) , with
(4.7)
\int_{0}^{\infty}|r_{g}(\tau)|\mathrm{d}\tau<\alpha
and \int_{0}^{\infty}|r_{g}^{\prime}(\tau)|\mathrm{d}\tau<\infty .
Furthermore, for some C,c>0 and all t\geq s\geq 0 and \tau\geq 0 ,
(4.8)
\begin{gathered}|R_{g}(t,s)|\leq Ce^{-c(t-s)},\qquad|r_{g}(\tau)|\leq Ce^{-c\tau},\\
|R_{g}(t,s)-r_{g}(t-s)|\leq Ce^{-cs},\qquad\int_{0}^{t}|R_{g}(t,s)-r_{g}(t-s)|\mathrm{d}s\leq Ce^{-ct}.\end{gathered}
(b)
c_{g}:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} is continuous, symmetric, and positive-semidefinite on
\mathbb{R} , twice continuously-differentiable on (0,\infty) , and has
a right derivative c_{g}^{\prime}(0^{+})=\lim_{\tau\to 0^{+}}c_{g}^{\prime}(\tau) at \tau=0 .
We have the fluctuation-dissipation relation
(4.9)
r_{g}(\tau)={-}c_{g}^{\prime}(\tau)\text{ for all }\tau>0,\qquad r_{g}(0)={-}c_{g}^{\prime}(0^{+}).
Furthermore \mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(v_{*}-q_{*})\geq 0 and
q_{*}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(v_{*}-q_{*})\geq 0 , and we have
(4.10)
\begin{gathered}c_{g}(0)=\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(v_{*}-q_{*})+q_{*}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(v_{*}-q_{*}),\qquad\lim_{\tau\to\infty}c_{g}(\tau)=q_{*}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(v_{*}-q_{*}),\\
\qquad|C_{g}(t,s)-c_{g}(t-s)|\leq Ce^{-c\min(s,t)},\qquad|c_{g}(\tau)-q_{*}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(v_{*}-q_{*})|\leq Ce^{-c\tau}.\end{gathered}
The remainder of this section proves Lemmas 4.1
and 4.2. In these proofs and in our subsequent proof of Theorem
2.6, to ease the exposition of statements that hold almost
surely for all large n , we assume the following additional condition.
Assumption 4.3.
For some constants C,c>0 , with probability 1 over (\mathbf{X},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0})
(for every n\geq 1 ), we have
\|\mathbf{X}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\Lambda_{\max} , \frac{1}{n}\|\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0}\|_{2}^{2}\leq C ,
and the statements of Assumption 2.5 hold.
This is without loss of generality: Indeed, letting \mathcal{E}_{n} be the
(\mathbf{X},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0}) -dependent event where the statements of Assumption
4.3 hold, Assumptions 2.1, 2.2, and
2.5 ensure that \mathcal{E}_{n} holds a.s. for all large n .
We may define (\tilde{\mathbf{X}},\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0})=(\mathbf{X},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0}) on \mathcal{E}_{n} and
define (\tilde{\mathbf{X}},\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0}) arbitrarily on \mathcal{E}_{n}^{c} (e.g., setting \tilde{\mathbf{X}}=0 and \tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0}=0 ) to satisfy
Assumption 4.3. Then Lemmas 4.1,
4.2, and Theorem 2.6 for (\tilde{\mathbf{X}},\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0}) imply the corresponding results for (\mathbf{X},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0}) , since
(\tilde{\mathbf{X}},\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0})=(\mathbf{X},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0}) a.s. for all large n .
Proof of Lemma 4.1.
Throughout, \{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{t}\}_{t\in\mathbb{R}} denotes a stationary
process satisfying (2.11) with equilibrium initial state
\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0}\sim\mu_{\mathrm{Gibbs}} .
To ease notation, we will use consistently the convention that
\langle f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t})\rangle=\mathbb{E}[f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t})\mid\mathbf{X},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0}]
denotes an expectation conditional on \boldsymbol{\theta}^{0}
(the given initial condition satisfying Assumptions 2.2 and
2.5), while
\langle f(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{t})\rangle=\mathbb{E}[f(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{t})\mid\mathbf{X}]
denotes an expectation marginalizing over \tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0}\sim\mu_{\mathrm{Gibbs}} .
The notation
\langle f(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime})\rangle without time index continues to denote
“static” expectations over \boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}\overset{iid}{\sim}\mu_{\mathrm{Gibbs}} .
(We will write these expectations more explicitly under couplings of these
components.) We assume without loss of generality that Assumption
4.3 holds.
Constants C,C^{\prime},c,c^{\prime}>0 depend on \Lambda_{\max} and the potential U(\cdot)
but do not depend on n , and may change from instance to instance.
Parts (a) and (b): Since f=-U^{\prime} satisfies Assumption
2.2 and U(\cdot) also satisfies (2.10) with
\alpha>\Lambda_{\max} , there are constants C,\varepsilon>0 such that
Cx^{2}+C\geq U(x)\geq\frac{\Lambda_{\max}+\varepsilon}{2}\,x^{2}-C\text{ for all }x\in\mathbb{R}.
Then
\displaystyle\mathcal{Z}
\displaystyle=\int\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}U(\theta_{i})\right)\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\geq\int\exp\left({-}\Big(\frac{\Lambda_{\max}}{2}+C\Big)\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_{2}^{2}-Cn\right)\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\geq e^{-C^{\prime}n},
\displaystyle\mathcal{Z}
\displaystyle\leq\int\exp\left({-}\Big(\frac{\Lambda_{\max}+\varepsilon}{2}-\frac{\Lambda_{\max}}{2}\Big)\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_{2}^{2}+Cn\right)\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\leq e^{C^{\prime}n},
so \mu_{\mathrm{Gibbs}} is well-defined.
Also for any M>0 , by a chi-squared tail bound,
\displaystyle\int_{\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_{2}^{2}\geq Mn}\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_{2}^{2}\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}U(\theta_{i})\right)\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}
\displaystyle\leq\int_{\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_{2}^{2}\geq Mn}\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_{2}^{2}\exp\left({-}\Big(\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\Big)\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_{2}^{2}+Cn\right)\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}
\displaystyle\leq e^{C^{\prime}n}\cdot e^{-cMn}
Thus for M>0 large enough, we have
\langle\mathbf{1}\{\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_{2}^{2}\geq Mn\}\cdot\frac{1}{n}\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_{2}^{2}\rangle\leq 1 , implying for C=M+1 that
(4.11)
\frac{1}{n}\langle\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_{2}^{2}\rangle\leq C.
Assumption 2.5 implies that for every s\geq 0 ,
there exists a coupling of (\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s})
with \tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0} having law \mu_{\mathrm{Gibbs}} conditional on \boldsymbol{\theta}^{0}
(i.e. \tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0} is independent of \boldsymbol{\theta}^{0} ), such that
(4.12)
\frac{1}{n}\,\mathbb{E}[\|\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}-\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0}\|_{2}^{2}\mid\mathbf{X},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0}]\leq Ce^{-cs}.
Combined with (4.11) to bound \frac{1}{n}\langle\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0}\|_{2}^{2}\rangle , this implies also
(4.13)
\frac{1}{n}\langle\|\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}\|_{2}^{2}\rangle\leq C\text{ for all }s\geq 0.
Denote
P_{t}f(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\mathbb{E}[f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t})\mid\mathbf{X},\,\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0}=\boldsymbol{\theta}]
for any f:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{m} and m\geq 1 for which this expectation exists.
Let \operatorname{id}:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} be the identity map. Then for any fixed
s,\tau\geq 0 ,
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\langle\theta_{i}^{s+\tau}\theta_{i}^{s}\rangle=\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s\top}\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s+\tau}\mid\mathbf{X},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}]\mid\mathbf{X},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0}]=\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s\top}P_{\tau}\operatorname{id}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s})\rangle,
so Theorem 2.4(c) implies that
(4.14)
C_{\theta}(s+\tau,s)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s\top}P_{\tau}\operatorname{id}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s})\rangle\text{ a.s.}
Let us bound P_{t}(\boldsymbol{\theta})-P_{t}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}) for any \boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} :
For two diffusions
\{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} and \{{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0}
satisfying (2.11) with
initial conditions \boldsymbol{\theta} and \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime} , coupling these by
the same Brownian motion, we have
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\|\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}-{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}}^{t}\|_{2}^{2}=2(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}-{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}}^{t})^{\top}[\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}-\mathbf{X}{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}}^{t}-U^{\prime}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t})+U^{\prime}({\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}}^{t})]\leq C\|\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}-{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}}^{t}\|_{2}^{2},
and thus for all t\geq 0 ,
(4.15)
\|\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}-{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}}^{t}\|_{2}\leq e^{C^{\prime}t}\|\boldsymbol{\theta}-{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}}\|_{2}.
Then also by Jensen’s inequality, for all t\geq 0 ,
(4.16)
\|P_{t}\operatorname{id}(\boldsymbol{\theta})-P_{t}\operatorname{id}({\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}})\|_{2}\leq e^{C^{\prime}t}\|\boldsymbol{\theta}-{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}}\|_{2}.
Let (\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}) and \tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0} be coupled as in (4.12).
Then by this bound (4.16)
applied to \boldsymbol{\theta}=\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s} and \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}=\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0} and
Cauchy-Schwarz,
(4.17)
\left|\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s\top}P_{\tau}\operatorname{id}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s})\rangle-\frac{1}{n}\langle\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0\top}P_{\tau}\operatorname{id}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0})\rangle\right|\leq Ce^{C\tau}\cdot e^{-cs}.
Then by the existence a.s. of the limit (4.14) for any fixed
s,\tau\geq 0 ,
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\langle\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0\top}P_{\tau}\operatorname{id}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0})\rangle-\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\langle\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0\top}P_{\tau}\operatorname{id}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0})\rangle\leq 2Ce^{C\tau}\cdot e^{-cs}\text{ a.s.}
Since s\geq 0 is arbitrary, this implies that for each fixed \tau\geq 0 ,
there exists a (possibly random) almost sure limit
(4.18)
c_{\theta}(\tau):=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\langle\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0\top}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{\tau}\rangle=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\langle\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0\top}P_{\tau}\operatorname{id}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0})\rangle\text{ a.s.}
Taking n\to\infty followed by s\to\infty
in (4.17) shows that c_{\theta}(\tau) is deterministic and
given by
(4.19)
c_{\theta}(\tau)=\lim_{s\to\infty}C_{\theta}(s+\tau,s).
Defining c_{\theta}(\tau)=c_{\theta}(-\tau) for \tau\leq 0 , and noting that
\langle\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0\top}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{\tau}\rangle=\langle\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0\top}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{-\tau}\rangle by
reversibility, (4.19) and
the first equality of (4.18) then also hold for all \tau\in\mathbb{R} .
Since \tau\mapsto\frac{1}{n}\langle\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0\top}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{\tau}\rangle is symmetric positive-semidefinite for each n ,
this implies by (4.18)
that c_{\theta}(\tau) is also symmetric positive-semidefinite.
To show part (a), define v_{*}=c_{\theta}(0) .
Then by (4.18),
v_{*}=c_{\theta}(0)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\langle\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0}\|_{2}^{2}\rangle=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\langle\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_{2}^{2}\rangle\text{ a.s.}
For any fixed \tau\geq 0 , Assumption 2.5 implies
there exists a coupling of
(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0},\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{\tau}) with \boldsymbol{\theta} having law
\mu_{\mathrm{Gibbs}} conditional on \tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0} (i.e. \boldsymbol{\theta} is independent
of \tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0} ), such that
(4.20)
\frac{1}{n}\,\mathbb{E}[\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{\tau}-\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_{2}^{2}\mid\mathbf{X}]\leq Ce^{-c\tau}.
Then by (4.11) and Cauchy-Schwarz,
(4.21)
\left|\frac{1}{n}\langle\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0\top}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{\tau}\rangle-\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}\rangle\right|=\left|\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0\top}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{\tau}\mid\mathbf{X}]-\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathbf{X}]\right|\leq Ce^{-c\tau}.
Thus, since the limit (4.18) exists a.s.,
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}\rangle-\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}\rangle\leq 2Ce^{-c\tau}\text{ a.s.}
Here \tau\geq 0 is arbitrary, so there exists an almost sure limit
q_{*}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}\rangle\text{ a.s.}
Taking the limit n\to\infty followed by \tau\to\infty
in (4.21) shows that
q_{*} is deterministic and given by q_{*}=\lim_{\tau\to\infty}c_{\theta}(\tau) .
This proves part (a).
To check the bounds (4.2) in part (b), similarly by Assumption
2.5, there exists a coupling of
(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s+\tau}) with \boldsymbol{\theta} having law \mu_{\mathrm{Gibbs}}
conditional on \boldsymbol{\theta}^{s} (i.e. \boldsymbol{\theta} is independent of \boldsymbol{\theta}^{s} )
such that
(4.22)
\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{n}\,\mathbb{E}[\|\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s+\tau}-\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_{2}^{2}\mid\mathbf{X},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}]\;\bigg|\;\mathbf{X},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0}\right]\leq Ce^{-c\tau}.
By this, (4.13),
and Cauchy-Schwarz,
\mathbb{E}\left[\left|\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s+\tau}\mid\mathbf{X},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}]-\frac{1}{n}\,\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathbf{X},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}]\right|\;\bigg|\;\mathbf{X},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0}\right]\leq Ce^{-c\tau}.
Then coupling (\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}) with \tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0} via
(4.12) (where \tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0} is independent of
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0} , and all (\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s},\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0}) are
independent of the above \boldsymbol{\theta}\sim\mu_{\mathrm{Gibbs}} )
and applying Cauchy-Schwarz again,
(4.23)
\displaystyle\left|\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s+\tau}\rangle-\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}\rangle\right|
\displaystyle=\left|\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s+\tau}\mid\mathbf{X},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0}]-\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathbf{X},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0}]\right|
\displaystyle\leq Ce^{-c\tau}+Ce^{-cs}.
Taking the limit n\to\infty in (4.17),
(4.21), and (4.23) shows
\begin{gathered}|C_{\theta}(s+\tau,s)-c_{\theta}(\tau)|\leq Ce^{C\tau}\cdot e^{-cs},\quad|c_{\theta}(\tau)-q_{*}|\leq Ce^{-c\tau},\\
|C_{\theta}(s+\tau,s)-q_{*}|\leq Ce^{-c\tau}+Ce^{-cs}.\end{gathered}
Choosing a constant \iota>0 small enough, the first bound is at most
C^{\prime}e^{-c^{\prime}s} when \tau\leq\iota s . Applying this bound for \tau\leq\iota s and the latter two bounds for \tau>\iota s , also
|C_{\theta}(s+\tau,s)-c_{\theta}(\tau)|\leq C^{\prime\prime}e^{-c^{\prime\prime}\iota}.
This shows all statements of part (b).
Part (c): In light of the last statement of Theorem
2.4(c), we first compute a simple form for
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}s}\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t\top}\mathbf{b}^{s}\rangle
over s\in(0,t) . Since
\{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} solves (2.11), we have
\sqrt{2}\,\mathbf{b}^{s}=\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}-\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0}-\int_{0}^{s}[\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{r}-U^{\prime}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{r})]\mathrm{d}r.
Then
(4.24)
\sqrt{2}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}s}\left[\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t\top}\mathbf{b}^{s}\rangle\right]=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}s}\left[\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}\rangle\right]-\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t\top}[\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}-U^{\prime}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s})]\rangle.
Define e_{i}:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R} by e_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\theta_{i} . Then
\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}\rangle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}P_{s}(e_{i}\cdot P_{t-s}e_{i})(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0}).
Letting
-Af(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\theta})^{\top}[\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}-U^{\prime}(\boldsymbol{\theta})]+\operatorname{Tr}\nabla^{2}f(\boldsymbol{\theta})
be the generator of the diffusion, we have
\partial_{\tau}P_{\tau}e_{i}={-}AP_{\tau}e_{i}={-}P_{\tau}Ae_{i},\qquad\partial_{s}P_{s}(e_{i}\cdot P_{\tau}e_{i})={-}P_{s}A(e_{i}\cdot P_{\tau}e_{i})
as equalities pointwise on \mathbb{R}^{n} .
Then by the chain rule and dominated convergence,
(4.25)
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}s}P_{s}(e_{i}\cdot P_{t-s}e_{i})={-}P_{s}A(e_{i}\cdot P_{t-s}e_{i})+P_{s}(e_{i}\cdot P_{t-s}Ae_{i}).
Here, using \nabla e_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\mathbf{e}_{i} (the i^{\text{th}} standard basis
vector in \mathbb{R}^{n} ) and \nabla^{2}e_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta})=0 , we have
\displaystyle{-}A(e_{i}\cdot P_{t-s}e_{i})(\boldsymbol{\theta})
\displaystyle=\bigl[P_{t-s}e_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\cdot\nabla e_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta})+e_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\cdot\nabla P_{t-s}e_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\bigr]^{\top}[\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}-U^{\prime}(\boldsymbol{\theta})]
\displaystyle\qquad+\operatorname{Tr}\bigl[\nabla P_{t-s}e_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\cdot\nabla e_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta})^{\top}+\nabla e_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\cdot\nabla P_{t-s}e_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta})^{\top}+e_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\cdot\nabla^{2}P_{t-s}e_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\bigr]
\displaystyle=P_{t-s}e_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\cdot\mathbf{e}_{i}^{\top}[\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}-U^{\prime}(\boldsymbol{\theta})]+2\mathbf{e}_{i}^{\top}\nabla P_{t-s}e_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta})-(e_{i}\cdot AP_{t-s}e_{i})(\boldsymbol{\theta})
Applying P_{s} to this function,
the last term cancels the second term of (4.25), and thus
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}s}P_{s}(e_{i}\cdot P_{t-s}e_{i})(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0})=\langle P_{t-s}e_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s})\cdot\mathbf{e}_{i}^{\top}[\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}-U^{\prime}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s})]\rangle+2\langle\mathbf{e}_{i}^{\top}\nabla P_{t-s}e_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s})\rangle.
Then
\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}s}\left[\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}\rangle\right]
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}s}P_{s}(e_{i}\cdot P_{t-s}e_{i})(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0})
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t\top}[\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}-U^{\prime}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s})]\rangle+\frac{2}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\langle\mathbf{e}_{i}^{\top}\nabla P_{t-s}e_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s})\rangle.
Applying this to (4.24), for all s\in(0,t) we have
(4.26)
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}s}\left[\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t\top}\mathbf{b}^{s}\rangle\right]=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\langle\mathbf{e}_{i}^{\top}\nabla P_{t-s}e_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s})\rangle.
We note that \mathbf{e}_{i}^{\top}\nabla P_{t-s}e_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}) is a standard form of a
response function for the Markov diffusion, see e.g. [17].
We now check that for any fixed t\geq 0 , the right side of
(4.26) as a function
of s\in[0,t] is uniformly bounded and equicontinuous
for all n . Given \{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} ,
define a process \{\mathbf{J}^{t,s}\}_{t\geq s\geq 0} by
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathbf{J}^{t,s}=[\mathbf{X}-\operatorname{diag}(U^{\prime\prime}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}))]\mathbf{J}^{t,s}\text{ for }t\geq s,\qquad\mathbf{J}^{s,s}=\mathrm{Id}.
By Assumptions 4.3 and 2.2 for f=-U^{\prime} ,
we have \|\mathbf{X}-\operatorname{diag}(U^{\prime\prime}(\boldsymbol{\theta}))\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq C for a constant C>0 and any
\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} , and thus
(4.27)
\|\mathbf{J}^{t,s}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq e^{C(t-s)}\text{ for all }t\geq s\geq 0.
For any s\geq 0 , conditional on \boldsymbol{\theta}^{s} , there
exists a modification of \{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}\}_{t\geq s}
and \{\mathbf{J}^{t,s}\}_{t:\,t\geq s} where \boldsymbol{\theta}^{t} is
continuously-differentiable in \boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}
with Jacobian \frac{\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}}{\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}}=\mathbf{J}^{t,s}
[45, Theorem II.3.1].
Then by dominated convergence,
\displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{e}_{i}^{\top}\nabla P_{t-s}e_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s})
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta_{i}^{s}}\mathbb{E}[\theta_{i}^{t}\mid\mathbf{X},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}]
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial\theta_{i}^{t}}{\partial\theta_{i}^{s}}\,\bigg|\,\mathbf{X},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{Tr}\mathbf{J}^{t,s}\,\bigg|\,\mathbf{X},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}\right]
Thus, (4.26) is equivalently
\frac{1}{n}\langle\operatorname{Tr}\mathbf{J}^{t,s}\rangle , where \langle\cdot\rangle
here and below denotes the expectation over both
\{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} and \{\mathbf{J}^{t,s}\}_{t\geq s\geq 0}
conditional on (\mathbf{X},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0}) . For any s,s^{\prime}\in[0,t] with
s\leq s^{\prime} , we have
\|\mathbf{J}^{s^{\prime},s}-\mathbf{J}^{s^{\prime},s^{\prime}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\|\mathbf{J}^{s^{\prime},s}-\mathbf{J}^{s,s}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\int_{s}^{s^{\prime}}\left\|\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}r}\mathbf{J}^{r,s}\right\|_{\mathrm{op}}\mathrm{d}r\leq\int_{s}^{s^{\prime}}Ce^{C(r-s)}\mathrm{d}r\leq C(t)|s^{\prime}-s|
for some constant C(t)>0 not depending on n . Then by Grönwall’s
inequality, for a (different) constant C(t)>0 , also
\left|\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{Tr}\mathbf{J}^{t,s}-\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{Tr}\mathbf{J}^{t,s^{\prime}}\right|\leq\|\mathbf{J}^{t,s}-\mathbf{J}^{t,s^{\prime}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq C(t)|s^{\prime}-s|.
This and (4.27) imply
the uniform boundedness and equicontinuity of (4.26) in the form
\frac{1}{n}\langle\operatorname{Tr}\mathbf{J}^{t,s}\rangle over
s\in[0,t] , as claimed. This uniform boundedness, Arzelà-Ascoli, and
Theorem 2.4(c) imply that
\lim_{n\to\infty}\sup_{s\in[0,t]}\left|\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\cdot\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t\top}\mathbf{b}^{s}\rangle-\int_{0}^{s}R_{\theta}(t,\tau)\mathrm{d}\tau\right|=0\text{ a.s.}
Then this uniform equicontinuity, the
continuity of s\mapsto R_{\theta}(t,s) over s\in[0,t] ensured by the domain \mathcal{S}_{\theta}^{+} of
Theorem 2.4, and
(4.26) and Arzelà-Ascoli imply that for any t\geq 0 ,
(4.28)
\lim_{n\to\infty}\sup_{s\in[0,t]}\left|R_{\theta}(t,s)-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\langle\mathbf{e}_{i}^{\top}\nabla P_{t-s}e_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s})\rangle\right|=0\text{ a.s.}
We now apply arguments analogous to part (b).
To define r_{\theta}(\tau) , let us establish the bound
(4.29)
\displaystyle\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{e}_{i}^{\top}\nabla P_{t}e_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta})-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{e}_{i}^{\top}\nabla P_{t}e_{i}({\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}})\right|
\displaystyle\leq\frac{Ce^{Ct}}{\sqrt{n}}\|\boldsymbol{\theta}-{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}}\|_{2}
for any \boldsymbol{\theta},{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and t\geq 0 .
Let \{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} and
\{{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} be two diffusions with initial states
\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime} coupled by the same Brownian motion, and define
correspondingly \{{\mathbf{J}}^{t,0}\}_{t\geq 0} and \{{\mathbf{J}^{\prime}}^{t,0}\}_{t\geq 0}
(restricting the above Jacobian processes to s=0 ).
The above arguments show the representations
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\mathbf{e}_{i}^{\top}\nabla P_{\tau}e_{i})(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\allowbreak\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Tr}\mathbf{J}^{\tau,0}\mid\mathbf{X},\allowbreak\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0}=\boldsymbol{\theta}] ,
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\mathbf{e}_{i}^{\top}\nabla P_{\tau}e_{i})({\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}})=\allowbreak\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Tr}{\mathbf{J}^{\prime}}^{\tau,0}\mid\mathbf{X},\allowbreak{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0}}^{\prime}=\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}] .
Under this coupling,
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(\mathbf{J}^{t,0}-{\mathbf{J}^{\prime}}^{t,0})=\operatorname{diag}(U^{\prime\prime}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t})-U^{\prime\prime}({\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}}^{t}))\mathbf{J}^{t,0}+\operatorname{diag}(U^{\prime\prime}({\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}}^{t}))(\mathbf{J}^{t,0}-{\mathbf{J}^{\prime}}^{t,0}).
Since U^{\prime\prime}(\cdot) is bounded and Lipschitz under Assumption
2.2 for f=-U^{\prime} ,
the right side is bounded in Frobenius norm as
\displaystyle\|\operatorname{diag}(U^{\prime\prime}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t})-U^{\prime\prime}({\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}}^{t}))\mathbf{J}^{t,0}+\operatorname{diag}(U^{\prime\prime}({\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}}^{t}))(\mathbf{J}^{t,0}-{\mathbf{J}^{\prime}}^{t,0})\|_{F}
\displaystyle\leq\|\operatorname{diag}(U^{\prime\prime}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t})-U^{\prime\prime}({\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}}^{t}))\|_{F}\|\mathbf{J}^{t,0}\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|\operatorname{diag}(U^{\prime\prime}({\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}}^{t}))\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|\mathbf{J}^{t,0}-{\mathbf{J}^{\prime}}^{t,0}\|_{F}
\displaystyle\leq e^{Ct}\|\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}-{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}}^{t}\|_{2}+C\|\mathbf{J}^{t,0}-{\mathbf{J}^{\prime}}^{t,0}\|_{F}.
Then Grönwall’s inequality and (4.15) imply
\displaystyle\left|\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Tr}\mathbf{J}^{t,0}\mid\mathbf{X},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0}=\boldsymbol{\theta}]-\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Tr}{\mathbf{J}^{\prime}}^{t,0}\mid\mathbf{X},{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0}}^{\prime}=\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}]\right|
\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\|\mathbf{J}^{t,0}-{\mathbf{J}^{\prime}}^{t,0}\|_{F}\leq\frac{Ce^{Ct}}{\sqrt{n}}\sup_{s\in[0,t]}\|\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}-{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}}^{s}\|_{2}\leq\frac{Ce^{C^{\prime}t}}{\sqrt{n}}\|\boldsymbol{\theta}-{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}}\|_{2},
which shows (4.29). Then, recalling the coupling of
(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}) and \tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0} which
gives (4.12), let us apply (4.29)
with \boldsymbol{\theta}=\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s} and \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}=\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0} . This shows
(4.30)
\displaystyle\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\langle\mathbf{e}_{i}^{\top}\nabla P_{\tau}e_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s})\rangle-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\langle\mathbf{e}_{i}^{\top}\nabla P_{\tau}e_{i}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0})\rangle\right|
\displaystyle\leq\frac{Ce^{C\tau}}{\sqrt{n}}\,\mathbb{E}[\|\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}-\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0}\|_{2}\mid\mathbf{X},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0}]
\displaystyle\leq Ce^{C\tau}\cdot e^{-cs}.
By the existence of the almost sure limit
R_{\theta}(s+\tau,s) in (4.28), we then have
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\langle\mathbf{e}_{i}^{\top}\nabla P_{\tau}e_{i}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0})\rangle-\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\langle\mathbf{e}_{i}^{\top}\nabla P_{\tau}e_{i}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0})\rangle\leq 2Ce^{C\tau}\cdot e^{-cs}\text{ a.s.}
Since s\geq 0 is arbitrary, this shows that for each fixed \tau\geq 0 ,
there exists a limit
(4.31)
r_{\theta}(\tau)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\langle\mathbf{e}_{i}^{\top}\nabla P_{\tau}e_{i}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0})\rangle\text{ a.s.}
Taking the limit n\to\infty followed by s\to\infty in
(4.30) shows that r_{\theta}(\tau) is deterministic, with
r_{\theta}(\tau)=\lim_{s\to\infty}R_{\theta}(s+\tau,s) .
To bound R_{\theta}(s+\tau,s) , r_{\theta}(\tau) , and their difference, let us
check that
(4.32)
\displaystyle\left\langle\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{e}_{i}^{\top}\nabla P_{\tau}e_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s})\right|\right\rangle,\left\langle\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{e}_{i}^{\top}\nabla P_{\tau}e_{i}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0})\right|\right\rangle
\displaystyle\leq Ce^{-c\tau}.
Define as above \{\mathbf{J}^{t,s}\}_{t\geq s\geq 0} from
\{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} . Recalling the representation
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{e}_{i}^{\top}\nabla P_{\tau}e_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s})=\allowbreak\frac{1}{n}\langle\operatorname{Tr}\mathbf{J}^{s+\tau,s}\rangle ,
