\lim_{n\to\infty}\sup_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{E}_{\pi(m,n)}(\tilde{g}_{m}^{t}-\tilde{g}_{n}^{t})^{2}\leq C^{\prime}\varepsilon^{2}.
Since Lemma 5.1 ensures that c_{g}^{0} is the pointwise
limit of positive-semidefinite functions \tilde{c}_{g}^{m} , it is also
positive-semidefinite. For any given time horizon T>0 ,
we may couple \tilde{g}_{n}^{t}\sim\operatorname{GP}(0,\tilde{c}_{g}^{n})
and g_{0}^{t}\sim\operatorname{GP}(0,c_{g}^{0}) generically over [0,T] , by noting that Lemma
4.2 implies
(5.47)
|c_{g}^{0}(t-t)+c_{g}^{0}(s-s)-2c_{g}^{0}(t-s)|=2|c_{g}(0)-c_{g}(t-s)|\leq C|t-s|
for a constant C>0 . Then there exists a coupling of \tilde{g}_{n}^{t} and g_{0}^{t} such that
\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\mathbb{E}(\tilde{g}_{n}^{t}-g_{0}^{t})^{2}\leq C^{\prime}(1+\sqrt{T})\cdot\sqrt{\sup_{t,s\in[0,T]}|c_{g}^{0}(t-s)-\tilde{c}_{g}^{n}(t-s)|}
(c.f. [31, Lemma D.1]). Since [0,T]\subset[0,T_{n}] for all large n , property
(i) of Lemma 5.1 then ensures that there exists
n=n(\varepsilon,T) large enough such that
\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\mathbb{E}(\tilde{g}_{n}^{t}-g_{0}^{t})^{2}<\varepsilon^{2}.
Combining with the above, there exists a coupling of \{\tilde{g}_{m}^{t}\}\sim\operatorname{GP}(0,\tilde{c}_{g}^{m}) and \{g_{0}^{t}\}\sim\operatorname{GP}(0,c_{g}^{0}) such that
\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\mathbb{E}(\tilde{g}_{m}^{t}-g_{0}^{t})^{2}<C^{\prime\prime}\varepsilon^{2}.
The lemma follows upon adjusting \varepsilon .
∎
We now couple the generalized Langevin process \{\theta^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} in the dynamical mean-field limit of
Definition 2.3 with a process \tilde{\theta}^{t} defined from
(\tilde{c}_{g}^{m},\tilde{r}_{g}^{m}) , which will admit a Markovian representation.
Lemma 5.3.
Suppose the conditions of Theorem 2.6 hold.
Fix any sufficiently large T_{0},T>0 and sufficiently small \varepsilon>0 .
Let (\tilde{c}_{g},\tilde{r}_{g})\equiv(\tilde{c}_{g}^{m},\tilde{r}_{g}^{m}) be
the kernels of Corollary 5.2 for this \varepsilon . Let
\{\tilde{g}^{t}\}_{t\in\mathbb{R}},\{\tilde{b}^{t}\}_{t\geq T_{0}},z
be mutually independent such that
\{\tilde{g}^{t}\}_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\sim\operatorname{GP}(0,\tilde{c}_{g}) ,
\{\tilde{b}^{t}\}_{t\geq T_{0}} is a standard Brownian motion with \tilde{b}^{T_{0}}=0 , and z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,q_{*}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(v_{*}-q_{*})) .
Then there is a coupling of
(\{\tilde{g}^{t}\}_{t\in\mathbb{R}},\{\tilde{b}^{t}\}_{t\geq T_{0}},z)
with the process \{\theta^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} in (2.2) of
Definition 2.3 such that the following holds: Define the process
\{\tilde{\theta}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} by
\displaystyle\tilde{\theta}^{t}
\displaystyle=\theta^{t}\text{ for all }t\in[0,T_{0}],
\displaystyle\mathrm{d}\tilde{\theta}^{t}
\displaystyle=\left[-U^{\prime}(\tilde{\theta}^{t})+\int_{0}^{t}\tilde{r}_{g}(t-s)\tilde{\theta}^{s}ds+\tilde{g}^{t}+z\right]\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{d}\tilde{b}^{t}\text{ for }t\geq T_{0}.
Then for some constants C,c>0 not depending on T_{0},T,\varepsilon ,
(5.48)
\sup_{t\geq 0}\mathbb{E}(\theta^{t})^{4}<C,\qquad\sup_{t\geq 0}\mathbb{E}(\tilde{\theta}^{t})^{4}<C,
and
(5.49)
\sup_{t\in[T_{0},T_{0}+T]}\mathbb{E}(\tilde{\theta}^{t}-\theta^{t})^{2}<C(\varepsilon+T^{1/4}e^{-cT_{0}})^{2/3}.
Proof.
We construct the coupling as follows: By Lemma 4.2, there exist
C,c>0 such that
\sup_{s,t\in[T_{0},T_{0}+T]}|C_{g}(t,s)-c_{g}(t-s)|<Ce^{-cT_{0}}.
Writing c_{g}(\tau)=c_{g}^{0}(\tau)+q_{*}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(v_{*}-q_{*})
where q_{*}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(v_{*}-q_{*})=\lim_{\tau\to\infty}c_{g}(\tau)\geq 0 ,
we may represent a centered stationary Gaussian process with covariance
c_{g} on \mathbb{R} as
\{g_{0}^{t}+z\}_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\sim\operatorname{GP}(0,c_{g})
where
\{g_{0}^{t}\}_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\sim\operatorname{GP}(0,c_{g}^{0}),\qquad z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,q_{*}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(v_{*}-q_{*})),
and these are independent. Then by the bound (5.47) and
[31, Lemma D.1], for some constants
C,c>0 , there exists a coupling of \{g^{t}\}_{t\in[T_{0},T_{0}+T]}\sim\operatorname{GP}(0,C_{g}) and \{g_{0}^{t}+z\}_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\sim\operatorname{GP}(0,c_{g}) such that
\sup_{t\in[T_{0},T_{0}+T]}\mathbb{E}(g_{0}^{t}+z-g^{t})^{2}<C\sqrt{T}\,e^{-cT_{0}}.
By Corollary 5.2, we may couple \{g_{0}^{t}\}_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\sim\operatorname{GP}(0,c_{g}^{0}) and \{\tilde{g}^{t}\}_{t\in\mathbb{R}}\sim\operatorname{GP}(0,\tilde{c}_{g})
such that
\mathbb{E}(g_{0}^{t}-\tilde{g}^{t})^{2}<\varepsilon^{2}
for all t\in[T_{0},T_{0}+T] , yielding a coupling of
(\{\tilde{g}^{t}\}_{t\in\mathbb{R}},z) with \{g^{t}\}_{t\in[T_{0},T_{0}+T]}
such that
(5.50)
\sup_{t\in[T_{0},T_{0}+T]}\mathbb{E}(\tilde{g}^{t}+z-g^{t})^{2}<C(\varepsilon^{2}+\sqrt{T}\cdot e^{-cT_{0}}).
Next, we adapt a sticky/reflection coupling
argument of [28, 27] and [31, Lemma
3.3] to couple \{\theta^{t}\}_{t\geq T_{0}} and
\{\tilde{\theta}^{t}\}_{t\geq T_{0}} .
Fix \delta>0 , and let h_{\delta}:[0,\infty)\to[0,1] be a smooth
Lipschitz function such that
(5.51)
h_{\delta}(0)=0,\qquad h_{\delta}(x)=1\text{ for }x\geq\delta.
Let \{b_{1}^{t}\}_{t\geq T_{0}} and \{b_{2}^{t}\}_{t\geq T_{0}}
be two standard Brownian motions independent of each other and of
(\{\theta^{t}\}_{t\in[0,T_{0}]},\{b^{t}\}_{t\in[0,T_{0}]},\{g^{t}\}_{t\in[0,T_{0}+T]},\{\tilde{g}^{t}\}_{t\in\mathbb{R}},z) .
We couple \{\theta^{t}\}_{t\geq T_{0}} and
\{\tilde{\theta}^{t}\}_{t\geq T_{0}} by the evolutions
\displaystyle\mathrm{d}\theta^{t}
\displaystyle=\left[{-}U^{\prime}(\theta^{t})+\int_{0}^{t}R_{g}(t,s)\theta^{s}\mathrm{d}s+g^{t}\right]\mathrm{d}t
\displaystyle\hskip 36.135pt\underbrace{+h_{\delta}(|\theta^{t}-\tilde{\theta}^{t}|)\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{d}b_{1}^{t}+\sqrt{2(1-h_{\delta}(|\theta^{t}-\tilde{\theta}^{t}|)^{2})}\,\mathrm{d}b_{2}^{t}}_{=\sqrt{2}\mathrm{d}b^{t}},
\displaystyle\mathrm{d}\tilde{\theta}^{t}
\displaystyle=\left[{-}U^{\prime}(\tilde{\theta}^{t})+\int_{0}^{t}\tilde{r}_{g}(t-s)\tilde{\theta}^{s}\mathrm{d}s+\tilde{g}^{t}+z\right]\mathrm{d}t
\displaystyle\hskip 36.135pt\underbrace{-h_{\delta}(|\theta^{t}-\tilde{\theta}^{t}|)\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{d}b_{1}^{t}+\sqrt{2(1-h_{\delta}(|\theta^{t}-\tilde{\theta}^{t}|)^{2})}\,\mathrm{d}b_{2}^{t}}_{=\sqrt{2}\mathrm{d}\tilde{b}^{t}}.
Lévy’s characterization of Brownian motion shows that \{b^{t}\}_{t\geq T_{0}}
and \{\tilde{b}^{t}\}_{t\geq T_{0}} defined above
are both standard Brownian motions adapted to the filtration generated by
\theta^{t},\tilde{\theta}^{t},g^{t},\tilde{g}^{t},b_{1}^{t},b_{2}^{t} ,
and hence the above processes indeed
coincide in law with \{\theta^{t}\}_{t\geq T_{0}} and
\{\tilde{\theta}^{t}\}_{t\geq T_{0}} .
Let us first check the fourth moment
bound (5.48) for all sufficiently small
\varepsilon>0 . For \{\theta^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} ,
starting with the second moment, Itô’s formula gives
(5.52)
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathbb{E}(\theta^{t})^{2}=\mathbb{E}\left[2\theta^{t}\left(-U^{\prime}(\theta^{t})+\int_{0}^{t}R_{g}(t,s)\theta^{s}\mathrm{d}s+g^{t}\right)\right]+2.
By Lemma 4.2, there exists some \iota>0 small enough
such that \int_{0}^{\infty}|r_{g}(s)|\mathrm{d}s<\alpha-4\iota , and hence also for all
large t ,
\int_{0}^{t}|R_{g}(t,s)|\mathrm{d}s\leq\int_{0}^{t}|R_{g}(t,s)-r_{g}(t-s)|\mathrm{d}s+\int_{0}^{t}|r_{g}(t-s)|\mathrm{d}s<\alpha-3\iota.
By the condition (2.10) for U(\cdot) , there exists a
constant C=C(\alpha,\iota)>0 such that \theta U^{\prime}(\theta)\geq(\alpha-\iota)\theta^{2}-C for all \theta\in\mathbb{R} .
Furthermore Lemma 4.1 implies \mathbb{E}(g^{t})^{2}=C_{g}(t,t)<C
for some constant C>0 and all t\geq 0 ,
so \mathbb{E}\theta^{t}g^{t}\leq\iota\mathbb{E}(\theta^{t})^{2}+C^{\prime} for some
C^{\prime}=C^{\prime}(\iota)>0 .
Then for a constant C(\iota)>0 and all large t ,
\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathbb{E}(\theta^{t})^{2}
\displaystyle\leq-2(\alpha-2\iota)\,\mathbb{E}(\theta^{t})^{2}+2(\alpha-3\iota)\sup_{s\in[0,t]}\mathbb{E}|\theta^{t}\theta^{s}|+C(\iota)
\displaystyle\leq-2(\alpha-2\iota)\,\mathbb{E}(\theta^{t})^{2}+2(\alpha-3\iota)[\mathbb{E}(\theta^{t})^{2}]^{1/2}\cdot\sup_{s\in[0,t]}[\mathbb{E}(\theta^{s})^{2}]^{1/2}+C(\iota).
Consider M(t)=\sup_{s\in[0,t]}\mathbb{E}(\theta^{s})^{2} . Since
t\mapsto\mathbb{E}(\theta^{t})^{2} is continuously-differentiable by
(5.52), then so is M(t)
with \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}M(t)=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathbb{E}(\theta^{t})^{2} if
M(t)=\mathbb{E}(\theta^{t})^{2} , and \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}M(t)=0 otherwise. Thus the above
gives
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}M(t)\leq\max\left(0,{-}2\iota M(t)+C(\iota)\right)
for all large t , implying that M(t) is uniformly bounded over t\geq 0 .
Thus for a constant C>0 ,
\sup_{t\geq 0}\mathbb{E}(\theta^{t})^{2}\leq C.
Now for the fourth moment, Itô’s formula gives
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathbb{E}(\theta^{t})^{4}=\mathbb{E}\left[4(\theta^{t})^{3}\left({-}U^{\prime}(\theta^{t})+\int_{0}^{t}R_{g}(t,s)\theta^{s}\mathrm{d}s+g^{t}\right)+12(\theta^{t})^{2}\right].
Applying \theta^{3}U^{\prime}(\theta)\geq(\alpha-\iota)\theta^{4}-C\theta^{2} ,
\mathbb{E}(\theta^{t})^{3}g^{t}\leq\iota\mathbb{E}(\theta^{t})^{4}+C\mathbb{E}(g^{t})^{4}\leq\iota\mathbb{E}(\theta^{t})^{4}+C^{\prime} , Hölder’s
inequality, and the above second moment bound,
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathbb{E}(\theta^{t})^{4}\leq-4(\alpha-2\iota)\mathbb{E}(\theta^{t})^{4}+4(\alpha-3\iota)[\mathbb{E}(\theta^{t})^{4}]^{3/4}\sup_{s\in[0,t]}[\mathbb{E}(\theta^{s})^{4}]^{1/4}+C(\iota).
Then the same argument as above shows \sup_{t\geq 0}\mathbb{E}(\theta^{t})^{4}\leq C ,
giving the first statement of (5.48). The argument for
the second statement is the same, noting that
Corollary 5.2 implies
\mathbb{E}(\tilde{g}^{t})^{2}=\|u_{m}\|_{2}^{2}<C for all t\in\mathbb{R} and some C>0
(thus \mathbb{E}(\tilde{g}^{t})^{4}\leq C^{\prime} ), and also for \varepsilon>0 sufficiently small,
\int_{0}^{t}|\tilde{r}_{g}(t-s)|\mathrm{d}s\leq\int_{0}^{t}|\tilde{r}_{g}(t-s)-r_{g}(t-s)|\mathrm{d}s+\int_{0}^{t}|r_{g}(t-s)|\mathrm{d}s<\varepsilon+(\alpha-4\iota)<\alpha-3\iota.
Then the same arguments as above applied for \tilde{\theta}^{t} and
t\geq T_{0} show the second statement of (5.48).
Now set
\xi^{t}=\theta^{t}-\tilde{\theta}^{t},
v^{t}=-U^{\prime}(\theta^{t})+\int_{0}^{t}R_{g}(t,s)\theta^{s}\mathrm{d}s+g^{t},\qquad\tilde{v}^{t}=-U^{\prime}(\tilde{\theta}^{t})+\int_{0}^{t}\tilde{r}_{g}(t-s)\tilde{\theta}^{s}\mathrm{d}s+\tilde{g}^{t}+z.
Thus
\mathrm{d}\xi^{t}=(v^{t}-\tilde{v}^{t})\mathrm{d}t+2\sqrt{2}h_{\delta}(|\xi^{t}|)\,\mathrm{d}b_{1}^{t}.
Applying Itô’s formula with a smooth approximation S_{\delta^{\prime}}(x)
of |x| , and then taking \delta^{\prime}\to 0 , gives
(c.f. [27, Eq. (4.4)])
(5.53)
\mathrm{d}|\xi^{t}|=\operatorname{sign}(\xi^{t})(v^{t}-\tilde{v}^{t})\mathrm{d}t+2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sign}(\xi^{t})h_{\delta}(|\xi^{t}|)\mathrm{d}b_{1}^{t},
where the property h_{\delta}(0)=0 ensures there is no additional term from the
local time of \xi^{t} at 0.
Let A:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty) be a function chosen later, and set
r^{t}=|\xi^{t}|+\int_{0}^{t}A(t-s)|\xi^{s}|\mathrm{d}s
Let f:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty) be a function chosen later, such that
f(r) is differentiable and f^{\prime}(r) is absolutely continuous, and
f^{\prime}(r)\in[0,1],\qquad f^{\prime\prime}(r)\leq 0\text{ for a.e. }r\geq 0.
Then applying Itô’s formula again with (5.53) for \mathrm{d}|\xi^{t}| gives
(5.54)
\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathbb{E}f(r^{t})
\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[f^{\prime}(r^{t})\left(\operatorname{sign}(\xi^{t})(v^{t}-\tilde{v}^{t})+A(0)|\xi^{t}|+\int_{0}^{t}A^{\prime}(t-s)|\xi^{s}|\mathrm{d}s\right)\right.
\displaystyle\left.+4f^{\prime\prime}(r^{t})h_{\delta}(|\xi^{t}|)^{2}\right].
By Lemma 4.2 and dominated convergence,
\lim_{\iota\to 0}\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{\iota s}|r_{g}(s)|\mathrm{d}s<\alpha . Then
there must exist a sufficiently small constant \iota>0 such that
\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{\iota s}|r_{g}(s)|\mathrm{d}s<\alpha-2\iota.
Let us set
\qquad A(t)=e^{-\iota t}\left(\alpha-2\iota-\int_{0}^{t}e^{\iota s}|r_{g}(s)|\mathrm{d}s\right).
This satisfies
A(0)=\alpha-2\iota,\qquad A(t)>0,\qquad A^{\prime}(t)={-}\iota A(t)-|r_{g}(t)|.
Define
\Delta_{t}=\int_{0}^{t}|R_{g}(t,s)-r_{g}(t-s)|\cdot\mathbb{E}|\theta^{s}|\mathrm{d}s+\int_{0}^{t}|\tilde{r}_{g}(t-s)-r_{g}(t-s)|\cdot\mathbb{E}|\tilde{\theta}^{s}|\mathrm{d}s+\mathbb{E}|\tilde{g}^{t}+z-g^{t}|.
Then, applying a triangle inequality and f^{\prime}(r)\in[0,1] ,
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[f^{\prime}(r^{t})\operatorname{sign}(\xi^{t})(v^{t}-\tilde{v}^{t})]
\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\Bigg[f^{\prime}(r^{t})\operatorname{sign}(\xi^{t})\Big({-}U^{\prime}(\theta^{t})+U^{\prime}(\tilde{\theta}^{t})\Big)
\displaystyle\hskip 72.26999pt+f^{\prime}(r^{t})\left|\int_{0}^{t}R_{g}(t,s)\theta^{s}\mathrm{d}s-\int_{0}^{t}\tilde{r}_{g}(t-s)\tilde{\theta}^{s}\mathrm{d}s+g^{t}-(\tilde{g}^{t}+z)\right|\Bigg]
(5.55)
\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\left[f^{\prime}(r^{t})\operatorname{sign}(\xi^{t})\Big({-}U^{\prime}(\theta^{t})+U^{\prime}(\tilde{\theta}^{t})\Big)+f^{\prime}(r^{t})\int_{0}^{t}|r_{g}(t-s)|\cdot|\xi^{s}|\mathrm{d}s\right]+\Delta_{t}.
Let
\kappa(r)=\inf_{x,y:|x-y|=r}\frac{U^{\prime}(x)-U^{\prime}(y)}{x-y}.
Then
\operatorname{sign}(\xi^{t})\Big({-}U^{\prime}(\theta^{t})+U^{\prime}(\tilde{\theta}^{t})\Big)={-}|\theta^{t}-\tilde{\theta}^{t}|\frac{U^{\prime}(\theta^{t})-U^{\prime}(\tilde{\theta}^{t})}{\theta^{t}-\tilde{\theta}^{t}}\leq-|\xi^{t}|\kappa(|\xi^{t}|).
Applying this bound and the identities A(0)=\alpha-2\iota and
|r_{g}(t-s)|={-}\iota A(t-s)-A^{\prime}(t-s) into
(5.55) and (5.54),
and re-identifying the definition of r^{t} ,
(5.56)
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathbb{E}f(r^{t})\leq\mathbb{E}\left[-\iota f^{\prime}(r^{t})r^{t}+f^{\prime}(r^{t})|\xi^{t}|(\alpha-\iota-\kappa(|\xi^{t}|))+4f^{\prime\prime}(r^{t})h_{\delta}(|\xi^{t}|)^{2}\right]+\Delta_{t}.
Here, for some constants C,c>0 , note that \Delta_{t} satisfies the bound
(5.57)
\sup_{t\in[T_{0},T_{0}+T]}\Delta_{t}\leq C(\varepsilon+T^{1/4}e^{-cT_{0}})
by (5.48), (5.50),
\int_{0}^{t}|R_{g}(t,s)-r_{g}(t-s)|\mathrm{d}s<Ce^{-cT_{0}}
from Lemma 4.2, and
\int_{0}^{t}|r_{g}(t-s)-\tilde{r}_{g}(t-s)|\mathrm{d}s<\varepsilon from
Corollary 5.2.
We proceed to derive a differential inequality for \mathbb{E}f(r^{t}) from
(5.56).
By the condition (2.10) for U(\cdot) ,
for some C,R>0 , we must have
\kappa(r)\geq-C\text{ for all }r\geq 0,\qquad\kappa(r)\geq\alpha-\iota\text{ for all }r\geq R.
Denote
\tilde{\kappa}(r)=\max(\alpha-\iota-\kappa(r),0)
so that
0\leq\tilde{\kappa}(r)\leq C_{0}:=C+\alpha-\iota\text{ for all }r\geq 0,\qquad\tilde{\kappa}(r)=0\text{ for all }r\geq R.
Note that this implies
r\tilde{\kappa}(r)\leq C_{0}R\text{ for all }r\geq 0.
Recalling the cutoff \delta>0 defining h_{\delta}(x) in
(5.51), denote
K(r)=\sup_{t\in[T_{0},T_{0}+T]}\mathbb{E}\Big[|\xi^{t}|\tilde{\kappa}(|\xi^{t}|)\,\Big|\,r^{t}=r,\,|\xi^{t}|>\delta\Big]\in[0,C_{0}R].
Then, using that h_{\delta}(x)=1 when x>\delta , for any t\in[T_{0},T_{0}+T] we have
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[-\iota f^{\prime}(r^{t})r^{t}+f^{\prime}(r^{t})|\xi^{t}|(\alpha-\iota-\kappa(|\xi^{t}|))+4f^{\prime\prime}(r^{t})h_{\delta}(|\xi^{t}|)^{2}\,\Big|\,r^{t}=r,\,|\xi^{t}|>\delta\right]
\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\left[-\iota f^{\prime}(r^{t})r^{t}+f^{\prime}(r^{t})|\xi^{t}|\tilde{\kappa}(|\xi^{t}|)+4f^{\prime\prime}(r^{t})\,\Big|\,r^{t}=r,\,|\xi^{t}|>\delta\right]
\displaystyle={-}\iota f^{\prime}(r)r+f^{\prime}(r)K(r)+4f^{\prime\prime}(r).
Let us set f:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty) as
f(0)=0,\qquad f^{\prime}(r)=\exp\left(-\frac{1}{4}\int_{0}^{\max(r,2C_{0}R/\iota)}K(s)\mathrm{d}s\right)
Thus f^{\prime}(r) is absolutely continuous and satisfies f^{\prime}(r)\in[c_{0},1] for a
constant c_{0}>0 (depending on C_{0},R,\iota ), and
f^{\prime\prime}(r)=\begin{cases}{-}\frac{1}{4}f^{\prime}(r)K(r)&\text{ if }r\leq 2C_{0}R/\iota\\
0&\text{ if }r>2C_{0}R/\iota.\end{cases}
For this choice of f(r) , substituting above gives
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[-\iota f^{\prime}(r^{t})r^{t}+f^{\prime}(r^{t})|\xi^{t}|(\alpha-\iota-\kappa(|\xi^{t}|))+4f^{\prime\prime}(r^{t})h_{\delta}(|\xi^{t}|)^{2}\,\Big|\,r^{t}=r,\,|\xi^{t}|>\delta\right]
\displaystyle\leq{-}\iota f^{\prime}(r)r+\begin{cases}0&r\leq 2C_{0}R/\iota\\
f^{\prime}(r)K(r)&r>2C_{0}R/\iota\end{cases}
\displaystyle\leq{-}(\iota/2)f^{\prime}(r)r
where the second inequality applies K(r)\leq C_{0}R<\iota r/2 when r>2C_{0}R/\iota . On the complementary event |\xi^{t}|\leq\delta ,
let us simply apply f^{\prime}(r)\leq 1 , f^{\prime\prime}(r)\leq 0 , and
\tilde{\kappa}(r)\leq C_{0} to get
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[-\iota f^{\prime}(r^{t})r^{t}+f^{\prime}(r^{t})|\xi^{t}|(\alpha-\iota-\kappa(|\xi^{t}|))+4f^{\prime\prime}(r^{t})h_{\delta}(|\xi^{t}|)^{2}\,\Big|\,r^{t}=r,\,|\xi^{t}|\leq\delta\right]
\displaystyle\leq-\iota f^{\prime}(r)r+C_{0}\delta.
Combining these bounds, taking the expectation over r^{t} , and applying this to
(5.56) yields
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathbb{E}f(r^{t})\leq{-}(\iota/2)\mathbb{E}[f^{\prime}(r^{t})r^{t}]+C_{0}\delta+\Delta_{t}.
Finally, applying f(0)=0 and f^{\prime}(r^{t})\in[c_{0},1] , hence
r^{t}\geq f(r^{t})\geq c_{0}r^{t} , we obtain the desired differential inequality
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathbb{E}f(r^{t})\leq{-}(c_{0}\iota/2)\mathbb{E}[f(r^{t})]+C_{0}\delta+\Delta_{t}.
Here \delta>0 is arbitrary, C_{0},c_{0},\iota do not depend on \delta ,
and f(r^{T_{0}})=f(0)=0 , so Grönwall’s inequality and (5.57)
show
\sup_{t\in[T_{0},T_{0}+T]}\mathbb{E}f(r^{t})\leq C\sup_{t\in[T_{0},T_{0}+T]}\Delta_{t}\leq C^{\prime}(\varepsilon+T^{1/4}e^{-cT_{0}}).
Since
also \mathbb{E}|\xi^{t}|\leq\mathbb{E}r^{t}\leq c_{0}^{-1}\mathbb{E}f(r^{t}) , this establishes for some
constants C,c>0 that
\sup_{t\in[T_{0},T_{0}+T]}\mathbb{E}|\theta^{t}-\tilde{\theta}^{t}|\leq C(\varepsilon+T^{1/4}e^{-cT_{0}}).
The desired bound for \mathbb{E}(\theta^{t}-\tilde{\theta}^{t})^{2}
then follows from \mathbb{E}(\theta^{t}-\tilde{\theta}^{t})^{2}\leq\mathbb{E}[|\theta^{t}-\tilde{\theta}^{t}|]^{2/3}\mathbb{E}[|\theta^{t}-\tilde{\theta}^{t}|^{4}]^{1/3} and
the fourth moment bounds of (5.48).
∎
We now prove Theorem 2.6.
Proof of Theorem 2.6.
Fix constants T_{0},T,\varepsilon>0 to be determined, and let
(\{\tilde{\theta}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0},\allowbreak z)
be as constructed in Lemma 5.3 for these values.
Recall that z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,q_{*}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(v_{*}-q_{*})) , and that
\{\tilde{\theta}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} is defined via the kernels
(\tilde{c}_{g},\tilde{r}_{g})\equiv(\tilde{c}_{g}^{m},\tilde{r}_{g}^{m})
corresponding to a pair (A,u)\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\times\mathbb{R}^{m} in Corollary 5.2,
where m,A,u,\tilde{c}_{g},\tilde{r}_{g} depend only on \varepsilon and not on T_{0},T .
Recall from Corollary 5.2 that
|\tilde{c}_{g}(0)-\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(v_{*}-q_{*})|<\varepsilon .
Then for \varepsilon>0 sufficiently small, the second condition in
(2.12) implies
(5.58)
\liminf_{|\theta|\to\infty}U^{\prime\prime}(\theta)>\tilde{c}_{g}(0)+\varepsilon.
Then given any z\in\mathbb{R} , we may define a probability density on \mathbb{R} by
(5.59)
\mu_{m}(\tilde{\theta}\mid z)\propto\exp\bigg({-}U(\tilde{\theta})+z\tilde{\theta}+\frac{\tilde{c}_{g}(0)}{2}\tilde{\theta}^{2}\bigg).
Let (\tilde{\theta},\tilde{\theta}^{\prime},z) be random variables such that
z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,q_{*}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(v_{*}-q_{*})) as above, and
\tilde{\theta},\tilde{\theta}^{\prime} are conditionally independent given z , each
having law \mu_{m}(\tilde{\theta}\mid z) . We claim that for some constants
C(\varepsilon),c(\varepsilon)>0 depending only on \varepsilon and not on T_{0},T ,
(5.60)
W_{2}(\operatorname{Law}(\tilde{\theta}^{T_{0}+T/2},\tilde{\theta}^{T_{0}+T},z),\,\operatorname{Law}(\tilde{\theta},\tilde{\theta}^{\prime},z))\leq C(\varepsilon)e^{-c(\varepsilon)T}.
To show this claim, let \Sigma\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m} be any matrix such that
\Sigma\Sigma^{\top}=A+A^{\top} . Observe that the
joint law of (\{\tilde{\theta}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0},z)
is equivalent to that in the system
(5.61)
\displaystyle\tilde{\theta}^{t}
\displaystyle=\theta^{t}\text{ for all }t\in[0,T_{0}]
\displaystyle\mathrm{d}\tilde{\theta}^{t}
\displaystyle=[{-}U^{\prime}(\tilde{\theta}^{t})+u^{\top}x^{t}+z]\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{d}\tilde{b}^{t}\text{ for }t\geq T_{0},
\displaystyle\mathrm{d}x^{t}
\displaystyle={-}A[x^{t}-u\,\tilde{\theta}^{t}]\mathrm{d}t+\Sigma\,\mathrm{d}b_{x}^{t}\text{ for }t\geq 0,\qquad x^{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{m}),
where \{b_{x}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} is a standard Brownian motion in \mathbb{R}^{m} independent
of (\{\theta^{t}\}_{t\in[0,T_{0}]},\allowbreak\{\tilde{b}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0},\allowbreak z,\allowbreak x^{0}) ,
and \{x^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} is an auxiliary process in \mathbb{R}^{m} . Indeed, the third
equation of (5.61) has the explicit solution
(5.62)
x^{t}=e^{-At}x^{0}+\int_{0}^{t}Ae^{-A(t-s)}u\,\tilde{\theta}^{s}\,\mathrm{d}s+\int_{0}^{t}e^{-A(t-s)}\Sigma\,\mathrm{d}b_{x}^{s}.
Substituting this solution into the second equation gives
\displaystyle\mathrm{d}\tilde{\theta}^{t}
\displaystyle=\bigg[{-}U^{\prime}(\tilde{\theta}^{t})+\int_{0}^{t}u^{\top}Ae^{-A(t-s)}u\,\tilde{\theta}^{s}\mathrm{d}s+u^{\top}e^{-At}x^{0}+\int_{0}^{t}u^{\top}e^{-A(t-s)}\Sigma\,\mathrm{d}b_{x}^{s}+z\bigg]\mathrm{d}t
\displaystyle+\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{d}\tilde{b}^{t}\text{ for }t\geq T_{0}.
Since u^{\top}Ae^{-A(t-s)}u=\tilde{r}_{g}(t-s) , and since u^{\top}e^{-At}x^{0}+\int_{0}^{t}u^{\top}e^{-A(t-s)}\Sigma\,\mathrm{d}b_{x}^{s} is a Gaussian process with covariance kernel
\tilde{c}_{g} as shown in the proof of Corollary 5.2,
this gives the same law for (\{\tilde{\theta}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0},z)
as defined in Lemma 5.3.
Conditional on z , the process \{(\tilde{\theta}^{t},x^{t})\}_{t\geq T_{0}} in
(5.61) is a Markov diffusion after time T_{0} , taking
the form
(5.63)
\mathrm{d}\begin{pmatrix}\tilde{\theta}^{t}\\
x^{t}\end{pmatrix}={-}\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\
0&A\end{pmatrix}\nabla H_{m}(\tilde{\theta}^{t},x^{t}\mid z)+\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt{2}&0\\
0&\Sigma\end{pmatrix}\mathrm{d}\begin{pmatrix}\tilde{b}^{t}\\
b_{x}^{t}\end{pmatrix}
where H_{m}(\cdot\mid z) is the Hamiltonian on \mathbb{R}^{m+1} given by
\displaystyle H_{m}(\tilde{\theta},x\mid z)
\displaystyle=U(\tilde{\theta})-(u^{\top}x+z)\tilde{\theta}+\frac{1}{2}\|x\|_{2}^{2}
\displaystyle=U(\tilde{\theta})-z\tilde{\theta}-\frac{\tilde{c}_{g}(0)}{2}\tilde{\theta}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\|x-\tilde{\theta}u\|_{2}^{2},
the second equality applying \|u\|_{2}^{2}=\tilde{c}_{g}(0) . Then
\mu_{m}(\tilde{\theta},x\mid z)\propto e^{-H_{m}(\tilde{\theta},x\mid z)}
defines the joint probability density for a pair (\tilde{\theta},x) where
\tilde{\theta}\sim\mu_{m}(\tilde{\theta}\mid z) has the conditional
law (5.59) given z , and x\sim\mathcal{N}(\tilde{\theta}u,\mathrm{Id}_{m})
given both (\tilde{\theta},z) . Since A+A^{\top}=\Sigma\Sigma^{\top} ,
it is standard to check that \mu_{m}(\tilde{\theta},x\mid z)
is a stationary law of the diffusion process (5.63).
To quantify the convergence of (5.63) to \mu_{m}(\tilde{\theta},x\mid z) ,
let us write C(\varepsilon),c(\varepsilon)>0 for constants depending on \varepsilon
but not T_{0},T or z . We check that \mu_{m}(\tilde{\theta},x\mid z) satisfies a
(Euclidean) log-Sobolev inequality on \mathbb{R}^{m+1}
with some log-Sobolev constant C(\varepsilon)>0 . Indeed,
the condition (5.58) implies that there exists a
continuous, compactly supported function
f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} for which \int_{\mathbb{R}}f=0
and f(\theta)\leq U^{\prime\prime}(\theta)-\tilde{c}_{g}(0)-\varepsilon/2 for all \theta\in\mathbb{R} .
Set W(\theta)=\int_{-\infty}^{\theta}\mathrm{d}x\int_{-\infty}^{x}\mathrm{d}y\,f(y) , so that
W^{\prime}(\theta)=\int_{-\infty}^{\theta}f(y)\mathrm{d}y remains compactly supported (with
the same support as f ),
and hence W(\theta) is bounded. Define V(\theta) by
(5.64)
U(\theta)-z\theta-\frac{\tilde{c}_{g}(0)}{2}\theta^{2}=V(\theta)+W(\theta),
so V^{\prime\prime}(\theta)=U^{\prime\prime}(\theta)-\tilde{c}_{g}(0)-f(\theta)\geq\varepsilon/2 for all
\theta\in\mathbb{R} . Then by the Holley-Stroock perturbation lemma,
\mu_{m}(\tilde{\theta}\mid z) satisfies a log-Sobolev inequality on \mathbb{R} with
log-Sobolev constant C(\varepsilon) not depending on z .
Writing x=\tilde{\theta}u+w where w\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathrm{Id}_{m}) is independent of
(\tilde{\theta},z) , we note that (\tilde{\theta},x) is a Lipschitz map of
(\tilde{\theta},w) , so this implies also a log-Sobolev inequality
for \mu_{m}(\tilde{\theta},x\mid z) .
Since \nabla^{2}H(\tilde{\theta},x\mid z) is bounded below by some
constant {-}c(\varepsilon)<0 also not depending on z ,
a log-Harnack/entropy-cost inequality [62, Corollary 1.2]
shows, for any t>s\geq T_{0} , that \operatorname{Law}(\tilde{\theta}^{t},x^{t}\mid\tilde{\theta}^{s},x^{s},z) admits a density
with respect to the stationary measure \mu_{m}(\tilde{\theta},x\mid z)
and satisfies
\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\operatorname{Law}(\tilde{\theta}^{t},x^{t}\mid\tilde{\theta}^{s},x^{s},z)\,\|\,\mu_{m}(\tilde{\theta},x\mid z))
\displaystyle\leq\frac{C(\varepsilon)}{e^{c(\varepsilon)(t-s)}-1}W_{2}(\delta_{(\tilde{\theta}^{s},x^{s})},\,\mu_{m}(\tilde{\theta},x\mid z))^{2}
\displaystyle\leq\frac{2C(\varepsilon)}{e^{c(\varepsilon)(t-s)}-1}\Big(\|(\tilde{\theta}^{s},x^{s})\|_{2}^{2}+\mathbb{E}[\|(\tilde{\theta},x)\|_{2}^{2}\mid z]\Big)
where \delta_{(\tilde{\theta}^{s},x^{s})} denotes the unit point measure
at (\tilde{\theta}^{s},x^{s})\in\mathbb{R}^{m+1} , and (\tilde{\theta},x) denotes a sample
from \mu_{m}(\tilde{\theta},x\mid z) . By the log-Sobolev inequality for
\mu_{m}(\tilde{\theta},x\mid z) and \varepsilon -dependent lower bound for
\lambda_{\min}(A+A^{\top}) , for any
t^{\prime}>t>s\geq T_{0} , we have also the decay in relative entropy,
\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\operatorname{Law}(\tilde{\theta}^{t^{\prime}},x^{t^{\prime}}\mid\tilde{\theta}^{s},x^{s},z)\,\|\,\mu_{m}(\tilde{\theta},x\mid z))
\displaystyle\leq e^{-c(\varepsilon)(t^{\prime}-t)}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\operatorname{Law}(\tilde{\theta}^{t},x^{t}\mid\tilde{\theta}^{s},x^{s},z)\,\|\,\mu_{m}(\tilde{\theta},x\mid z)),
as well as the T_{2} -transportation inequality [57]
W_{2}(\operatorname{Law}(\tilde{\theta}^{t^{\prime}},x^{t^{\prime}}\mid\tilde{\theta}^{s},x^{s},z),\,\mu_{m}(\tilde{\theta},x\mid z))^{2}\leq C(\varepsilon)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\operatorname{Law}(\tilde{\theta}^{t^{\prime}},x^{t^{\prime}}\mid\tilde{\theta}^{s},x^{s},z)\,\|\,\mu_{m}(\tilde{\theta},x\mid z)).
Applying the above with t=s+1 and t^{\prime}=s+\tau shows, for some
C(\varepsilon),c(\varepsilon)>0 and any s\geq T_{0} and \tau\geq 1 , that
(5.65)
\displaystyle W_{2}(\operatorname{Law}(\tilde{\theta}^{s+\tau},x^{s+\tau}\mid\tilde{\theta}^{s},x^{s},z),\,\mu_{m}(\tilde{\theta},x\mid z))^{2}
\displaystyle\leq C(\varepsilon)e^{-c(\varepsilon)\tau}\Big(\|(\tilde{\theta}^{s},x^{s})\|_{2}^{2}+\mathbb{E}[\|(\tilde{\theta},x)\|_{2}^{2}\mid z]\Big).
Let (\tilde{\theta},x,\tilde{\theta}^{\prime},x^{\prime},z) be such that z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,q_{*}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(v_{*}-q_{*})) , and (\tilde{\theta},x),(\tilde{\theta}^{\prime},x^{\prime})
are conditionally independent given z with law \mu_{m}(\tilde{\theta},x\mid z) .
Then, applying (5.65) with s=T_{0} and
\tau=T/2 to couple (\tilde{\theta}^{T_{0}+T/2},x^{T_{0}+T/2}) with
(\tilde{\theta},x) conditional on (\tilde{\theta}^{T_{0}},x^{T_{0}}) and z ,
and then with s=T_{0}+T/2 and \tau=T/2 to couple
(\tilde{\theta}^{T_{0}+T},x^{T_{0}+T}) with (\tilde{\theta}^{\prime},x^{\prime})
conditional on (\tilde{\theta}^{T_{0}+T/2},x^{T_{0}+T/2}) and z ,
and finally marginalizing over z , we get for some (different)
constants C(\varepsilon),c(\varepsilon)>0 that
\displaystyle W_{2}(\operatorname{Law}(\tilde{\theta}^{T_{0}+T/2},\tilde{\theta}^{T_{0}+T},z),\,\operatorname{Law}(\tilde{\theta},\tilde{\theta}^{\prime},z))^{2}
\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,q_{*}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(v_{*}-q_{*}))}W_{2}(\operatorname{Law}(\tilde{\theta}^{T_{0}+T/2},x^{T_{0}+T/2},\tilde{\theta}^{T_{0}+T},x^{T_{0}+T}\mid z),\,\operatorname{Law}(\tilde{\theta},x,\tilde{\theta}^{\prime},x^{\prime}\mid z))^{2}
(5.66)
\displaystyle\leq C(\varepsilon)e^{-c(\varepsilon)T}\Big(\mathbb{E}\|(\tilde{\theta}^{T_{0}},x^{T_{0}})\|_{2}^{2}+\mathbb{E}\|(\tilde{\theta}^{T_{0}+T/2},x^{T_{0}+T/2})\|_{2}^{2}+\mathbb{E}\|(\tilde{\theta},x)\|_{2}^{2}+\mathbb{E}\|(\tilde{\theta}^{\prime},x^{\prime})\|_{2}^{2}\Big).
Here, \mathbb{E}(\tilde{\theta}^{t})^{2} is uniformly bounded
for all t\geq 0 by (5.48).
Then also by the explicit form (5.62), for any t\geq T_{0} ,
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|x^{t}\|_{2}^{2}
\displaystyle\leq 2\mathbb{E}\left\|\int_{0}^{t}Ae^{-(t-s)A}u\,\theta^{s}\mathrm{d}s\right\|_{2}^{2}+2\mathbb{E}\left\|\int_{0}^{t}e^{-A(t-s)}\Sigma\,\mathrm{d}b_{x}^{s}+e^{-At}x^{0}\right\|_{2}^{2}
\displaystyle\leq C\left(\int_{0}^{\infty}\|Ae^{-sA}u\|_{2}\,\mathrm{d}s\right)^{2}+2m.
This is at most some C(\varepsilon)>0 by the bound \|e^{-sA}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq e^{-(s/2)\lambda_{\min}(A+A^{\top})} . Since (\tilde{\theta}^{t},x^{t})
converges weakly in law to (\tilde{\theta},x) as t\to\infty ,
(5.48) and Fatou’s lemma imply also
(5.67)
\mathbb{E}\tilde{\theta}^{4}=\mathbb{E}(\tilde{\theta}^{\prime})^{4}\leq C
for a constant C>0 . Then, since x\sim\mathcal{N}(\tilde{\theta}u,\mathrm{Id}_{m}) given (\tilde{\theta},z) , also
\mathbb{E}\|x\|_{2}^{2}=\mathbb{E}\|x^{\prime}\|_{2}^{2}\leq C(\varepsilon) .
Applying these bounds to the right side of (5.66)
yields (5.60) as claimed.
Under the second condition in (2.12), we may define also
the probability density on \mathbb{R}
\mu(\theta\mid z)\propto\exp\Big({-}U(\theta)+z\theta+\frac{\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(v_{*}-q_{*})}{2}\theta^{2}\Big).
Let (\theta,\theta^{\prime},z) be random variables such that z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,q_{*}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(v_{*}-q_{*})) and \theta,\theta^{\prime} are conditionally
independent given z with law \mu(\theta\mid z) , and let
(\tilde{\theta}\tilde{\theta}^{\prime},z) be defined from \mu_{m}(\theta\mid z)
as above. As \varepsilon\to 0 ,
considering a sequence of m=m(\varepsilon) defining \mu_{m}(\theta\mid z)
and recalling that |\tilde{c}_{g}(0)-\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(v_{*}-q_{*})|<\varepsilon ,
we have \mu_{m}(\cdot\mid z)\to\mu(\cdot\mid z) weakly as \varepsilon\to 0
for each fixed z\in\mathbb{R} . Then also marginalizing over z ,
\operatorname{Law}(\tilde{\theta},\tilde{\theta}^{\prime})\to\operatorname{Law}(\theta,\theta^{\prime}) weakly as
\varepsilon\to 0 . Since (5.67) implies that
(\tilde{\theta},\tilde{\theta}^{\prime}) is uniformly integrable in L^{2} for all
\varepsilon>0 , this implies
\mathbb{E}[\|(\tilde{\theta},\tilde{\theta}^{\prime})\|_{2}^{2}]\to\mathbb{E}[\|(\theta,\theta^{\prime})\|_{2}^{2}]
and hence also W_{2}(\operatorname{Law}(\tilde{\theta},\tilde{\theta}^{\prime}),\operatorname{Law}(\theta,\theta^{\prime}))\to 0 . Thus we have
(5.68)
W_{2}(\operatorname{Law}(\tilde{\theta},\tilde{\theta}^{\prime}),\operatorname{Law}(\theta,\theta^{\prime}))^{2}\leq o_{\varepsilon}(1)
for a quantity o_{\varepsilon}(1) depending only on \varepsilon and vanishing
as \varepsilon\to 0 . Combining the conclusion of Lemma 5.3
with (5.60) and (5.68),
W_{2}(\operatorname{Law}(\theta^{T_{0}+T/2},\theta^{T_{0}+T}),\operatorname{Law}(\theta,\theta^{\prime}))^{2}\leq C(\varepsilon+T^{1/4}e^{-cT_{0}})^{2/3}+C(\varepsilon)e^{-c(\varepsilon)T}+o_{\varepsilon}(1).
Given \varepsilon>0 , we may take T=T(\varepsilon)>0 large enough such that the second
term is small, followed by T_{0}=T_{0}(\varepsilon) large enough such that the first term
is small. Thus, there exist some T(\varepsilon),T_{0}(\varepsilon)\to\infty for which,
as \varepsilon\to 0 ,
(5.69)
\operatorname{Law}(\theta^{T_{0}(\varepsilon)+T(\varepsilon)/2},\theta^{T_{0}(\varepsilon)+T(\varepsilon)})\to\operatorname{Law}(\theta,\theta^{\prime})\text{ weakly and in Wasserstein-2}.
We now turn to the statements of Theorem 2.6. We may again assume,
without loss of generality, that Assumption 4.3 holds.
Part (a).
Identifying z=\sqrt{q_{*}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(v_{*}-q_{*})}\,\xi where \xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1) , the above law \mu(\theta\mid z) is precisely
\mu(\theta\mid v_{*},q_{*},\xi) defined in Theorem 2.6.
Then (5.69) implies,
by the characterizations of v_{*} and q_{*} in Lemma 4.1, that
\displaystyle v_{*}
\displaystyle=c_{\theta}(0)=\lim_{t\to\infty}\mathbb{E}(\theta^{t})^{2}=\mathbb{E}[\theta^{2}]=\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}\langle\theta^{2}\rangle_{v_{*},q_{*},\xi},
\displaystyle q_{*}
\displaystyle=\lim_{\tau\to\infty}c_{\theta}(\tau)=\lim_{s,\tau\to\infty}\mathbb{E}(\theta^{s}\theta^{s+\tau})=\mathbb{E}[\theta\theta^{\prime}]=\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}\langle\theta\rangle_{v_{*},q_{*},\xi}^{2},
establishing the fixed point conditions (2.16) for
(v_{*},q_{*}) .
Let \boldsymbol{\theta}\sim\mu_{\mathrm{Gibbs}} . Assumption
2.5 implies
that for some constants C,c>0 ,
(5.70)
\frac{1}{n}W_{2}(\operatorname{Law}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}\mid\mathbf{X},\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0}),\,\operatorname{Law}(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathbf{X}))^{2}\leq Ce^{-ct}.
This implies, for any function f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} satisfying |f(x)-f(y)|\leq C(1+|x|+|y|)|x-y| , that
\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\langle f(\theta_{i}^{t})\rangle-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\langle f(\theta_{i})\rangle\right|\leq C(f)e^{-ct}
for a constant C(f)>0 . Theorem 2.4 implies, for each fixed
t\geq 0 ,
\lim_{n\to\infty}\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\langle f(\theta_{i}^{t})\rangle-\mathbb{E}[f(\theta^{t})]\right|=0\text{ a.s.}
where \mathbb{E}[\cdot] is the expectation over \theta^{t} in the dynamical mean-field
limit of Definition 2.3. The Wasserstein convergence
(5.69) implies
\lim_{t\to\infty}\mathbb{E}[f(\theta^{t})]=\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}\langle f(\theta)\rangle_{v_{*},q_{*},\xi}.
Combining the above bounds, and taking n\to\infty followed by t\to\infty , shows (2.18).
For the final statement (2.17), recall the process
\mathbf{g}^{t}=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}-\int_{0}^{t}r_{g}(t-s)\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}\mathrm{d}s . Then
\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t\top}\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}\rangle=\left\langle\frac{1}{n}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t\top}\mathbf{g}^{t}+\int_{0}^{t}r_{g}(t-s)\frac{1}{n}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}\mathrm{d}s\right\rangle.
Recall from the equicontinuity (5.18)
and Theorem 2.4(c) that
\lim_{n\to\infty}\sup_{s\in[0,t]}\left|\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}\rangle-C_{\theta}(t,s)\right|=0\text{ a.s.},\qquad\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t\top}\mathbf{g}^{t}\rangle=\mathbb{E}[\theta^{t}g^{t}]\text{ a.s.}
where \mathbb{E}[\theta^{t}g^{t}] is the expectation in the dynamical mean-field limit of
Definition 2.3. To compute this expectation, note that Itô’s lemma
applied to (2.2) gives
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\frac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}(\theta^{t})^{2}=\mathbb{E}\theta^{t}\left({-}U^{\prime}(\theta^{t})+\int_{0}^{t}R_{g}(t,s)\theta^{s}\mathrm{d}s+g^{t}\right)+1.
Therefore
\mathbb{E}[\theta^{t}g^{t}]=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\frac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}(\theta^{t})^{2}+\mathbb{E}[\theta^{t}U^{\prime}(\theta^{t})]-\int_{0}^{t}R_{g}(t,s)C_{\theta}(t,s)\mathrm{d}s-1.
Applying this above,
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t\top}\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}\rangle=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}(\theta^{t})^{2}+\mathbb{E}[\theta^{t}U^{\prime}(\theta^{t})]-1+\int_{0}^{t}(r_{g}(t-s)-R_{g}(t,s))C_{\theta}(t,s)\mathrm{d}s\text{ a.s.}
By the equicontinuity (5.18),
for any T>0 , this convergence holds uniformly over t\in[T,2T] . Then also
\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\int_{T}^{2T}\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t\top}\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}\rangle\mathrm{d}t
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2T}\big(\mathbb{E}(\theta^{2T})^{2}-\mathbb{E}(\theta^{T})^{2}\big)+\frac{1}{T}\int_{T}^{2T}\Big(\mathbb{E}[\theta^{t}U^{\prime}(\theta^{t})]-1\Big)\mathrm{d}t
\displaystyle\quad+\frac{1}{T}\int_{T}^{2T}\mathrm{d}t\int_{0}^{t}(r_{g}(t-s)-R_{g}(t,s))C_{\theta}(t,s)\mathrm{d}s\text{ a.s.}
The Wasserstein convergence (5.69) and bounds for
|C_{\theta}(t,s)| and \int_{0}^{t}|r_{g}(t-s)-R_{g}(t,s)|\mathrm{d}s in Lemmas
4.1 and 4.2 imply that the first and third
terms on the right side vanish as T\to\infty , while the second term
converges to
\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}\langle\theta U^{\prime}(\theta)\rangle_{v_{*},q_{*},\xi}-1.
This may be evaluated by noting that, for any fixed \xi\in\mathbb{R} ,
\displaystyle\left\langle\theta\left({-}U^{\prime}(\theta)+\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(v_{*}-q_{*})\theta+\sqrt{q_{*}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(v_{*}-q_{*})}\,\xi\right)\right\rangle_{v_{*},q_{*},\xi}
\displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\theta\mu^{\prime}(\theta\mid v_{*},q_{*},\xi)\mathrm{d}\theta=-\int\mu(\theta\mid v_{*},q_{*},\xi)\mathrm{d}\theta=-1.
Therefore, integrating by parts also in \xi ,
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}\langle{\theta U^{\prime}(\theta)}\rangle_{v_{*},q_{*},\xi}-1
\displaystyle=\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(v_{*}-q_{*})\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}\langle\theta^{2}\rangle_{v_{*},q_{*},\xi}+\sqrt{q_{*}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(v_{*}-q_{*})}\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}[\xi\langle\theta\rangle_{v_{*},q_{*},\xi}]
\displaystyle=\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(v_{*}-q_{*})\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}\langle\theta^{2}\rangle_{v_{*},q_{*},\xi}+q_{*}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(v_{*}-q_{*})\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}[\langle\theta^{2}\rangle_{v_{*},q_{*},\xi}-\langle\theta\rangle_{v_{*},q_{*},\xi}^{2}]
\displaystyle=v_{*}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(v_{*}-q_{*})+q_{*}(v_{*}-q_{*})\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(v_{*}-q_{*}).
This shows
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\int_{T}^{2T}\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t\top}\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}\rangle=v_{*}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(v_{*}-q_{*})+q_{*}(v_{*}-q_{*})\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(v_{*}-q_{*})+o_{T}(1)\text{
a.s.},
where o_{T}(1) denotes an error vanishing as T\to\infty . The Wasserstein
bound (5.70) and Assumption 4.3
imply that for any t\in[T,2T] ,
\left|\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t\top}\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}\rangle-\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}\rangle\right|\leq Ce^{-ct}.
Then taking the limit n\to\infty followed by T\to\infty shows
(2.17).
Part (b). Let
\mu_{\beta}(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\frac{1}{\mathcal{Z}_{\beta}}\exp\left(\frac{\beta}{2}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}U(\theta_{i})\right)\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta},\quad\mathcal{Z}_{\beta}=\int\exp\left(\frac{\beta}{2}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}U(\theta_{i})\right)\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta},
and write \langle f(\boldsymbol{\theta})\rangle_{\beta} for the Gibbs average under
\mu_{\beta} . Then
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\beta}\frac{1}{n}\log\mathcal{Z}_{\beta}=\frac{1}{2n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}\rangle_{\beta}.
The result (2.17) for \beta\mathbf{X} in place of \mathbf{X} shows, for
each \beta\in[0,1] , almost surely
\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}(\beta\mathbf{X})\boldsymbol{\theta}\rangle_{\beta}
\displaystyle=v_{*}(\beta)\mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}(v_{*}(\beta)-q_{*}(\beta))
\displaystyle+q_{*}(\beta)(v_{*}(\beta)-q_{*}(\beta))\mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}^{\prime}(v_{*}(\beta)-q_{*}(\beta))
where v_{*}(\beta),q_{*}(\beta) are the limits ensured by Theorem
2.6(a) for \mu_{\beta} ,
and \mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}(x) is the R-transform of
\beta\Lambda . Writing \{\kappa_{p}\}_{p\geq 1} for the free cumulants of
\Lambda , those of \beta\Lambda are then \{\beta^{p}\kappa_{p}\}_{p\geq 1} ,
so
\mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}(x)=\sum_{p\geq 1}\beta^{p+1}\kappa_{p+1}x^{p}=\beta\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(\beta x),\qquad\mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}^{\prime}(x)=\beta^{2}\mathcal{R}^{\prime}_{\Lambda}(\beta x).
Applying this above, integrating over \beta\in[0,1] , and applying dominated
convergence (noting that the bound (4.11) for
\langle\frac{1}{n}\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_{2}^{2}\rangle_{\beta} is uniform in \beta ),
\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\log\mathcal{Z}
\displaystyle=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\log\mathcal{Z}_{0}+\int_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{2n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}\rangle_{\beta}\mathrm{d}\beta
(5.71)
\displaystyle=\log\int e^{-U(\theta)}\mathrm{d}\theta+\int_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{2}\Big(v_{*}(\beta)\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(\beta(v_{*}(\beta)-q_{*}(\beta)))
\displaystyle\hskip 108.405pt+\beta q_{*}(\beta)(v_{*}(\beta)-q_{*}(\beta))\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(\beta(v_{*}(\beta)-q_{*}(\beta))\Big)\mathrm{d}\beta.
To compare this to the replica formula, note first that
when Assumption 2.5 holds with
uniform constants C,c>0 for the dynamics defined by \beta\mathbf{X} and each
\beta\in[0,1] , the functions v_{*}(\beta),q_{*}(\beta) must be
Hölder-continuous over \beta\in[0,1] .
Indeed, letting \{\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\beta}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0}
denote the solution of (2.11) for \beta\mathbf{X} and letting
\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\beta}\sim\mu_{\beta} denote a sample from the Gibbs measure,
Assumption 2.5 implies
(5.72)
\left|\frac{1}{n}\langle\|\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\beta}^{t}\|_{2}^{2}\rangle-\frac{1}{n}\langle\|\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\beta}\|_{2}^{2}\rangle\right|\leq Ce^{-ct}\text{ for all }t\geq 0,\,\beta\in[0,1].
For \beta,\beta^{\prime}\in[0,1] , coupling \{\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\beta}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} and
\{\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\beta^{\prime}}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} by the same Brownian motion and applying
the bound (4.13) which holds for
\{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}_{\beta}\}_{t\geq 0} uniformly over \beta\in[0,1] , we have
\displaystyle\left|\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\langle\|\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\beta}^{t}-\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\beta^{\prime}}^{t}\|_{2}^{2}\rangle\right|
\displaystyle=\left|\langle 2(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\beta}^{t}-\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\beta^{\prime}}^{t})^{\top}(\beta\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\beta}^{t}-U^{\prime}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\beta}^{t})-\beta^{\prime}\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\beta^{\prime}}^{t}+U^{\prime}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\beta^{\prime}}^{t}))\rangle\right|
\displaystyle\leq C\langle\|\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\beta}^{t}-\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\beta^{\prime}}^{t}\|_{2}^{2}\rangle+Cn|\beta-\beta^{\prime}|
for a constant C>0 . Then by Grönwall’s inequality, \frac{1}{n}\langle\|\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\beta}^{t}-\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\beta^{\prime}}^{t}\|_{2}^{2}\rangle\leq Ce^{Ct}|\beta-\beta^{\prime}| .
By (4.13) and Cauchy-Schwarz, this implies for a (different)
constant C>0 that
(5.73)
\left|\frac{1}{n}\langle\|\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\beta}^{t}\|_{2}^{2}\rangle-\frac{1}{n}\langle\|\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\beta^{\prime}}^{t}\|_{2}^{2}\rangle\right|\leq Ce^{Ct}|\beta-\beta^{\prime}|\text{ for all }t\geq 0,\,\beta,\beta^{\prime}\in[0,1].
Combining (5.72) and (5.73), taking the limit
n\to\infty , and optimizing over t shows that v_{*}(\beta) is Hölder
continuous over \beta\in[0,1] with some exponent \rho\in(0,1) ,
i.e. |v_{*}(\beta)-v_{*}(\beta^{\prime})|\leq C|\beta-\beta^{\prime}|^{\rho} for a constant C>0 .
A similar argument establishes Hölder continuity
of q_{*}(\beta) with the same exponent \rho\in(0,1) .
Now let \alpha be the bound for
U^{\prime\prime}(\cdot) in (2.10). Fixing some small enough constant
\varepsilon>0 , define
\displaystyle S=\Bigg\{(\beta,v,q):\beta\in[0,1],\;v>q\geq 0,\;\sum_{p\geq 1}\beta^{p+1}|\kappa_{p+1}|(v-q+\varepsilon)^{p}<\alpha,\;q\mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}^{\prime}(v-q)\geq 0\Bigg\}.
By the given condition (2.12) and Lemma 4.2(b),
(\beta,v_{*}(\beta),q_{*}(\beta))\in S for all \beta\in[0,1] .
For (\beta,v,q)\in S , we may define
\displaystyle f(\beta,v,q)
\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}\log\int\exp\left(-U(\theta)+\frac{1}{2}\,\mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}(v-q)\theta^{2}+\sqrt{q\mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}^{\prime}(v-q)}\,\xi\theta\right)\mathrm{d}\theta
\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{v-q}\mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}(s)\mathrm{d}s-\frac{1}{2}\,(v-q)\mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}(v-q)-\frac{1}{2}\,q(v-q)\mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}^{\prime}(v-q)
and also the probability density on \mathbb{R}
\mu_{\beta}(\theta\mid v,q,\xi)\propto\exp\left(-U(\theta)+\frac{1}{2}\,\mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}(v-q)\theta^{2}+\sqrt{q\mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}^{\prime}(v-q)}\,\xi\theta\right)\mathrm{d}\theta.
Let us momentarily write \langle\cdot\rangle without subscript
for its associated expectation.
Note that at any (\beta,v,q)\in S where q\mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}^{\prime}(v-q)>0
strictly, f(\beta,v,q) is continuously-differentiable,
and a calculation via integration-by-parts on \xi shows
\displaystyle\partial_{\beta}f(\beta,v,q)
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\bigg(\mathbb{E}_{\xi}[\partial_{\beta}\mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}(v-q)\langle\theta^{2}\rangle+q\partial_{\beta}\mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}^{\prime}(v-q)(\langle\theta^{2}\rangle-\langle\theta\rangle^{2})]
\displaystyle\qquad+\int_{0}^{v-q}\partial_{\beta}\mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}(s)\mathrm{d}s-(v-q)\partial_{\beta}\mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}(v-q)-q(v-q)\partial_{\beta}\mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}^{\prime}(v-q)\bigg),
\displaystyle\partial_{v}f(\beta,v,q)
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\bigg(\mathbb{E}_{\xi}[\mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}^{\prime}(v-q)\langle\theta^{2}\rangle+q\mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}^{\prime\prime}(v-q)(\langle\theta^{2}\rangle-\langle\theta\rangle^{2})]
\displaystyle\hskip 72.26999pt-v\mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}^{\prime}(v-q)-q(v-q)\mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}^{\prime\prime}(v-q)\bigg),
\displaystyle\partial_{q}f(\beta,v,q)
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\bigg(\mathbb{E}_{\xi}[{-}\mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}^{\prime}(v-q)\langle\theta\rangle^{2}-q\mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}^{\prime\prime}(v-q)(\langle\theta^{2}\rangle-\langle\theta\rangle^{2})]
\displaystyle\hskip 72.26999pt+q\mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}^{\prime}(v-q)+q(v-q)\mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}^{\prime\prime}(v-q)\bigg).
These derivative formulas extend continuously to points (\beta,v,q)\in S where
q\mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}^{\prime}(v-q)=0 , and we take these extensions to be the
definitions of \partial_{\beta}f,\partial_{v}f,\partial_{q}f at such points.
Since v_{*}(\beta),q_{*}(\beta) satisfy the fixed point
conditions (2.16), the above forms of \partial_{v}f,\partial_{q}f imply
(5.74)
\partial_{v}f(\beta,v_{*}(\beta),q_{*}(\beta))=0,\qquad\partial_{q}f(\beta,v_{*}(\beta),q_{*}(\beta))=0.
From the identity \mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}(x)=\beta\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(\beta x) , we have
\partial_{\beta}\mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}(x)=\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(\beta x)+\beta x\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(\beta x) and
\int_{0}^{x}\partial_{\beta}\mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}(s)\mathrm{d}s=\int_{0}^{x}\left[\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(\beta s)+\beta s\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(\beta s)\right]\mathrm{d}s=x\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(\beta x),
the last equality applying integration-by-parts for the second term. Then also
\displaystyle\partial_{\beta}f(\beta,v_{*}(\beta),q_{*}(\beta))
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\left(\int_{0}^{v_{*}(\beta)-q_{*}(\beta)}\partial_{\beta}\mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}(s)\mathrm{d}s+q_{*}(\beta)\partial_{\beta}\mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}(v_{*}(\beta)-q_{*}(\beta))\right)
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\Big(v_{*}(\beta)\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(\beta(v_{*}(\beta)-q_{*}(\beta)))+\beta q_{*}(\beta)(v_{*}(\beta)-q_{*}(\beta))\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(\beta(v_{*}(\beta)-q_{*}(\beta)))\Big)
which matches the integrand in (5.71).
The above continuity of v_{*}(\beta),q_{*}(\beta) implies that
\beta\mapsto f(\beta,v_{*}(\beta),q_{*}(\beta)) is continuous on [0,1] . We
claim that it is in fact continuously-differentiable on (0,1) , with derivative
(5.75)
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\beta}f(\beta,v_{*}(\beta),q_{*}(\beta))=\partial_{\beta}f(\beta,v_{*}(\beta),q_{*}(\beta)).
To check differentiability, we extend f(\beta,v,q) smoothly to an open domain: Let \ell_{\beta,v,q}(z)=\log\int\exp\left(-U(\theta)+\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}(v-q)\theta^{2}+z\theta\right)d\theta , which is well-defined and analytic over z\in\mathbb{R} for all (\beta,v,q) such that \beta\in(0,1) , v>q , and \sum_{p\geq 1}\beta^{p+1}|\kappa_{p+1}|(v-q+\varepsilon)^{p}<\alpha . Consider \tilde{\ell}_{\beta,v,q}(s)=\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}[\ell_{\beta,v,q}(\sqrt{s}\xi)] for s\geq 0 . By Gaussian integration by parts,
\frac{\partial^{j}}{\partial s^{j}}\tilde{\ell}_{\beta,v,q}(s)=\frac{1}{2^{j}}\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}\left[\frac{\partial^{2j}}{\partial z^{2j}}\ell_{\beta,v,q}(\sqrt{s}\xi)\right],\quad j=1,2,\ldots
By dominated convergence, we can take the limit s\to 0+ and conclude that \tilde{\ell}_{\beta,v,q}(s) has finite derivatives of all orders at s=0 from the positive side. Pick N to be a large enough integer such that (N+1)\rho>1 . We extend \tilde{\ell}_{\beta,v,q}(s) by
\displaystyle\tilde{\ell}_{\beta,v,q}(s)=\begin{cases}\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}[\ell_{\beta,v,q}(\sqrt{s}\xi)],&s\geq 0,\\
\sum_{j=0}^{N+1}\frac{\tilde{\ell}^{(j)}(0)}{j!}s^{j},&s<0.\end{cases}
From now on, we understand f(\beta,v,q)=\tilde{\ell}_{\beta,v,q}(q\mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}^{\prime}(v-q))+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{v-q}\mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}(s)ds-\frac{1}{2}(v-q)\mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}(v-q)-\frac{1}{2}q(v-q)\mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}^{\prime}(v-q) with this extension on the enlarged domain
\displaystyle S^{\prime}
\displaystyle=\Bigg\{(\beta,v,q):\beta\in(0,1),\;v>q,
\displaystyle\hskip 72.26999pt\text{there exists }\delta>0\text{ s.t. }\sum_{p\geq 1}\beta^{p+1}|\kappa_{p+1}|(v-q+\delta)^{p}<\alpha\Bigg\}.
Importantly, this domain S^{\prime} is open, and f is C^{N+1} over (\beta,v,q)\in S^{\prime} . Now fix any \beta_{0}\in(0,1) . For any \beta sufficiently close to \beta_{0} , we have
\displaystyle f(\beta,v_{*}(\beta),q_{*}(\beta))-f(\beta_{0},v_{*}(\beta_{0}),q_{*}(\beta_{0}))
\displaystyle=(f(\beta,v_{*}(\beta),q_{*}(\beta))-f(\beta_{0},v_{*}(\beta),q_{*}(\beta)))+(f(\beta_{0},v_{*}(\beta),q_{*}(\beta))-f(\beta_{0},v_{*}(\beta_{0}),q_{*}(\beta_{0})))
\displaystyle=\partial_{\beta}f(\beta_{0},v_{*}(\beta),q_{*}(\beta))(\beta-\beta_{0})+o(|\beta-\beta_{0}|)+(f(\beta_{0},v_{*}(\beta),q_{*}(\beta))-f(\beta_{0},v_{*}(\beta_{0}),q_{*}(\beta_{0}))).
It then suffices to show f(\beta_{0},v_{*}(\beta),q_{*}(\beta))-f(\beta_{0},v_{*}(\beta_{0}),q_{*}(\beta_{0}))=o(|\beta-\beta_{0}|) . Denote \Delta v_{\beta}=v_{*}(\beta)-v_{*}(\beta_{0}) and \Delta q_{\beta}=q_{*}(\beta)-q_{*}(\beta_{0}) . By the Hölder continuity of v_{*} and q_{*} , we have |\Delta v_{\beta}|+|\Delta q_{\beta}|=O(|\beta-\beta_{0}|^{\rho}) . By Taylor expansion of f(\beta_{0},\cdot,\cdot) at (v_{*}(\beta_{0}),q_{*}(\beta_{0})) , we have
\displaystyle f(\beta_{0},v_{*}(\beta),q_{*}(\beta))-f(\beta_{0},v_{*}(\beta_{0}),q_{*}(\beta_{0}))=P_{N}(\Delta v_{\beta},\Delta q_{\beta})+O(|\Delta v_{\beta}|^{N+1}+|\Delta q_{\beta}|^{N+1}),
where P_{N} is a polynomial of degree at most N . From the condition (5.74), the first order term of P_{N} vanishes, and also
\displaystyle|\partial_{v}f(\beta_{0},v_{*}(\beta),q_{*}(\beta))|=|\partial_{v}f(\beta_{0},v_{*}(\beta),q_{*}(\beta))-\partial_{v}f(\beta,v_{*}(\beta),q_{*}(\beta))|=O(|\beta-\beta_{0}|).
Combining with the fact that
|\partial_{v}P_{N}(\Delta v_{\beta},\Delta q_{\beta})-\partial_{v}f(\beta_{0},v_{*}(\beta),q_{*}(\beta))|=O(|\Delta v_{\beta}|^{N}+|\Delta q_{\beta}|^{N}) ,
we have
|\partial_{v}P_{N}(\Delta v_{\beta},\Delta q_{\beta})|=O(|\beta-\beta_{0}|+|\Delta v_{\beta}|^{N}+|\Delta q_{\beta}|^{N}) .
Similarly, we have
|\partial_{q}P_{N}(\Delta v_{\beta},\Delta q_{\beta})|=O(|\beta-\beta_{0}|+|\Delta v_{\beta}|^{N}+|\Delta q_{\beta}|^{N}) .
Then by the Bochnak–Łojasiewicz inequality
[46, Lemma 4.3],
\displaystyle|P_{N}(\Delta v_{\beta},\Delta q_{\beta})|
\displaystyle\leq C(|\Delta v_{\beta}|+|\Delta q_{\beta}|)\cdot(|\partial_{v}P_{N}(\Delta v_{\beta},\Delta q_{\beta})|+|\partial_{q}P_{N}(\Delta v_{\beta},\Delta q_{\beta})|)
\displaystyle=O(|\beta-\beta_{0}|^{1+\rho}+|\beta-\beta_{0}|^{(N+1)\rho})=o(|\beta-\beta_{0}|),
where the last equality uses \rho\in(0,1) and N large enough such that (N+1)\rho>1 . This shows f(\beta_{0},v_{*}(\beta),q_{*}(\beta))-f(\beta_{0},v_{*}(\beta_{0}),q_{*}(\beta_{0}))=o(|\beta-\beta_{0}|) , and hence (5.75) holds immediately by the definition of the derivative.
Note that for \beta=0 , we have \mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}(x)=0
and \mathcal{R}_{\beta\Lambda}^{\prime}(x)=0 for all x\in\mathbb{R} , so
f(0,\allowbreak v_{*}(0),\allowbreak q_{*}(0))=\log\int e^{-U(\theta)}\mathrm{d}\theta .
Applying this and (5.75) to (5.71), and
using the continuous differentiability of \beta\mapsto f(\beta,\allowbreak v_{*}(\beta),\allowbreak q_{*}(\beta)) ,
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\log\mathcal{Z}=f(0,v_{*}(0),q_{*}(0))+\int_{0}^{1}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\beta}f(\beta,v_{*}(\beta),q_{*}(\beta))\mathrm{d}\beta=f(1,v_{*}(1),q_{*}(1)).
The right side is the desired replica formula in Theorem
2.6(b), concluding the proof.
∎
Proof of Corollary 2.7.
We let \boldsymbol{\theta}^{0} have i.i.d. entries with (arbitrary) law supported on [-1,1] , and restrict to an event holding a.s. for all large n where
\|\mathbf{X}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\Lambda_{\max}.
Write
\mathrm{d}\nu_{x}(y)=\frac{e^{\alpha xy-\frac{\alpha}{2}y^{2}}\mathrm{d}\nu(y)}{\int_{-M}^{M}e^{\alpha xy-\frac{\alpha}{2}y^{2}}\mathrm{d}\nu(y)},\qquad\langle f(y)\rangle_{\nu_{x}}=\int_{-M}^{M}f(y)\mathrm{d}\nu_{x}(y),\qquad\operatorname{Var}_{\nu_{x}}[y]=\langle y^{2}\rangle_{\nu_{x}}-\langle y\rangle_{\nu_{x}}^{2}.
Then
\displaystyle U^{\prime\prime}(x)
\displaystyle=\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}}{\mathrm{d}x^{2}}\left[-\log\int_{-M}^{M}\sqrt{\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{\alpha}{2}(x-y)^{2}}\mathrm{d}\nu(y)\right]
\displaystyle=\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}}{\mathrm{d}x^{2}}\left[\frac{\alpha}{2}x^{2}-\log\int_{-M}^{M}e^{\alpha xy-\frac{\alpha}{2}y^{2}}\mathrm{d}\nu(y)\right]=\alpha-\alpha^{2}\operatorname{Var}_{\nu_{x}}[y].
As x\to\pm\infty , the measure \nu_{x} converges weakly to a point mass
at the maximum/minimum point of support of \nu . Then \operatorname{Var}_{\nu_{x}}[y]\to 0 .
Thus U(\cdot) satisfies
(2.10). The same argument shows that the 3rd and 4th cumulants of \nu_{x}
converge to 0 as x\to\pm\infty , so also
\lim_{|x|\to\pm\infty}U^{\prime\prime\prime}(x)=0 and \lim_{|x|\to\pm\infty}U^{(4)}(x)=0 . Hence f={-}U^{\prime} satisfies the conditions
of Assumption 2.2.
To check the condition (2.12), observe that we may represent
\boldsymbol{\theta}\sim\prod_{i=1}^{n}e^{-U(\theta_{i})}\mathrm{d}\theta_{i}
as \boldsymbol{\theta}=\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{z} where \mathbf{y},\mathbf{z} are independent vectors with
y_{i}\overset{iid}{\sim}\nu and \mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\alpha^{-1}\mathrm{Id}) .
Thus
\displaystyle\mathcal{Z}
\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{z})^{\top}\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{z})\right)\bigg|\mathbf{X}\right],
\displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}\rangle
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n\mathcal{Z}^{2}}\left\|\mathbb{E}\left[(\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{z})\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{z})^{\top}\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{z})\right)\bigg|\mathbf{X}\right]\right\|_{2}^{2},
\displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\langle\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_{2}^{2}\rangle
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n\mathcal{Z}}\,\mathbb{E}\left[\|\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{z}\|_{2}^{2}\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{z})^{\top}\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{z})\right)\bigg|\mathbf{X}\right]
where expectations are over the joint law of (\mathbf{y},\mathbf{z}) .
Evaluating the expectation over \mathbf{z} for fixed \mathbf{X},\mathbf{y} ,
where \|\mathbf{X}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\Lambda_{\max}<\alpha , an explicit calculation shows
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{z})^{\top}\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{z})\right)\bigg|\mathbf{X},\mathbf{y}\right]
\displaystyle=\underbrace{\frac{\exp(\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{y}^{\top}\mathbf{X}(\mathrm{Id}-\alpha^{-1}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{y})}{\det(\mathrm{Id}-\alpha^{-1}\mathbf{X})^{1/2}}}_{:=\mathcal{Z}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{y})}
and
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[(\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{z})\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{z})^{\top}\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{z})\right)\bigg|\mathbf{X},\mathbf{y}\right]
\displaystyle=\mathcal{Z}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{y})(\mathrm{Id}-\alpha^{-1}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{y},
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\|\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{z}\|_{2}^{2}\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{z})^{\top}\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{z})\right)\bigg|\mathbf{X},\mathbf{y}\right]
\displaystyle=\mathcal{Z}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{y})\left(\begin{aligned} &\alpha^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}(\mathrm{Id}-\alpha^{-1}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\\
&+\mathbf{y}^{\top}(\mathrm{Id}-\alpha^{-1}\mathbf{X})^{-2}\mathbf{y}\end{aligned}\right).
Thus
(5.76)
\displaystyle\mathcal{Z}
\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{Z}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{y})\mid\mathbf{X}],
\displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}\rangle
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\,\frac{\|\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{Z}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{y})(\mathrm{Id}-\alpha^{-1}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{y}\mid\mathbf{X}]\|_{2}^{2}}{\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{Z}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{y})\mid\mathbf{X}]^{2}},
\displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\langle\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_{2}^{2}\rangle
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\,\frac{\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{Z}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{y})(\alpha^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}(\mathrm{Id}-\alpha^{-1}\mathbf{X})^{-1}+\mathbf{y}^{\top}(\mathrm{Id}-\alpha^{-1}\mathbf{X})^{-2}\mathbf{y})\mid\mathbf{X}]}{\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{Z}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{y})\mid\mathbf{X}]}.
Since
\frac{1}{n}\left|\alpha^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}(\mathrm{Id}-\alpha^{-1}\mathbf{X})^{-1}+\mathbf{y}^{\top}(\mathrm{Id}-\alpha^{-1}\mathbf{X})^{-2}\mathbf{y}\right|\leq\frac{1}{\alpha-\Lambda_{\max}}+\frac{\alpha^{2}M^{2}}{(\alpha-\Lambda_{\max})^{2}}
for all \mathbf{y} in the support [-M,M]^{n}
of \prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathrm{d}\nu(y_{i}) , this implies
0\leq\frac{1}{n}\langle\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_{2}^{2}\rangle-\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}\rangle\leq\frac{1}{n}\langle\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_{2}^{2}\rangle\leq\frac{1}{\alpha-\Lambda_{\max}}+\frac{\alpha^{2}M^{2}}{(\alpha-\Lambda_{\max})^{2}}.
Then the given conditions of (2.20) in the
corollary imply the required conditions (2.12) for \alpha
in Theorem 2.6.
It remains to check Assumption 2.5. We verify a log-Sobolev inequality for
\mu_{\mathrm{Gibbs}} following the argument of [6]: Let
\omega=\Lambda_{\max}+\varepsilon
and write
\mu_{\mathrm{Gibbs}}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\propto\exp\left({-}\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}(\omega\,\mathrm{Id}-\mathbf{X})\boldsymbol{\theta}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\frac{\omega}{2}\theta_{i}^{2}-U(\theta_{i})\right)\right)
Then \varepsilon\,\mathrm{Id}\preceq\omega\,\mathrm{Id}-\mathbf{X}\preceq(2\omega-\varepsilon)\,\mathrm{Id}
in the positive-definite ordering, so we have
(\omega\,\mathrm{Id}-\mathbf{X})^{-1}=(2\omega\,\mathrm{Id})^{-1}+\mathbf{B}^{-1}
for some \mathbf{B}\succ 0 . Hence,
expressing the Gaussian measure with covariance (\omega\,\mathrm{Id}-\mathbf{X})^{-1}
as a convolution of those with covariances (2\omega\,\mathrm{Id})^{-1} and \mathbf{B}^{-1} ,
\exp\left({-}\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}(\omega\,\mathrm{Id}-\mathbf{X})\boldsymbol{\theta}\right)\propto\int\exp\left({-}\frac{2\omega}{2}\|\boldsymbol{\theta}-\boldsymbol{\varphi}\|_{2}^{2}\right)\exp\left({-}\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\varphi}^{\top}\mathbf{B}\boldsymbol{\varphi}\right)\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\varphi}.
Thus
(5.77)
\displaystyle\mu_{\mathrm{Gibbs}}(\boldsymbol{\theta})
\displaystyle\propto\int\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\varphi}\exp\underbrace{\left({-}\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\varphi}^{\top}\mathbf{B}\boldsymbol{\varphi}+\log\sum_{i=1}^{n}\int\exp\left(\frac{\omega}{2}\theta_{i}^{2}-U(\theta_{i})-\omega(\theta_{i}-\varphi_{i})^{2}\right)\mathrm{d}\theta\right)}_{:={-}V(\boldsymbol{\varphi})}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mu_{\varphi_{i}}(\theta_{i})
where
\mu_{\varphi}(\theta)=\frac{\exp((\omega/2)\theta^{2}-U(\theta)-\omega(\theta-\varphi)^{2})}{\int\exp((\omega/2)\theta^{2}-U(\theta)-\omega(\theta-\varphi)^{2})\mathrm{d}\theta}.
Under the condition (2.12) checked above, each univariate law
\mu_{\varphi_{i}} satisfies a log-Sobolev inequality on \mathbb{R} with
log-Sobolev constant depending only on \omega and U(\cdot) and not on
\varphi_{i} , by the same argument as (5.64). Furthermore,
writing
\langle f(\theta)\rangle_{\varphi}=\int f(\theta)\mu_{\varphi}(\theta)\mathrm{d}\theta,\quad\operatorname{Var}_{\varphi}[\theta]=\langle\theta^{2}\rangle_{\varphi}-\langle\theta\rangle_{\varphi}^{2},
we have
(5.78)
\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}}{\mathrm{d}\varphi^{2}}\left[{-}\log\int\exp\Big(\frac{\omega}{2}\theta^{2}-U(\theta)-\omega(\theta-\varphi)^{2}\Big)\mathrm{d}\theta\right]=2\omega-4\omega^{2}\operatorname{Var}_{\varphi}[\theta].
Recalling that e^{-U(\theta)} is the law of
y+z where y\sim\nu and z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\alpha^{-1}) , we have furthermore
\displaystyle\mu_{\varphi}(\theta)
\displaystyle\propto\int_{-M}^{M}\exp\left(\frac{\omega}{2}\theta^{2}-\omega(\theta-\varphi)^{2}\right)\exp\left({-}\frac{\alpha}{2}(\theta-y)^{2}\right)\nu(\mathrm{d}y)
\displaystyle\propto\int_{-M}^{M}\exp\Big({-}\frac{\alpha+\omega}{2}\theta^{2}+(\alpha y+2\omega\varphi)\theta-\frac{\alpha}{2}y^{2}\Big)\nu(\mathrm{d}y)
\displaystyle\propto\int_{-M}^{M}\exp\Big({-}\frac{\alpha+\omega}{2}\Big(\theta-\frac{\alpha y+2\omega\varphi}{\alpha+\omega}\Big)^{2}\Big)\tilde{\nu}_{\varphi}(\mathrm{d}y),
for some probability measure \tilde{\nu}_{\varphi} supported on [-M,M] and
depending on (\alpha,\omega,\varphi) . Thus \mu_{\varphi}(\theta)
is the law of
\theta=\frac{2\omega\varphi}{\alpha+\omega}+\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\omega}y+z,\qquad y\sim\tilde{\nu}_{\varphi},\qquad z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,(\alpha+\omega)^{-1}),
and y,z are independent. Then
\operatorname{Var}_{\varphi}[\theta]=\frac{\alpha^{2}}{(\alpha+\omega)^{2}}\operatorname{Var}_{\tilde{\nu}}[y]+\frac{1}{\alpha+\omega}\leq\frac{\alpha^{2}M^{2}}{(\alpha+\omega)^{2}}+\frac{1}{\alpha+\omega}\leq M^{2}+\frac{1}{\alpha+\omega}.
Recalling \omega=\Lambda_{\max}+\varepsilon and choosing \varepsilon small enough, the
second given condition of (2.20) ensures
2\omega-4\omega^{2}\operatorname{Var}_{\varphi}[\theta]\geq\varepsilon.
Applying this to (5.78) shows that
V(\boldsymbol{\varphi}) defined in (5.77) is a
uniformly strongly convex potential, so e^{-V(\boldsymbol{\varphi})}
satisfies a log-Sobolev inequality on \mathbb{R}^{n} with log-Sobolev constant depending
only on \varepsilon . Then the argument of [6] verifies that
\mu_{\mathrm{Gibbs}} also satisfies a log-Sobolev inequality on \mathbb{R}^{n} , with
log-Sobolev constant depending only on \omega,\varepsilon,U(\cdot) .
This implies by a T_{2} -transportation inequality, contraction of relative
entropy, and log-Harnack/entropy-cost inequality (as in the proof of Theorem 2.6) that for any
deterministic vector \boldsymbol{\theta}^{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and t\geq 1 ,
\displaystyle W_{2}(\operatorname{Law}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0}),\,\mu_{\mathrm{Gibbs}})^{2}
\displaystyle\leq CD_{\mathrm{KL}}(\operatorname{Law}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0})\|\,\mu_{\mathrm{Gibbs}})
\displaystyle\leq Ce^{-c(t-1)}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\operatorname{Law}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{1}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0})\|\,\mu_{\mathrm{Gibbs}})
\displaystyle\leq C^{\prime}e^{-ct}W_{2}(\delta_{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0}},\,\mu_{\mathrm{Gibbs}})^{2}
\displaystyle\leq 2C^{\prime}e^{-ct}(\|\boldsymbol{\theta}^{0}\|_{2}^{2}+\langle\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_{2}^{2}\rangle).
Recall from (4.11) that \frac{1}{n}\langle\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_{2}^{2}\rangle\leq C , where this requires only the assumptions \|\mathbf{X}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\Lambda_{\max}<\alpha . Then,
applying the above bound with the specified initial condition \boldsymbol{\theta}^{0} having i.i.d. entries on [-1,1] , this implies for all t\geq 1 that
\frac{1}{n}\langle\|\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}\|_{2}^{2}\rangle\leq C.
This holds also for t\in[0,1] , by Itô’s lemma which shows \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\frac{1}{n}\langle\|\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}\|_{2}^{2}\rangle\leq C(\frac{1}{n}\langle\|\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}\|_{2}^{2}\rangle+1) and Grönwall’s inequality. Then, applying the above bound with
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s} in place of \boldsymbol{\theta}^{0}
shows the first statement of Assumption 2.5 for t\geq s+1 .
The bound for t\in[s,s+1] again follows from Itô’s lemma for \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\frac{1}{n}\langle\|\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}-\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}\|_{2}^{2}\rangle and Grönwall’s inequality. The second statement of
Assumption 2.5 follows similarly by applying the above with \tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{0}\sim\mu_{\mathrm{Gibbs}} in place of \boldsymbol{\theta}^{0} .
This checks all needed conditions for Theorem 2.6(a).
Note that if (2.20)
holds, then it also holds for (\beta\Lambda_{\max},\beta^{p+1}\kappa_{p+1}) in
place of (\Lambda_{\max},\kappa_{p+1}) for every \beta\in[0,1] , because
the left side of each condition in (2.20)
for (\beta\Lambda_{\max},\beta^{p+1}\kappa_{p+1}) is increasing
in \beta . Thus, all of the above statements hold also for \beta\mathbf{X} in place
of \mathbf{X} , verifying the needed condition for Theorem 2.6(b).
∎
Proof of Corollary 2.8.
Define the discrete law on \{\pm 1\}
\nu=\frac{e^{h}}{e^{-h}+e^{h}}\,\delta_{+1}+\frac{e^{-h}}{e^{-h}+e^{h}}\,\delta_{-1},\qquad M=1.
Since \Lambda_{\max}<1/2
and \limsup_{p\to\infty}|\kappa_{p}|^{1/p}<1 by Proposition
A.1,
the condition (2.20) holds for all sufficiently
large \alpha . Thus, for all large \alpha ,
Corollary 2.7 holds with the potential
e^{-U_{\alpha}(\theta)}=\frac{e^{h}}{e^{-h}+e^{h}}\sqrt{\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{\alpha}{2}(\theta-1)^{2}}+\frac{e^{-h}}{e^{-h}+e^{h}}\sqrt{\frac{\alpha}{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{\alpha}{2}(\theta+1)^{2}}
Let us define p_{\alpha}(\mathrm{d}\theta)=e^{-U_{\alpha}(\theta)}\mathrm{d}\theta for
\alpha<\infty , and p_{\alpha}(\mathrm{d}\theta)=\nu(\mathrm{d}\theta) for \alpha=\infty .
We denote also
\mu_{\alpha}(\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta})=\frac{1}{\mathcal{Z}_{\alpha}}\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}\right)\prod_{i=1}^{n}p_{\alpha}(\mathrm{d}\theta_{i}),\qquad\mathcal{Z}_{\alpha}=\int\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\theta}\right)\prod_{i=1}^{n}p_{\alpha}(\mathrm{d}\theta_{i})
and write \langle\cdot\rangle_{\alpha} for the associated Gibbs average.
Note then that \mu_{\infty}\equiv\mu_{\text{Ising}} is precisely the Ising
Gibbs measure (2.21), and
(5.79)
\mathcal{Z}_{\infty}=\mathcal{Z}_{\text{Ising}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{e^{-h}+e^{h}}.
Let v_{*}(\alpha),q_{*}(\alpha) be the values corresponding to \mu_{\alpha} ,
for all large enough \alpha<\infty such that
Corollary 2.7 holds.
Recall the explicit forms (5.76)
for \mathcal{Z}_{\alpha} , \frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}\rangle_{\alpha} ,
and \frac{1}{n}\langle\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_{2}^{2}\rangle_{\alpha} , where the expectation
\mathbb{E} is over \mathbf{y}\in\{\pm 1\}^{n} with entries y_{i}\overset{iid}{\sim}\nu .
Write \mathcal{Z}_{\alpha}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{y})\equiv\mathcal{Z}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{y}) to now make explicit the dependence on \alpha . Note that
for any \mathbf{y}\in\{\pm 1\}^{n} , \mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}
with \|\mathbf{X}\|_{\mathrm{op}}<\Lambda_{\max} , and
\alpha>\Lambda_{\max} , we have
\frac{1}{n}\left|\alpha^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}(\mathrm{Id}-\alpha^{-1}\mathbf{X})^{-1}+\mathbf{y}^{\top}(\mathrm{Id}-\alpha^{-1}\mathbf{X})^{-2}\mathbf{y}-1\right|\leq\frac{1}{\alpha-\Lambda_{\max}}+\frac{\alpha^{2}}{(\alpha-\Lambda_{\max})^{2}}-1.
Then the third identity of (5.76) implies
|v_{*}(\alpha)-1|\leq\limsup_{n\to\infty}\left|\frac{1}{n}\langle\|\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_{2}^{2}\rangle_{\alpha}-1\right|\leq\frac{1}{\alpha-\Lambda_{\max}}+\frac{\alpha^{2}}{(\alpha-\Lambda_{\max})^{2}}-1,
so
(5.80)
1=\lim_{\alpha\to\infty}v_{*}(\alpha)
For q_{*}(\alpha) , observe first
that
\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\|(\mathrm{Id}-\alpha^{-1}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{y}\|_{2}\leq\frac{\Lambda_{\max}}{\alpha-\Lambda_{\max}},\qquad\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\|(\mathrm{Id}-\alpha^{-1}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{y}\|_{2}\leq 2+\frac{\Lambda_{\max}}{\alpha-\Lambda_{\max}}.
Hence, by the second identity of (5.76) and Cauchy-Schwarz,
\displaystyle\left|\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}\rangle_{\alpha}-\frac{1}{n}\frac{\|\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{Z}_{\alpha}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{y})\mathbf{y}\mid\mathbf{X}]\|_{2}^{2}}{\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{Z}_{\alpha}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{y})\mid\mathbf{X}]^{2}}\right|
\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{n}\frac{\|\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{Z}_{\alpha}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{y})((\mathrm{Id}-\alpha^{-1}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{y})\mid\mathbf{X}]\|_{2}\cdot\|\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{Z}_{\alpha}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{y})((\mathrm{Id}-\alpha^{-1}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{y})\mid\mathbf{X}]\|_{2}}{\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{Z}_{\alpha}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{y})\mid\mathbf{X}]^{2}}
(5.81)
\displaystyle\leq\frac{\Lambda_{\max}}{\alpha-\Lambda_{\max}}\left(2+\frac{\Lambda_{\max}}{\alpha-\Lambda_{\max}}\right)
Momentarily denoting
[f(\mathbf{y})]_{\omega}=\frac{\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{Z}_{\omega^{-1}}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{y})f(\mathbf{y})\mid\mathbf{X}]}{\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{Z}_{\omega^{-1}}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{y})\mid\mathbf{X}]}=\frac{\mathbb{E}[\exp(\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{y}^{\top}\mathbf{X}(\mathrm{Id}-\omega\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{y})\cdot f(\mathbf{y})\mid\mathbf{X}]}{\mathbb{E}[\exp(\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{y}^{\top}\mathbf{X}(\mathrm{Id}-\omega\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{y})\mid\mathbf{X}]}
and writing \operatorname{Var}_{[\cdot]_{\omega}} and
\operatorname{Cov}_{[\cdot]_{\omega}} for the associated variance and covariance, observe that
\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\omega}[y_{i}]_{\omega}
\displaystyle=\operatorname{Cov}_{[\cdot]_{\omega}}\left[y_{i},\,\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\omega}\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{y}^{\top}\mathbf{X}(\mathrm{Id}-\omega\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{y}\right]
\displaystyle=\operatorname{Cov}_{[\cdot]_{\omega}}\left[y_{i},\,\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{y}^{\top}\mathbf{X}^{2}(\mathrm{Id}-\omega\mathbf{X})^{-2}\mathbf{y}\right].
Then
\displaystyle\left\|\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\omega}[\mathbf{y}]_{\omega}\right\|_{2}
\displaystyle=\sup_{\mathbf{u}:\|\mathbf{u}\|_{2}=1}\operatorname{Cov}_{[\cdot]_{\omega}}\left[\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{y},\,\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{y}^{\top}\mathbf{X}^{2}(\mathrm{Id}-\omega\mathbf{X})^{-2}\mathbf{y}\right]
\displaystyle\leq C\sqrt{n}\sup_{\mathbf{u}:\|\mathbf{u}\|_{2}=1}\operatorname{Var}_{[\cdot]_{\omega}}[\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{y}]^{1/2}
for a constant C>0 and all small \omega . Since \|\mathbf{X}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\Lambda_{\max}<1/2 , also
\|\mathbf{X}(\mathrm{Id}-\omega\mathbf{X})^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}<c_{0}<1/2 for some constant
c_{0}\in(\Lambda_{\max},1/2) and all small enough \omega . Then by the result
of [6], the Gibbs measure on \{\pm 1\}^{n} defining
[\cdot]_{\omega} (having Hamiltonian \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{y}^{\top}\mathbf{X}(\mathrm{Id}-\omega\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{y}+h\sum_{i=1}^{n}y_{i} with respect to the uniform measure over
\mathbf{y}\in\{\pm 1\}^{n} )
satisfies a Poincaré inequality with a dimension-free
Poincaré constant depending only on c_{0},h . Thus,
\operatorname{Var}_{[\cdot]_{\omega}}[\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{y}]\leq C\|\mathbf{u}\|_{2}^{2}\leq C for a constant C>0 , any unit vector \mathbf{u} ,
and all small \omega . Applying this above shows that for all
small enough \omega , \|[\mathbf{y}]_{\omega}-[\mathbf{y}]_{0}\|_{2}\leq C^{\prime}\omega\sqrt{n} .
Thus, there is a constant C>0 such that for all large enough
\alpha<\infty ,
\displaystyle\left|\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}\rangle_{\infty}-\frac{1}{n}\frac{\|\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{Z}_{\alpha}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{y})\mathbf{y}\mid\mathbf{X}]\|_{2}^{2}}{\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{Z}_{\alpha}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{y})\mid\mathbf{X}]^{2}}\right|
\displaystyle=\left|\frac{1}{n}\frac{\|\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{Z}_{\infty}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{y})\mathbf{y}\mid\mathbf{X}]\|_{2}^{2}}{\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{Z}_{\infty}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{y})\mid\mathbf{X}]^{2}}-\frac{1}{n}\frac{\|\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{Z}_{\alpha}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{y})\mathbf{y}\mid\mathbf{X}]\|_{2}^{2}}{\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{Z}_{\alpha}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{y})\mid\mathbf{X}]^{2}}\right|\leq\frac{C}{\alpha}.
Combining this with (5.81) shows
\lim_{\alpha\to\infty}\sup_{n\geq 1}\left|\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}\rangle_{\alpha}-\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}\rangle_{\infty}\right|=0.
Then, since the limit
q_{*}(\alpha)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}\rangle_{\alpha} exists a.s. for all large \alpha ,
this implies that there exists a limit
(5.82)
q_{*}:=\lim_{\alpha\to\infty}q_{*}(\alpha)
for which also
q_{*}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}\rangle_{\infty}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\langle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}\rangle_{\text{Ising}}\text{ a.s.}
For all large \alpha , by Theorem 2.6,
v_{*}(\alpha),q_{*}(\alpha) satisfy the fixed point equation
\displaystyle q_{*}(\alpha)
\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}\left(\frac{\int\theta\exp(\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(v_{*}(\alpha)-q_{*}(\alpha))\theta^{2}+\sqrt{q_{*}(\alpha)\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(v_{*}(\alpha)-q_{*}(\alpha))}\xi\theta)p_{\alpha}(\mathrm{d}\theta)}{\int\exp(\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(v_{*}(\alpha)-q_{*}(\alpha))\theta^{2}+\sqrt{q_{*}(\alpha)\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(v_{*}(\alpha)-q_{*}(\alpha))}\xi\theta)p_{\alpha}(\mathrm{d}\theta)}\right)^{2}.
Then taking \alpha\to\infty and applying
(5.80), (5.82), and the weak convergence of
p_{\alpha} to p_{\infty}=\nu ,
\displaystyle q_{*}
\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}\left(\frac{\int\theta\exp(\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(1-q_{*})\theta^{2}+\sqrt{q_{*}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(1-q_{*})}\xi\theta)\nu(\mathrm{d}\theta)}{\int\exp(\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(1-q_{*})\theta^{2}+\sqrt{q_{*}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(1-q_{*})}\xi\theta)\nu(\mathrm{d}\theta)}\right)^{2}
\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}\tanh\Big(h+\sqrt{q_{*}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(1-q_{*})}\xi\Big)^{2},
the second equality following from definition of \nu(\mathrm{d}\theta) which is
supported on \{\pm 1\} .
We have also
\displaystyle|\log\mathcal{Z}_{\alpha}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{y})-\log\mathcal{Z}_{\infty}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{y})|
\displaystyle\leq\left|\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{y}^{\top}\mathbf{X}(\mathrm{Id}-\alpha^{-1}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{y}-\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{y}^{\top}\mathbf{X}\mathbf{y}\right|+\left|\frac{1}{2}\log\det(\mathrm{Id}-\alpha^{-1}\mathbf{X})\right|
\displaystyle\leq\frac{n}{2}\cdot\frac{\Lambda_{\max}^{2}}{\alpha-\Lambda_{\max}}+\frac{n}{2}\left|\log\left(1-\frac{\Lambda_{\max}}{\alpha}\right)\right|
Thus, applying the first identity of (5.76) and
taking the expectation over \mathbf{y} ,
\lim_{\alpha\to\infty}\sup_{n\geq 1}\left|\frac{1}{n}\log\mathcal{Z}_{\alpha}-\frac{1}{n}\log\mathcal{Z}_{\infty}\right|=0.
Since f(\alpha):=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\log\mathcal{Z}_{\alpha} exists
a.s. for all large \alpha , this implies that almost surely,
\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\log\mathcal{Z}_{\infty}
\displaystyle=\lim_{\alpha\to\infty}f(\alpha)
\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}\log\int\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(1-q_{*})\theta^{2}+\sqrt{q_{*}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(1-q_{*})}\xi\theta\right)\nu(\mathrm{d}\theta)
\displaystyle\hskip 36.135pt+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1-q_{*}}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(s)\mathrm{d}s-\frac{1}{2}(1-q_{*})\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(1-q_{*})-\frac{1}{2}q_{*}(1-q_{*})\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(1-q_{*})
\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}\log 2\cosh\left(h+\sqrt{q_{*}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(1-q_{*})}\xi\right)-\log 2\cosh(h)
\displaystyle\hskip 36.135pt+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1-q_{*}}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(s)\mathrm{d}s+\frac{1}{2}q_{*}\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}(1-q_{*})
\displaystyle\hskip 36.135pt-\frac{1}{2}q_{*}(1-q_{*})\mathcal{R}_{\Lambda}^{\prime}(1-q_{*}).
From (5.79) we have
\frac{1}{n}\log\mathcal{Z}_{\infty}=\frac{1}{n}\log\mathcal{Z}_{\text{Ising}}-\log 2\cosh(h) , proving all statements of the corollary.
∎
6. Universality over the disorder
We prove Corollary 2.10 on universality over the
disorder \mathbf{X} , using the results of [71].
Proof of Corollary 2.10.
Let \tilde{\mathbf{X}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} satisfy Assumption 2.9.
Let \mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} be an orthogonally-invariant matrix
satisfying Assumption 2.1 with the same bound \Lambda_{\max} and
asymptotic eigenvalue distribution \Lambda as \tilde{\mathbf{X}} .
Let \mathbf{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} be
a random diagonal sign matrix as in Corollary 2.10(d),
and let \boldsymbol{\Pi}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} be a uniformly random permutation matrix,
where (\mathbf{S},\boldsymbol{\Pi}) are independent of each other and of \boldsymbol{\theta}^{0},\{\mathbf{b}^{t}\}_{t\geq 0} . Then [71, Proposition 2.7, Theorem 2.8]
implies that the AMP algorithm (3.35) applied with \tilde{\mathbf{X}} has the
same dynamical mean-field limit (3.37) (in the sense of almost-sure
Wasserstein-2 convergence of the coordinatewise empirical distribution of its
iterates) as applied with the matrix
\mathbf{W}=\boldsymbol{\Pi}\mathbf{S}\tilde{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{S}\boldsymbol{\Pi}^{\top}.
As (3.37) and the bound \|\mathbf{X}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\Lambda_{\max} are the only
properties of \mathbf{X} used in all preceding proofs, this implies that
Theorems 2.4, 2.6 and Corollaries
2.7, 2.8 hold equally with \mathbf{W} in place of
\mathbf{X} .
The dynamics (2.1) driven by \mathbf{W} have the form
\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}=[f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t})+\boldsymbol{\Pi}\mathbf{S}\tilde{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{S}\boldsymbol{\Pi}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}]\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{b}^{t}.
Define \mathbf{g}^{t}=\mathbf{W}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t}-\int_{0}^{t}r_{g}(t-s)\boldsymbol{\theta}^{s}\mathrm{d}s as in Theorem
2.4, and let
\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{t}=\boldsymbol{\Pi}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t},\qquad\tilde{\mathbf{g}}^{t}=\boldsymbol{\Pi}^{\top}\mathbf{g}^{t},\qquad\tilde{\mathbf{b}}^{t}=\boldsymbol{\Pi}^{\top}\mathbf{b}^{t}.
The conclusion of Theorem 2.4
for \{(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t},\mathbf{g}^{t},\mathbf{b}^{t})\}_{t\geq 0} implies the same convergence for
\{(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{t},\tilde{\mathbf{g}}^{t},\tilde{\mathbf{b}}^{t})\}_{t\geq 0} , since this has the
same empirical distribution of sample paths.
Multiplying the above dynamics by \boldsymbol{\Pi}^{\top} and noting that
\boldsymbol{\Pi}^{\top}f(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{t})=f(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{t}) since f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} is applied
entrywise, the dynamics of \{(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{t},\tilde{\mathbf{g}}^{t},\tilde{\mathbf{b}}^{t})\}_{t\geq 0} are given by
(6.1)
\mathrm{d}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{t}=[f(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{t})+\mathbf{S}\tilde{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{S}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{t}]\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\mathrm{d}\tilde{\mathbf{b}}^{t},\qquad\tilde{\mathbf{g}}^{t}=\mathbf{S}\tilde{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{S}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{t}-\int_{0}^{t}r_{g}(t-s)\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{s}\mathrm{d}s,
coinciding with the dynamics (2.1) driven by \mathbf{S}\tilde{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{S} .
This shows Corollary 2.10(d) for the dynamics.
Since the Gibbs measures \mu_{\mathrm{Gibbs}} and \mu_{\text{Ising}} defined by
\mathbf{W} are also identical to those defined by \mathbf{S}\tilde{\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{S} ,
Corollary 2.10(d) holds also for the Gibbs measures.
If f(\cdot) is odd and \theta^{0} is sign-invariant in law, then
